items.title: Sangster Directs Hammer Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
In the early ’70s, UK-based Hammer Films was winding down after defining a creative and colorful era of horror with lavishly produced films featuring lovely ladies, lethal living dead, and copious amounts of red, red blood. But even though their greatest years were behind them, the company that made Christopher Lee and Peter Cushing genre icons still had a few devilish delights to offer audiences before they reached the end of that dirt road in their runaway carriage (either 1976 for their last horror film, To the Devil a Daughter, or 1979, when they released their actual last film, Hitchcock remake The Lady Vanishes). One of the men most responsible for writing many of the movies that shaped Hammer’s style, Jimmy Sangster, even got a chance to direct during that final decade of Hammer’s classic output, and although the three films he helmed (two of which he also co-wrote, while the other — Lust for a Vampire — was scripted by Danger: Diabolik and ’s Tudor Gates) are not generally regarded as among the best the studio produced, they each have charms all their own and deserve reappraisal.

Now Severin Films is giving us that opportunity with their first-ever release of Hammer titles — Sangster Directs Hammer is an impressive set that brings The Horror of Frankenstein (1970), Lust for a Vampire (1971), and Fear in the Night (1972) to the US in 4K UHD for the first time, all wrapped up in a gorgeously gory green box. As usual for Severin, these movies have never looked this vibrant. Hammer was always well known for its lurid palette and stunning visuals, but now they practically leap off the screen. Fortunately, Severin also knows that preserving the true film experience is important, so grain is not absent but a wonderful texture layer along with everything else. One minor tweak: The box would perhaps be better named Sangster Directs Hammer’s Ralph Bates, because that actor — who forged a productive creative partnership and lasting friendship with the director — appears in all three films, and the story of their collaboration is the spine running through the patchwork body of material presented here. As for the extraordinary extras curated and collected to accompany the films — including a 312-page book! — there couldn’t be a better sign of the love and respect that everyone involved has for these movies and the creative team that made them.

Sangster was an endearingly self-deprecating man who, in his autobiography Do You Want It Good or Tuesday, titled the chapter on these three films “They Would Have Been Better Directed by Terry Fisher” (referring to the legendary Hammer director who helmed multiple entries in their Frankenstein and Dracula series starting with the first installments in 1957 and 1958 respectively). We’ll never know if that would actually be true, but that doesn’t mean these movies are the failures Sangster and others believed. Most folks apparently shuffle these to the bottom of their lists pretty quickly; the fact that Severin was only able to produce this box because no one else wanted to license these titles is baffling to me, but a boon for us and them. And no, I’m not saying these are classics on par with the films that launched Hammer’s legend, but they’re solid productions with something to offer both Hammer aficionados and casual fans alike. Let’s take a closer look…

The Horror of Frankenstein (1970)

Of the many tactics Hammer employed to distinguish their cinematic monsters from the unforgettable 1930s-1940s Universal incarnations that preceded them, one of the cleverest and most inventive was to follow the creator rather than the creature when making their series of Frankenstein films. And I know it’s blasphemy to many Hammer fans (appropriately enough) but this comedic remake of Hammer’s first Frankenstein foray (1957’s The Curse of Frankenstein) and the next-to-last installment in the seven-film Hammer Frankenstein series — with Ralph Bates replacing Peter Cushing as Victor — is my favorite of that entire run. While Cushing plays an utter sociopath or a more genial amoral Victor well (there are two timelines in the series; it’s complicated), Bates perfectly blends the sociopathy with a glib devil-may-care charm that makes him delightfully magnetic. Hammer was trying to make Bates a thing, positioning him as Frankenstein, Dracula (plans for that went awry when Christopher Lee came back instead, relegating Bates to a smaller role in 1970's Taste the Blood of Dracula), and Dr. Jekyll (in 1971's Dr. Jekyll and Sister Hyde). While things didn’t quite pan out, what we have is wonderful for all of us who value what Bates brought to the slab.

The film is ahead of its time with its black humor and gleeful lewdness; it feels like partial inspiration for the Re-Animator movies, and its lascivious tone resembles what people often thought Hammer movies were like but . The sexual dynamics are interesting too, as Victor’s friend, Stephan (Stephen Turner), eagerly becomes his cook and wants very much to be part of Victor’s life, while the movie makes clear that a man working in the kitchen seems unusual to everyone. They also joke about Victor not being interested in men...or is he? He shows zero interest in Elizabeth (Hammer regular Veronica Carlson) even when she virtually proposes to him, and although he carries on with housekeeper Alys (the superb Kate O’Mara), that could be more about continuing a power dynamic established by his father rather than personal desire.

Bates perfectly blends the sociopathy with a glib devil-may-care charm that makes him delightfully magnetic.

In a cute twist on Frankenstein tropes, Victor keeps track of creature assembly via a build-by-numbers approach. His friend Wilhelm (Graham James) even hits the nail on the flattop by speaking a version of the clichéd line: “You’re tampering with forces we don’t fully understand!” As for the creature itself, David Prowse (yes, Darth Vader) is a mute, hairless Karloffian monster with a creepy smugness that suggests he’s far smarter than his predecessors. He’s no tragic figure either; this creature’s a violent . As the bodies mount up, Victor is willing to let those around him suffer if it means protecting his creation; the apple didn’t reanimate far from the tree.

The only disappointment is an abrupt ending that leaves you wanting Bates-led sequels, but it wasn’t to be; when Hammer tried one more time to draw on Shelley’s creation for movie material, they brought Cushing back. But we have this one, and it’s a twisted delight.

Lust for a Vampire (1971)

After mining Stoker for over a decade, Hammer turned to Sheridan Le Fanu’s sapphic classic novel, Carmilla, for inspiration, resulting in a trio of films focusing on a female vampire first played by Ingrid Pitt in 1970’s lush and top-heavy saucy romp, The Vampire Lovers. Lust for a Vampire is the second installment in what would later be labeled “The Karnstein Trilogy,” and it featured several missteps, not least replacing Pitt as Mircalla/Carmilla with Yutte Stensgaard. Yutte’s no Ingrid, but she’s also not as bad as some think. She does a damn good job of conveying that underlying air of menace and calculation that makes Carmilla a great villain; she just isn’t quite as good or as stylish as Pitt was.

Also carrying over from the first Karnstein film is the character of the “Man in Black,” a sort of/not really Dracula played this time by Mike Raven (there are odd cutaway insert shots of Christopher Lee’s eyes to muddy the waters). Unlike the mute grinning fool from the first movie played by John Forbes-Robertson, this one — now more specifically Count Karnstein — speaks with the dubbed voice of Valentine Dyall, but his role is still murky. He’s partnered with the Countess (Barbara Jefford), but more intriguing than the Man in Black’s part in this tale is the behind-the-scenes goss on Raven himself; for that, go to the extras and the book.

Ralph Bates (who replaced Cushing in this particular role) famously threw this movie under the bus, but damn if he doesn’t give his performance as the creepy teacher at a girls' school 110%; he’s one of the highlights of the movie. Our hero, new teacher Richard LeStrange (Michael Johnson), is based on Carmilla author Le Fanu, and his romance with Carmilla provides Hammer with a chance to immediately dial down the lesbian themes from the first film by focusing Carmilla’s attention primarily on the dashing scholar. Fans also remember (and correctly malign) this one for the insufferable song “Strange Love” that plays not once but (the second time with a color-washed montage of previous scenes!) to provide padding as the story isn’t substantial enough for feature length.

There are nice stylistic touches like mesmerized girls approaching the camera in close-up so that the viewer shares Carmilla’s POV.

The resurrection sequence is pretty spectacular, although you don’t see as much of Yutte as you do in the associated publicity stills (Severin helpfully puts one of those on the cover of the book). There are also nice stylistic touches like mesmerized girls approaching the camera in close-up so that the viewer shares Carmilla’s POV, and the strange mythology of the Karnstein vampires adding the odd twist that simply turning a cross upside down “deactivates” its effects. There are other tropes galore, like an old-school torch-bearing crowd and characters professing deep and abiding love for one another after knowing each other for about an hour. OK, so it’s not Hammer’s finest moment, or even the best of the Karnstein films, but it has its charms as all of them do, and it’s good to have it as part of this set.

Hammer did more than just produce gothic period-set horrors, and that included a series of psychological thrillers often featuring a character fighting for their sanity and their very life. Sangster wrote several of these “Mini-Hitchcocks”; although they were so named because of the debt they owed to the Master of Suspense, the real inspiration for Sangster was Henri-Georges Clouzot’s (1955). In fact, he drew on that source more than once, and when it came time not just to write but direct one himself, he reworked his script from an earlier production — 1961’s Scream of Fear — that leaned heavily on its Diabolique origins. Fear in the Night was the result, and despite its present-day setting, it still manages to be pretty gothic with an unsettling psychosexual edge.

Also betraying a possible influence from Italian giallos, especially with the stalker’s black gloved hands, and sharing elements with many of the thrillers and slashers that came before and after it, Fear takes us to a secluded country school where a mentally fragile young newlywed (Judy Geeson of To Sir, with Love) moves with her husband teacher (Ralph Bates of course) into a cottage on the grounds. The headmaster (Peter Cushing) and his wife (Joan Collins) are strangely fascinated with Geeson, and soon a battle of wills begins, with twists that are best left for you to discover.

Speaking of Cushing, he’s barely in it, but he predictably makes the most of it with an understated performance that exudes a creepy yet strangely gentle quality; you wouldn’t want to be in the same room with this guy, especially if you’re a woman, but there’s something about him that suggests he’s not the person you should be worried about. One scene of him standing before a noose while trying to unknot Geeson’s scarf brings to mind a bit in 1932’s White Zombie, while the visual symbolism concerning the violation of Geeson’s innocence becomes even more overt when Joan Collins arrives at the halfway point to kill a cute little bunny right in front of her.

Geeson in particular delivers an emotionally raw performance that can be uncomfortably real and difficult to watch.

It has a quiet, deliberate atmosphere, and everyone is excellent; Geeson in particular delivers an emotionally raw performance that can be uncomfortably real and difficult to watch. But I have to say that I don’t enjoy movies predicated on gaslighting the protagonist and dragging us along for the frustrating ride before things resolve; some may call it suspense, but as someone prone to anxiety, I call it cinematic torture.

I have quibbles with the final act, but no spoilers. Right from the precision-crafted opening sequence, you’ll see what you’re in for, perhaps more than you realize. And in addition to the moment that shockingly punctuates the end of that montage, the movie has one other arresting image that will stick with you involving Peter Cushing and his circular glasses; you’ll know when you see it.

As befits a box set that’s so clearly a labor-of-love tribute to this era of Hammer history, the extras are exhaustive and entertaining. The one criticism I have is that there are captions on any of the extras, making them inaccessible for some fans. There’s no reason not to provide them, but Severin? Don’t ever generate them automatically; hire someone to write and edit them properly.

Since there are many extras included on every film disc as well as an extra disc with Fear, let’s examine the 19 hours of material (!) by category:

There are two commentary tracks for each film. The first features Sangster from years back (he died in 2011), moderated by Hammer historian Marcus Hearn with actress Suzanna Leigh joining on Lust. Leigh brings out more energy in Sangster, although he’s informative and enjoyable in all of them. The second tracks feature various authors and experts pontificating about the production history and cultural impact of each film.

Besides the many newly produced interviews with cast and crew across all three films, there are archival segments featuring Cushing and Sangster. Many of them are relatively short, but they cover a wide range of perspectives, with some folks like production runner Philip Campbell talking about all three movies. Perhaps the most consistent mood is “wistful.” Kirsten Lindholm of Lust is a delightfully quirky highlight, and if (like me) you’re a Dracula A.D. 1972 fan, Christopher Neame’s interview serves as an overview of his entire career, including that film, his work in Lust, and the day Cushing told him the work was helping him to deal with his grief over his wife’s death.

That dedicated extras disc accompanying Fear includes three documentaries: one on Sangster (he’s credited with shaping the modern conception of Dracula and Frankenstein as well as demonstrating great versatility in multiple genres), one on Ralph Bates (it’s a heartfelt tribute from his wife, son, and colleagues), and one on Joan Collins (authors Kier-La Janisse and Amanda Reyes look at how the horror work Collins disowned led to her iconic turn in Dynasty).

Perhaps the most laudable aspect of this set is that with so much subject matter that should center a woman’s experience and perspective, they do just that, featuring an array of scholars and historians like Dr. Colin Azariah-Kribbs and Dr. Emma Liggins on the work of Mary Shelley; writer/producer Gillian Wallace Horvat and narrator Megan Stern on the history of Frankenstein adaptations; Carmen Maria Machado (she edited an edition of Carmilla) and Annie Rose Malamet on the cultural phenomenon of sapphic vampire tales; and two essays by Dr. Alexandra Heller-Nicholas on school-based stories and gaslighting as a thematic element of Fear.

If all this isn’t enough, there’s a 312-page full-color glossy volume titled Horror! Lust! Fear! Sangster — an overwhelming compilation of interviews and essays, rare photos, and even comic adaptations. The book offers a of information not touched on in the other extras, but in order to fit everything in the box, the book (otherwise designed beautifully by Stephen Thrower) is rather small and just a little awkward to read. It’s still a lovely, and one might argue indispensable, part of this once-in-a-lifetime set.

There’s plenty of additional bits and bobs too, like trailers and promos, alternate “clothed” takes, and TV opening credits. It’s a treasure trove, and if the material becomes repetitive, it’s still worth it to include everything Severin could collect.

items.title: The Sinking City 2 Review
items.author: Michael Higham
items.content:
It was impossible for me to play The Sinking City 2 for more than 15 minutes without coming to the obvious realization that this is Resident Evil in a fedora. That might sound dismissive, but I really enjoy the recent Resident Evil games, so comparing Frogwares' Lovecraftian survival horror sequel to some of the best of them – which feels especially similar to 2019's Resident Evil 2 remake – is much more of a compliment than a put-down. What sets it apart begins with its unique, rich, 1920s New England setting flush with loving detail that instills a strong sense of personality over the top of the mechanics it so clearly imitates.

You play as Calvin Rafferty, a likeable occultist waking up to an apocalyptic flood set to wipe out the entire city of Arkham, Massachusetts in 1929. He's definitely a little bit of a pulp fiction stock character: hard-chinned, two-fisted, and foolishly brave. But there are layers to him that rise to the surface here and there. Similar to the Resident Evil comparison, likening him to the classic heroes of the genre is not really an insult.

The intriguing cosmic horror plot revolves around a half-remembered expedition to Lovecraft's surreal Dreamlands that left Calvin's partner and paramour, Faye, in a comatose state. This creates immediate emotional stakes and momentum from the very start, which carried me through the somewhat slow first half of the first chapter. I don't want to spoil too many surprises, but The Sinking City 2 manages to be a bit of a who's who of the Cthulhu mythos. Some of its eldritch guest characters are much more hinted at than portrayed in all their terrible glory, but Arkham-heads will find lots of little nods to make them cackle with otherworldly glee.

The unfolding story includes some effective emotional beats and a few neat twists that kept me guessing about some characters' motivations, but overall remains pretty easy to follow given the high concept subject matter. This isn't the kind of tale where you're going to have to look up a YouTube video to explain the ending afterwards, and I appreciated that. But it also doesn't back down from engaging with some of the heavier metaphysical aspects of Lovecraft, effectively selling the idea that you're up against beings beyond human comprehension. And it also does a decent job of sidestepping some of the ones that haven't aged particularly well.

The centerpiece is the town of Arkham itself, which presents a gorgeously damp and decrepit backdrop for exploration and combat. Excellent texture work and sound design come together to create an atmosphere that made my skin feel clammy even in the dry heat of a Colorado summer. The density of little details crammed into every corner of every area is truly inspiring. Every dilapidated hotel room or terrifying hospital ward feels both lived-in and ravaged by the ongoing disaster. The cutscenes and facial animations aren't always to the same level of quality, but pretty strong voice acting across the board helps carry them past their production limitations.

Each chapter takes you to a new locale in Arkham, and each feels distinct in both vibes and layout. You start out in the flooded city streets, navigating by boat to various ruins and culminating in a creepy, haunted hotel. Chapter 2, which I found to be the scariest, is set in an abandoned hospital that features its own version of the unkillable stalker in the spirit of Mr. X and Nemesis. And Chapter 3 takes you to the Arkham Fish Market, which goes about exactly how you'd expect if you're familiar with the works of Lovecraft. That is to say, very poorly for our boy Calvin in some unpleasantly fish-themed ways. This progression keeps things fresh while maintaining a cohesive aesthetic.

[The Sinking City 2] doesn't back down from engaging with some of the heavier metaphysical aspects of Lovecraft.

As I mentioned earlier, when it comes to the mechanics, this is an unapologetic tribute to modern, over-the-shoulder Resident Evil. Calvin can amass a small arsenal of guns, but there are never enough bullets to kill everything, leading to tense scrounging through drawers for every last round. Melee is an option, but not a very effective one. Mixing it up with even your basic zombie-like enemies is almost a guarantee of taking some licks yourself, so close quarters combat became a conscious choice to expend my healing items instead of my ammo. Calvin is not as vulnerable as Resident Evil Requiem's Grace, but he's certainly not a Leon S. Kennedy-level action hero, maintaining a good balance between competent and fragile.

The controls are very similar. The inventory system is very similar. The basic enemies are very similar. There are puzzles where you have to find three things to stick into a door to make it open. You can pick up herbs and craft them into healing items. It even has a system of achievements that unlock powerful perks in New Game+ almost identical to the newer Resident Evil games. Again, I'm not complaining. It's not like I'm sick of the modern Resident Evil formula if it's executed well, and Frogwares did a commendable job, so this feels like a free extra course while we wait for Capcom's next big dish.

One exception to the scarce ammo rule is that certain boss fights or big arena battles have infinitely respawning loot pick-ups (explained by an in-game note that lampshades their bizarre physical properties) to keep you from getting softlocked if your magazines run dry. This felt like a little bit of a cop-out that undermines its difficulty – these segments were some of my least favorite anyway, but hey, you know what else is very Resident Evil? Having boss fights that aren't very good.

All that said, The Sinking City 2 isn't just about Frogwares being a Capcom cover band. One way it sets itself apart is with a perk system that lets you unlock and equip powerful runes that do things like increase your damage when your flashlight is off, rewarding you for being able to hit enemies you can't even see. They come in four tiers of increasing power, and you can't really unlock the strongest ones on a single playthrough, creating a compelling incentive to charge headlong into horror all over again.

The Sinking City 2 isn't just about Frogwares being a Capcom cover band.

The other novel bit is the ability to find written clues around every area that can be organized and connected with red strands like your very own wacky conspiracy board. Each belongs to a group, and correctly connecting each group gives you some progression points. Some give hints on plot-critical objectives, while others point to potent, optional treasures. The rewards feel worthwhile, though some require a little bit of backtracking, even if the puzzles themselves aren't exactly brain-busters.

You can set the difficulty of these puzzles independently of the combat difficulty, which is neat, but all the harder option really does is remove highlighted text and icons that tell you which clues belong together. I didn't find it particularly difficult to figure out which hints were related and put together the information in them myself even without those hints, so it felt like increasing the difficulty from Very Easy to Easy. There is one pretty tough optional puzzle that required me to really use my brain later on, but I did end up yearning for more difficult detective work.

Also, there is no sanity mechanic, which seems a little odd for a Cthulhu game. There are some strange moments of reality-bending theatrics, but I was never made to doubt if the things my character was experiencing were even real. And that's a bit of a letdown.

items.title: Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Review/Recap... Yeah, This Is the One With the Puppets...
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Alright then, the puppet episode is finally here.

We’ve known this one was coming ever since it was first teased, what, two San Diego Comic-Cons ago? The latest in high-concept Strange New Worlds episodes – this directly follows the zany from two weeks ago, and last week’s – “Level Five Transporter Accident” certainly does feel like an accident… but not one that can be fixed with mere needle and thread the way the puppets here can. Indeed, its only saving grace is the performance from the always reliable Ethan Peck as Spock, who manages to walk the line between comedic Vulcan acting and conflicted Vulcan acting just fine.

When Scotty (Martin Quinn) tries to push his transporter tech to its limits – a nice nod to the Kelvinverse movies, where that Scotty (Simon Pegg) makes some big leaps with the old beam ‘em up technology – things go awry. Since he’s using his childhood puppet “Little Ricky” as a test subject, when the system gets screwy, somehow everyone onboard winds up beaming into puppet versions of themselves. And mostly annoying puppets at that.

I’ve complained about this before, but one of my issues with these Strange New Worlds concept episodes is that a lot of said concepts have been done before, if not, on other shows. The musical episode “Subspace Rhapsody” was great and all, but you know, not exactly an original idea. A film noir episode? LARPing with the crew? . And now we get a puppet episode, the idea of which I can recall seeing at least as far back as on Angel 22 years ago, when .

And look, there’s nothing wrong with recycling old premises, but if you’re gonna do it, you gotta bring something new to the table. It’s got to work, and “Level Five Transporter Accident” mostly doesn’t. For starters, by its very nature, the notion of having most of your cast turn into puppets is going to bring a heightened sense of absurdity to things; the characters even harness this idea in their quest to defeat the nasty if forgettable Orion villains of the week. But there’s something about suddenly hearing voices like Anson Mount’s and Christina Chong’s coming from the puppets that I found too jarring. It’s all supposed to be fun and funny, but it’s mostly not, and once again Mount’s take on Pike veers into “this is not a Starfleet captain” territory, wool stuffing notwithstanding.

So what does work here? I think I laughed out loud twice, and both times it was involving the guy at the navigation console next to Ortegas (Melissa Navia) who would usually have been a Red Shirt but instead here is just a funny puppet. His wordless panic about the situation is great. And the puppet designs themselves (created by the Jim Henson Company) are really nice – like, they should sell them on the Paramount+ store because people would want to collect them all. Oh, and the shots near the end of the episode, with the crew all floating around in space in puppet form, are just quite sweet (and really, is how the hour should’ve ended, instead of turning it into an “It was all a dream” scenario for some reason).

And then there’s the Spock stuff, which saves the episode from disaster. Peck’s comedic timing is notable, as he has to run around doing everyone’s jobs for them to keep the ship running, since their little puppet fingers are mostly useless. The actor really has mastered Spock – he and Mount have been playing these characters since 2019 at this point, when they debuted on Star Trek: Discovery – and he always rolls with the various curveballs the writers have thrown at him. Too Vulcan, too human, too Vulcan/human, he’s done it all, and here he’s dealing with not just getting dumped by another crewmate (though La’an was pretty graceful in the dumping, unlike Chapel previously), but also in having to go to his ex, T’Pring (Gia Sandhu), for help in the aftermath of the incident onboard the Griffin earlier this season. I’m glad to see they didn’t just drop that thread, and continuing to explore its impact on both Spock and La’an is welcome.

Questions and Notes from the Q Continuum:

  • About it all being a dream… was it? Little Ricky sure seemed malevolent in that last shot… or maybe Spock just needs more logic training.
  • But what is this “studying logic” thing anyway? Hasn’t Spock been doing that since he was in diapers?
  • Could Little Ricky be a reference to the onscreen son of Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz from I Love Lucy? The puppet even has a red crop of hair on its head. Don’t forget, the pair’s production company Desilu was behind the original Star Trek series.
  • Pelia (Carol Kane) pointing out that they shouldn’t be able to hear each other in space and how it doesn’t even make sense is an appreciated jab at the grumps in the audience like me.

items.title: Insidious: Out of the Further Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
With 2023’s having served as an effective swan song to Blumhouse’s first original horror franchise, Out of the Further arrives with one chance to prove that the light over the series’ spectral crimson door deserves to be kept on after all. With a grab bag of different-flavored scares that broadly work, some grounded performances, and a willingness to double down on the abject weirdness of the world-building that’s been established up to this point, against the odds for a sixth film in any franchise, Insidious: Out of the Further maintains a steady stride and winds up being a hell of a good time.

As the title suggests, Insidious: Out of the Further sets itself apart from the films which precede it by opening the proverbial (and literal) door from the spirit realm into the material plane in a much more significant way than ever before. It’s true that we’ve seen the spirits of the Further out in the real world, but generally, these apparitions are fairly closely shackled to the bodies of those they’re trying to possess, and incapable of too much more than going “boo”... or I guess luring them into the street, like in the case of Insidious: Chapter 3’s Quinn. The particulars of how (and to what degree) the Further gets Out are fun to discover along the way, but suffice to say that protagonist Gemma (Amelia Eve) had a rough childhood that has left her unable to move on in life in a way that’s made her a valuable target for the spirits of The Further. The opening scene paints a truly sad picture of Gemma’s childhood, as she tiptoes around her house to avoid drawing the attention of her mother, who’s clearly in the throes of a crisis that’s been going on for some time. It sets up a dynamic that carries into Gemma’s adulthood, as she navigates fears of transferring that experience onto her daughter Maya (Island Austin).

Amelia Eve does fine work shouldering Gemma’s growing instability as she tries to keep her feet on the ground, although writer/director Jacob Chase’s script hammers a bit too hard on the “passing familial trauma along” element of the story, routinely saying out loud what the imagery and performance already clearly communicate. It feels especially repetitive in the context of Insidious: The Red Door’s plot, which focused on the reconciliation of Patrick Wilson and Ty Simpkins’ Josh and Dalton Lambert after their shared experiences in the first two chapters of the series. Though it’s not always subtle, Chase does at least prioritize threading that family drama through Out of the Further in a way that keeps the central wound Gemma is nursing in focus, so that her desperation remains palpable throughout. We see the past repeating itself through Maya’s eyes as Gemma unravels, and Island Austin strikes a good balance between vulnerability and tenacity through her mom’s ups and downs.

The director knows the Insidious films well, capably easing into the visual language of the series.

Given all the new facets of how the Further is able to interact with the material plane in this film, Chase is able to stage a number of creative and fresh scenarios that delight in blurring the line between what’s happening in reality and what’s bleeding over from the spirit realm. Chase knows the Insidious films well, capably easing into the visual language of the series while also having a keen sense of how the rhythms of encounters with the denizens of the Further are expected to play out. At worst, the scares work about as well as they have in any other Insidious film (jump scares and audio stings abound), but Chase brings no shortage of new ideas to the table.

Two strong back-to-back sequences around the film’s midpoint represent Out of the Further at its best. The first is a claustrophobic’s nightmare set in Maya’s pillow fort. As Gemma pokes her head in, the pillow fort becomes a rat’s maze in which she’s very much not alone. Chase is able to draw the tension out of every wrong turn through the labyrinth very effectively, including some fun misdirects and camera coverage that make the most out of the tight space. By the time Gemma finally emerges, the viewer should feel just as relieved as the character.

But it’s the following sequence, which follows Gemma to her job as a dental hygienist, that is Out of the Further’s crown jewel. For a franchise that has always forefronted spectral spookies and haunted house-style bumps in the night, Insidious: Out of the Further features one of the more disgusting and visceral dental horror scenes I can recall ever having seen, as Gemma goes to work on a guy who seems like he may be better off getting his teeth checked by the Lipstick Face Demon from the first movie. Chase draws this sequence out to a fever pitch, layering one sickening and all-too-realistic gag over another. All that really dampens this excellent sequence is how it tails off into the Further, where evil-looking dentists and patients seem far more tame than the actual oral horror we just witnessed out in the real world.

The Insidious films have favored vague, elemental demons as antagonists up to this point, really as more of a visual focal point for the sleepless evil contained in the Further, but Out of the Further makes the smart choice to try out a more well-drawn villain this time out, played by A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms’ Sam Spruell. Cyrus Lam is no hoofed, red-faced Beelzebub, but a cunning spirit with an interesting backstory which connects to how much more interaction the Further and the real world have this time out. Cyrus and his motives aren’t all that deep, but he’s different enough from previous antagonists to make his moves feel a lot more unpredictable.

Out of the Further’s strength at delivering on that namesake concept does belie a weakness of the film’s, which is that most of the material set in the Further itself is rather forgettable. The space tends to be a VFX-darkened/color-graded void in the shape of whatever house or neighborhood that particular movie is set in, where the spirits have greater power. On that front, we’re pretty firmly in “been there, done that” territory. Die-hards will no doubt delight in the myriad familiar faces among the vaudevillian freakshow of ghouls that call the Further home, but with the stakes of the film being so focused on preventing the Further from getting out, much of the anxiety surrounding the idea of the characters being trapped within feels too distant for those moments to feel all that weighty.

The movie’s supporting cast are uniformly strong at keeping Insidious: Out of the Further from astral projecting itself into incoherence. Is there anything new for Lin Shaye’s Elise Rainier to do here other than amend exposition from previous movies to explain new abilities, raise a lantern in the darkness of the Further, and scream at ghosts in the face after dying five movies ago? Nope. Is her presence and personality as welcome and warm a blanket as ever? You betcha. As Gemma’s boyfriend Nick, Brandon Perea and his excellent comedic timing are particularly well-deployed as a very open-minded skeptic. Legends of Tomorrow’s Maisie Richardson-Sellers stops by as tattoo artist/medium Clare to pick up the torch from Elise in the material plane, and while she’s mostly there as a conduit for Elise, it’s easy to see her steely comfort with the abnormal becoming a more prominent part of the series going forward. And a special shoutout to the pair of actors who play Gemma’s neighbors, the O’Sullivans. They (with some canny direction on Chase’s part) absolutely nail a self-referential gag during the very intense finale and give me hope that, for every 10 or 12 poe-faced entities that reoccur from previous movies in future installments, we get one appearance from these two just doing their best to be helpful and not to bicker too much while doing so.

items.title: Google Pixel 11 Pro Review
items.author: Bo Moore
items.content:
Google has rolled out its latest line of Pixel phones with the Pixel 11 family. The Pixel 11 Pro sits at the middle, offering the same smaller footprint of the Pixel 11 while getting the extra features and cameras of the Pro models. Unsurprising for 2026, it comes with a price hike over last year’s model, bringing the starting price to $1,099 while coming with less memory, though it does have a higher base storage. Let’s dig into what the new Android flagship has going for it.

Pixel 11 Pro – Design and Features

The Pixel 11 Pro is a fairly standard year-on-year refresh of the , which was itself a pretty tame refresh of the Pixel 9 Pro. Like those models, the Pixel 11 Pro is pleasantly compact and comfortable to hold. Its physical differences from the Pixel 10 Pro are measured on the tenth-of-a-millimeter scale, and at just three grams heavier, you’d be hard-pressed to feel any difference in the hand. Its camera bar is also still a considerable protrusion (adding 4.1mm to the 8.2mm thick phone), but at least it keeps the phone from wobbling when set on a table.

There are some fresh colors. The model sent to me for testing is the Canyon colorway, a bold salmon-like orange-pink with a gorgeous copper-colored aluminum frame. There’s also a pleasant-looking Olive green colorway. The faint, minty Fog color and matte black Obsidian look quite bland, though.

The Pixel 11 Pro sticks with largely the same materials for durability, with Gorilla Glass Victus 2 on both sides and an aluminum frame. It should be pretty sturdy, but I wouldn’t consider it even remotely hard to damage, having damaged plenty of phones quite easily over the years. There’s a new coating on the display to boost scratch resistance, and seeing scratches on the back from my short time testing but none of the front makes me think it might be helping. The Pixel 11 Pro still trods out the same IP68 protection against dust and water ingress, which should be plenty sufficient for most, though still lags behind the IP69 that the now-belly-up OnePlus had been offering on its even cheaper flagship.

Of the phone’s marquee features, the “new” HiLight feature is perhaps the lamest of all. It doubles as a camera flash and replaces the temperature sensor (even though that sensor happily sat alongside the flash in prior models). HiLight is also simply a case of Google digging up the dead and trodding them out in worse fashion. My first Android phone was a Sharp Aquos SH-01D in 2012, and it had a notification indicator light that I could set up to display different colors depending on the app giving me a notification. In 2012, the customization was already more granular than what Google is offering on its premium handset in 2026.

HiLight only lets you see a light while you’re talking to Gemini or when favorited contacts call you through the default phone app – tough luck if you use WhatsApp, Signal, or anything else as your default communication method, or if want HiLight to glow for texts from favorited contacts, too. With only five colors (if you count white as a color) to choose from to help identify specific contacts, you’ll run into a wall as soon as you have a lot of favorited contacts, and the purpose of HiLight could quickly be undermined.

The Nothing Phone has a similar feature with its customizable dot matrix animations that I find far more compelling. Never mind that with OLED displays, a similar feature could be made to run in Do Not Disturb mode such that small calling cards for favorite contacts or important apps could appear unobtrusively to have the same effect without needing a special piece of added hardware that will probably just get dumped two generations down the line anyway.

The display on the Pixel 11 Pro is hardly anything new, but that’s not a bad thing. It’s still a gorgeous 6.3-inch OLED capable of variable refresh rates from 1 to 120Hz and a new peak brightness up to 3,600 nits. That’s a minor improvement on last year’s model and not likely to make a meaningful difference, especially as you won’t be seeing those over-3000-nit brightness levels in day-to-day use unless you love to have the screen facing the sun.

The speakers aren’t a great match for the display. While the bottom speaker puts out a good deal of volume, the earpiece speaker is so much weaker that the stereo sound hardly feels like stereo. There’s enough volume to listen to a podcast or video while poking around a small room, but that’s about the extent of it.

The phone still offers a fingerprint sensor baked into the display as well as facial recognition. I’ve found both quick and reliable for unlocking the phone.

The Pixel 11 Pro also continues to operate using eSIM exclusively. It’s a minor bugbear, as I find eSIM a convenient , but it becomes limiting to only have eSIM.

The phone’s connectivity is solid with the typical 5G alongside Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.0, keeping up with the times. It also supports satellite connections when you’re remote and don’t have a terrestrial signal. The USB-C port handles charging, 10Gbps data, and can link out to displays to run a desktop mode. Oddly, the phone doesn’t automatically bring up a trackpad to navigate the desktop environment, leaving me to find a Bluetooth mouse and keyboard to get up and running.

The Pixel 11 Pro comes running Android 17 and will get 7 years of software and security updates. This has been Google’s promise for a few generations now, and it’s paired with assurances that the phones will get better over time thanks to special feature updates. I’ve known too many people who’ve had the power buttons fall off their Pixel phones within a couple years of ownership to think much of this promise anymore, never mind that the performance of the Pixel phones tends to lag behind flagship rivals and will be sorely wanting as time passes and the demands of modern software increase.

One of the new features of the Pixel 11 line is Google Keyboard's Rambler feature, a beefed-up version of speech-to-text that is designed to let you just kind of talk at it, tidying up the speech and letting you make revisions on the fly. One downside is that it doesn't show live output, so you have to wait until it's done processing to see what it's done, which can make checking it more of a chore. In testing it proved fairly reliable even as I stumbled over some of my speech. Unfortunately, this feature uses online processing for full functionality, which becomes a double shame when considering that Google could likely have made it an Android-wide feature instead of a Pixel 11 series exclusive.

Another feature Google has implemented is its Camera Looks feature. These let you snap photos with several different preset looks that handle photo processing differently, and you can make fine-tuned adjustments to each of the looks. Having an option like this certainly seems like a fine addition, though at a certain point simply shooting RAW and having the option to make whatever adjustments you want afterward might be the most sensible thing. And for casual photographers, this feature will probably feel like nothing more than simple filters.

The final big feature is Magic Capture, which basically lets you record a video carelessly and then will automatically scan through it and pull out photos (the idea being that you can then pay more attention to the real world and less to the phone). It appeared to do what it promised and served as a good way of grabbing a selfie with the rear sensor, too.

Pixel 11 Pro – Gaming and Performance

Google isn’t out here making a name for itself where raw performance is concerned. Its Tensor chips are not in that game, and the Tensor G6 is no exception. For raw speed and gaming performance, it’s much better to turn to something like the OnePlus 15 or RedMagic 11 Pro. The Pixel 11 Pro has plenty of muscle for day-to-day operation and doesn’t feel slow in general use. Gaming is another matter.

The Pixel 11 Pro got pretty toasty compiling shaders for Neverness to Everness over the course of about 10 minutes. From there, running the game at Balanced settings, it managed generally smooth visuals but had frequent hitches, especially in combat when using special moves or switching characters. With the game's Cinematic settings, hitches were even more frequent while simply wandering the game world. From a cold start, the game still hitched a bit while playing, and after 10 minutes, the phone had gotten a bit hot to hold and was hitching even more in gameplay.

Frankly, I was surprised it ran the game at Cinematic settings at all. The phone is still using a PowerVR GPU, which in last year’s model was a huge step backward for the phone’s performance. This go-around, it’s still certainly not a great gaming phone, but it’s passable.

Google finally bumped up the base storage of the phone to 256GB, though where all of the Pixel 10 Pro models had 16GB of memory, the Pixel 11 Pro starts out with just 12GB. It’s a shortcoming you probably won’t feel in practice, but it may start to hurt down the line.

The Pixel 11 Pro wields an unimpressive 4850mAh battery, which is a hair smaller than the prior phone’s 4870mAh. It’s still good for all-day use, but two full days may be a stretch depending on how heavy a user you are. The phone tops up at 30W over a wired connection, but can also use Wireless Qi2 charging at 25W, which is a solid step up over the 15W of the Pixel 10 Pro.

Unfortunately, during the initial testing period, my usual suite of benchmarks was unavailable for the phone, so I’ll have to circle back with results. That said, based on the gaming performance and history of Tensor chips, it's a safe bet that results will fall well behind phones running the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5.

The Pixel 11 Pro made a few tweaks to the Pixel 10 Pro’s camera system, opting for slightly larger sensors in a few cases but sticking to the same resolutions and apertures all around. The biggest change was in the telephoto sensor, which got a much bigger sensor that’s a boon for shooting in darker conditions and contending with its already narrow aperture. Here’s what the Pixel 11 Pro packs:

  • 50MP Wide, 1/1.3" sensor, f/1.68, Laser AF, OIS, EIS
  • 48MP ultrawide, 1/2.51" sensor, f/1.7, 123-degree FOV
  • 48MP telephoto, 1/1.95" sensor, f/2.8, 5x optical, OIS, EIS
  • 42MP Selfie, f/2.2, 103-degree FOV

Unsurprisingly, the camera system is an all around potent mix. Up close, the main sensor is happy to capture a ton of detail with natural colors and a satisfying background blur. The tele sensor can step in for close ups as well and makes for some crisp details on subjects that might not usually make it easy to get so close.

For larger subjects, the main and ultra-wide work well together. Colors are consistent between the two, making different shots of the same subject appear like a cohesive set. The wide aperture of the ultra-wide also helps avoid running into too much noise when shooting in darker environments.

The telephoto sensor proves a fairly powerful tool, but not nearly as capable as the marketing claims. Out to 10x, the zoom still looks great and gets in pretty close on far off subjects. After that, it starts to show softness and heavy digital correction, so 30x starts to look flat and beyond that becomes simply artificial. This is made perfectly apparent by zooming into far off signage. Looking at a parking sign far enough to require the max zoom level showed me reimagined visuals and an alien script. The phone saves both the original snap and the enhanced versions at this distance, and though the originals can be quite blurry, they can still have better detail than what the enhancement invents. One car license plate in my shot clearly had a “9” showing in the original photo, but the enhanced version obliterated it.

Selfies look decent, but I found them a little bit softer than I would have expected from a 42MP sensor. The focus seemed soft, and the fine detail of my facial hair was simply blurred together rather than standing out.

Mark Knapp is a contributing freelancer for IGN covering everything electronics and gaming hardware. He has over 10 years of experience in the tech industry with bylines at PCMag, Reviewed, CNET, and more. Find Mark on Twitter

items.title: Mutiny Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
is in theaters on August 21.

It’s rare for an already-compact movie to feel this overwrought. Even at a mere 95 minutes, the nautical Jason Statham starrer Mutiny plays like an unpolished assembly cut, with only a couple of slick or enjoyable action beats. Right from the opening, in which Statham’s bodyguard/former British marine Cole Reed recreates the actor’s fiery vehicular entrance in the Fast & Furious series — albeit with far less style and impact — something feels off, a sensation that carries through practically every moment.

Stationed in Bangkok, Reed’s job for the last five years has been to protect wealthy shipping magnate Tibu Campallo (Ramon Tikaram), as he and his son Kameron (Chaneil Kular) prepare to sell their empire. After a sentimental retirement party, where the benevolent billionaire gifts Reed a Rolex and welcomes him as family, the pair of them are ambushed by gunmen, and Tibu is killed. It takes a number of lethargic dialogue exchanges to get here, after which point you’d expect things to heat up as Reed tracks one of the hitmen to one of Tibu’s freighters leaving that night — but the film is slow and unsteady at every turn.

Reed’s maritime sleuthing is also complicated by the discovery of a shipping container filled with poor, malnourished Southeast Asian refugees, revealing a seedy side hustle operating without the knowledge of his late employer. Every international crewman seems involved, save for nondescript former U.S. naval officer Angie Ellis (Annabelle Wallis), with whom Reed teams up for a scattered, plotless and often directionless series of minor set pieces up and down the ship.

Directed by Jean-François Richet — whose jungle two-hander was pretty competent — Mutiny makes for an awkward watch, where each subsequent scene feels both visually and orally overstated, as though every shot had to be stretched to fill out a prescribed runtime. It’s hard to be sure of what wentwrong, butwere it to come out that the production just didn’t have enough usable footage, this might not be surprising.Take, for instance, one minor but emblematic moment, during which a human trafficker looks up at a guard tower and radios to his comrades, “I’m going up there,” before the camera follows him walking over to the ladder at length and climbing every single rung until he reaches the top. Multiply this by several dozen exchanges, and you’re left waiting for things to happen more often than they actually do.

Statham, an otherwise capable action lead, ends up sleepwalking through his part with nary a quip or powerful pose.

Statham, an otherwise capable action lead, ends up sleepwalking through his part as well, with nary a quip or powerful pose. There’s really nothing to Reed beyond what other people say about him — mostly, exposition delivered by a nearby U.S. navy vessel heroically patrolling the Indian Ocean, though don’t you dare consider the political implications of this in today’s Strait of Hormuz climate. Mutinyain’t that kind of movie, kid, even though it fawns at the foot of power at every turn, showing reverence for both military might and benevolent billionaires who can’t be held accountable for the transgressions of their underlings. And yet, power is something Mutiny lacks aesthetically; few hits land with the kind of gut-crunching sound or snappy visual impact you pay for in this kind of movie.

There’s exactly one action beat early on that’s pretty neat, involving Reed fish-hooking a hoodlum with a giant padlock, but Mutiny spends the rest of its runtime trying and failing to chase that high. As the aforementioned refugees all but disappear from the story, Reed and Ellis traipse up and down identical stairwells, repeatedly evading and engaging in gunfire exchanges while the movie spins its wheels, waiting for the nearby U.S. Navy to arrive and do nothing of note. (Shout out to the one hilariously swole Naval extra who gets to throw exactly zero punches.)

The ship is, theoretically, a character unto itself, but its geography is left so vague and indistinct that shots don’t often fit together. You might find yourself struggling to get a handle on who’s looking or standing where, as the movie cuts for the umpteenth time between identical, gruff characters obscured by shadow. It’s visual soup with no emotional core, and with very few visceral thrills to speak of, which is especially disappointing for a movie filled with this many guns, blades, and other objects that could be used as inventive weaponry. Instead, what we’re left with is a cavalcade of cartoonish bad guys meeting uninspired ends, courtesy of heroes whose only virtue is their former military background, in an environment that should be way more exciting. But alas: from deck to galley, Mutiny is a tremendous bore.

items.title: It Ends Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
will be released in select theaters on Friday, August 21, and enters wide release on August 28.

Remember that Talking Heads song ? It stars with these lyrics: “Well, we know where we're going / But we don't know where we've been” and “We're not little children / And we know what we want / And the future is certain / Give us time to work it out”...

It seems that David Byrne’s words are firmly entrenched in the minds of the team behind It Ends, the latest indie-horror-thriller-that-could, with its tale of a quartet of friends whose car trip turns into an existential joy ride on a never-ending road… a road to nowhere, you might say.

Written and directed (and edited) by newcomer Alexander Ullom, It Ends isn’t as outwardly cheery as the Talking Heads song sounds – it is a horror film after all – but it can be fun all the same. The four leads (Phinehas Yoon as James, Akira Jackson as Day, Noah Toth as Fisher, and Mitchell Cole as Tyler) have a playful banter that carries much of the film, particularly in its opening stretch where they innocently happen into what in another decade might’ve been an episode of ’s The Twilight Zone (or a Sartre play): The turn on the road they’re on never comes, and the group slowly realize they’re trapped on a paved nightmare, where if they dare stop the car for too long, raving maniacs emerge from the surrounding woods and engulf them. Their only choice? Drive, baby, drive. To continue the , these people may be on the road to purgatory, and they sure don't like the sound of that…

One question that always surrounds these tight-quarters movies is whether or not things can stay interesting, despite the film being set in one place. But rather than being limited by it, It Ends instead benefits from its contained setting. The first 15 minutes or so of It Ends are almost entirely shot in close-ups and two-shots of the cast inside the car as they chitter-chatter, happy to be reunited (Tyler hasn’t been on the scene recently but is back now that the other three are graduating from college). Even as the situation grows more concerning in that opening – where the heck is the exit off this road!? – Ullom’s camera remains restrained. The dude knows he’s got 90 minutes of movie to play out in this car and on the road outside it, and no place else, and he squeezes every bit that he can out of those settings. By the time Tyler and James exit to investigate the woods, the car’s flashing hazard lights cast an intermittent red glow where… wait… is that a face out there…? Did something just move behind that tree? And then BAM: The masses of lost souls or ghouls or whatever they are are upon our characters.

Yes, this is a hangout movie – and that’s a huge part of the appeal of the characters, and the film itself.

And that’s the thing about It Ends: The script allows for the characters to ask the same questions we’re asking while watching. These people who are appearing from out of the forest in a mania to overtake the car, begging to be let in, they’ve gotta be dead, right? Ghosts or shades of the living? Which means James and Tyler and Day and Fisher… well, maybe they’re dead too? Are they being punished for something they did in their “real” lives? The question is asked: Who in this car recently did something very, very bad, requiring karmic payback!? Speak up now!

So the questions and theories about what’s going on here are floated, particularly by James, the most driven and analytical of the group. But answers are a different story. Eventually the group settles into a sort of normalcy about their situation, driving and driving and driving. For a time, anyway.

Is the film about the road everyone finds themselves on as they enter adulthood? It Ends starts with the four talking about what’s next for them now that school is in the rearview mirror (if you will). Tyler, who’s already out in the real world as a working man, doesn’t seem particularly happy or satisfied with where life has taken him. James has given it all a lot of thought, and even has a job – and a selfie in his “first communion” work clothes – to prove it, but he doesn’t seem to be very happy either. Day’s living back home, and Fisher… is he just along for the ride? If he even has a plan for what’s next, I missed it.

Amid it all, these Gen Z kids are just hanging – yes, this is a hangout movie – and that’s a huge part of the appeal of the characters, and the film itself. Ullom has said he was partly inspired by Richard Linklater’s Slacker when making It Ends, and it shows, whether the group are debating who would win, a man with a gun or a man with 50 hawks, or contending with the monotony of living together in a car for weeks on end. (It must also be noted that Ullom shot most of this film on a mini Volume LED stage at his alma mater, Florida State, which is damned impressive.)

While never explicit in its intent, the film’s message is hard to shake. These four are trying to find their way in life, and as each comes to react to their situation in different ways, their fates seem to become increasingly sealed. And what is life in the real world if not a constant push to move forward? Do better, make more, get more, get . Those people clawing at you as you pull away? Ignore them, they’re in the way, they’re the competition. Look, it’s a helluva job market out there, and I don’t make the rules – I just follow them. Talk about a horror show.

items.title: Archie Lives: We Review Every Title in Oni Press' Ambitious Archie Comics Reboot
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
It’s been a while since we’ve run a proper comic book review on IGN, but that’s something I’m hoping to change in the months ahead. And what better time to get back in the habit than with Oni Press’ impending reboot of the Archie Comics line. In case you missed the news, Oni is launching a new wave of three comics that reinvent Archie and the Riverdale gang for a new generation. That includes the flagship Archie series as well as Sabrina the Teenage Witch and Archie in Hell.

To ring in this new era of comic book reviews on IGN, we figured the Archie reboot was the perfect starting point. We’ve been able to check out the first issue of all three series, and we’re here to render a verdict and let you know which, if any, are worth giving a look this fall.

We’re hoping to make new comic book reviews on IGN a regular thing again, so definitely head down to the comments and let us know what books you’d like to see us cover.

Writer Ben H. Winters & Artist Fábio Moon

September 2, 2026

This series is the obvious jumping-on point for most of the Archie-curious out there. It’s the classic Archie series reimagined for a new era. Though maybe “reimagined” is overselling things a bit. The new Archie doesn’t fundamentally rework the long-running series so much as it gives it a fresh coat of paint.

Which, for the most part, is just fine. The prospect of Casanova and Daytripper artist Fábio Moon getting the chance to work his magic on Riverdale was always the key selling point for me anyway, and in that regard the reboot doesn’t disappoint. Moon is basically the perfect artist to shoulder the burden of giving Archie Andrews a postmodern visual touch-up. His pages are free-flowing and dynamic and expertly capture the hectic nature of Archie’s overly busy day. Moon’s pencils and inks mesh well with Jason Wordie’s colors, which lend just the right sense of depth and texture to the art.

The main story featured in this issue offers a simple but largely effective gateway into Archie’s crazy little world. Riverdale High is holding a film festival, and Archie soon finds himself stretched thin as he tries to lend a helping hand to all of his friends while also pursuing his own big idea. The premise allows Winters and Moon to quickly cycle through the book’s major supporting cast and establish their various relationships with Archie, and it’s all done in an entertaining way.

The problem is mostly a lack of depth. The story is fun and lighthearted, but that’s about it. It doesn’t really strive to do anything that we wouldn’t have gotten out of a classic Archie Comics adventure. Give this same script to an artist like Dan Parent and it could just as easily be included in an Archie Double Digest in a grocery store checkout lane. Maybe I’m simply a victim of my own expectations, but I was hoping for something a little more experimental, or at least a story with more hints of a serialized narrative. For now, the previous “New Riverdale” reboot still stands as the more compelling example of reinventing Archie for the 21st century.

That said, Winters and Moon’s backup story does suggest the series is capable of a bit more. The backup focuses more on Jughead and digs a little deeper into the psychology of everyone’s favorite hamburger-scarfing best friend. Hopefully it’s a sign of more ambitious storytelling to come.

Sabrina the Teenage Witch #1 Review

Writer Corinna Bechko & Artist Kano

October 7, 2026

If Archie #1 is guilty of playing things a little too safe and traditional, that’s not a problem for this reboot of its sister series. This is easily the most satisfying debut issue of the trio, one that strikes a nice balance between honoring the franchise’s wholesome, all-ages roots and embracing the possibilities of this new future.

Similar to Archie #1, Sabrina the Teenage Witch #1 enters Sabrina Spellman’s life at a particularly chaotic time. She’s just discovered her magical abilities and is trying to balance her newfound responsibilities with her desire to hang out with her friends and enjoy a good Halloween party. Bechko’s script wisely skips over the origin story for the most part, preferring to jump right in with what comes next.

While this issue also serves as an efficient debut for much of the book’s supporting cast, it’s really the dynamic between Sabrina and her cat Salem that steals the show. Salem is a lot of fun as he bickers with his befuddled owner, who’s still growing accustomed to the fact that her cat talks in the first place. In general, Sabrina comes across as very likable here, a girl torn between high school fun and the more urgent, darker world that’s just opened before her.

Kano’s art complements the lighthearted but slightly sinister vibe of the script quite well. Here, too, the series toes that line between honoring the past and establishing its own look and feel. Of particular note is Kano’s facial work, which is wonderfully expressive and helps give each character a welcome burst of personality. This is a book to keep an eye on.

Writer Patrick Horvath & Artist Tyler Crook

November 4, 2026

It was clear from the beginning that anyone who wanted to see a more subversive take on the Archie franchise with this Oni reboot would be best served with Archie in Hell. The series is very much the spiritual successor to Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa and Francesco Francavilla’s Afterlife with Archie, a book that boasted a fantastic premise but was undone by its unpredictable shipping schedule. Hopefully, that won’t be a problem this time around.

Probably the biggest selling point of Archie in Hell, apart from the basic appeal of infusing this universe with supernatural horror, is the fact that it’s written by Beneath the Trees Where Nobody Sees’ Patrick Horvath. A real match made in heaven there, even if the end result isn’t quite as strong out of the gate as I would have liked. Issue #1 is a bit of a slow burn, taking its sweet time to transition from the wholesome charm of a standard Archie adventure to something darker and more grotesque. It’s fun, but there’s not quite enough meat on this particular bone just yet.

The series also finds a fitting artist in horror comics veteran Tyler Crook. Crook and colorist Francesco Segala are adept at blending the old-school Archie aesthetic with a darker, more twisted vibe. Early on, you can almost trick yourself into believing you’re reading another straightforward Archie adventure, only to be reminded otherwise when the black magic and ritualistic sacrifices start unfolding on the page.

This series holds plenty of potential, but a lot is riding on the final page twist and where things go from there. It lacks the fast-paced start and easy “Night of the Living Dead in Riverdale” elevator pitch that Afterlife with Archie benefited from.

items.title: Mortal Shell 2 Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
As a fan of Mortal Shell’s scaled-down approach to the soulslike back in 2020, I was very skeptical of Mortal Shell 2’s enthusiasm for making everything about it way larger, because bigger is not always better. If you felt the same, then allow me to assuage those fears from the top here: besides being bigger, Mortal Shell 2 is also better in almost every way. It still has its rough edges, mostly weird technical things and some balance issues, especially towards the end of this 25-30 hour quest. But its world, the occasionally daunting act of exploring it, and the gritty skirmishes you’ll have while doing so are all greatly improved.

As you did in the first game, you play as a creature whose shiny, sinewy body places it somewhere between a Ridley Scott monster and a corpse, one that can “embody” the forms of dead warriors of some renown and use their abilities to its ultimate ends. Like Illusion of Gaia, but with more thieves and war criminals. When you occupy one of these shells, you take on its identity and abilities. When its taken too much of a beating, you are jettisoned out, back into your original wormy form and given a chance to fight back into it. This was Mortal Shell gimmick back then, and it's still a fun take on the last stand now.

But the amount of possible people to climb in and pilot like a squishier Iron Man has doubled in the sequel, with only a couple of returning faces joining a mostly new roster of colorful scallywags. Standouts include a ferocious cannibal, an armor clad alien, and a time-stopping cultist, all of which sound strange out of context but fit perfectly in the macabre world Mortal Shell 2 creates. The overall story is still a bit of a cryptic mess, but the side stories of these individual characters, learned by increasing your bond with them through the help of a special collectable and a very large woman, really ground it in some human (or otherwise) interactions that are relatable.

The most important improvements to these shells from the previous game isn’t how they look or what nonsense they got up to before they died, but what makes them different outside of that stuff. Previously, the nimble Tiel or the mighty Eredrim were primarily differentiated by how big their life bars were, with all the more nuanced variations tucked away in passive abilities you could spend points to unlock. These passive abilities return in much more abundance and in a better organized progression chart, but each shell now also has distinct active abilities that make them even more impactful in combat and diverse among each other. Now Tiel can disappear for short periods of time, allowing him to stealth past enemies and reemerge with a big backstabbing attack, while Eredrim can wear a single target’s stagger bars down with a big shoulder charge or handle groups with a wide blast. Landing some of these can be finicky, specifically ones that require traveling some distance or auto-locking onto enemies, and I would just inexplicably miss with abilities like Tiel’s Shadow Stab every once in a while.

Switching between shells to try new combat tricks is more rewarding now.

Regardless, this is a gratifying step up from the original, and made actively switching between shells to try new combat tricks a rewarding experience, made all the easier since any points spent to enhance specific shells can be refunded and reallocated for free as many times as you want. I occasionally felt encouraged to do so in barely subtle ways. Have a tough enemy that leans heavily on its fire-based attacks and burn status? Max out Lazlo’s fireproof armorThis can have a hand in making later game bosses feel underpowered, as they don’t scale in the same way you can if you dedicate to the grind, invalidating their strengths while also overpowering them otherwise.

The arsenal of weapons has ballooned in kind in Mortal Shell 2, with eight main melee weapons and eight ranged sidearms to mix and match, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. Some are quick and great for stacking debuffs but don’t do much damage and can’t reliably interrupt enemies. Some have great range but take three-to-five business days to swing. I tended to lean towards weapons with really good running attacks, as I often started encounters with all-in alpha strikes in hopes to put enemies down as quickly as possible to avoid the very real danger most of them present. That was a little frustrating considering that, though largely mechanically sound, any actions involving clicking the sticks like running and auto-targeting were very finicky.

Each weapon has their own strings of light and heavy attacks which can be weaved together to create combos. Finding the right place to swap a light attack for its heavy counterpart in a three-hit combo in order to maximize damage while minimizing the relatively long windups of those attacks is the sort of surprisingly advanced experimentation you can find in what is generally a pretty simple system. Stamina is completely gone in Mortal Shell 2, so you’re free to swing to your heart’s content. Replacing it is Resolve, a meter filled by landing melee attacks and spent to do basically everything else, from shooting ranged weapons to shell abilities. I liked that it meant I had to stay aggressive in melee in order to reap the benefits of all the other cool stuff, and Resolve gain is steady enough without any modifications that I never felt like I was locked out of those options when I needed them.

Mortal Shell 2 varies its defensive offerings in an interesting way, treating a small number of different Seals as shields with differing functionality. One of them allows you to Harden, which turns your body to stone for a brief period in order to repel the next attack, and was the signature feature that helped Mortal Shell stand out among its soulslike peers five years ago. Another introduces a pretty genre-standard block, complete with parry if you have the right timing. A third is a parry-only option, allowing you to execute enemies much faster at the risk of getting punished yourself. I stuck with hardening most of my run - I couldn't give up the satisfaction of being able to harden midswing to eat incoming attacks and finishing my offense on the other side safely - but I did appreciate how this operated as a sort of de facto difficulty setting, with an option to switch it at will should you want to try your luck.

The melee options are reliable but mundane compared to the sidearms.

The melee options are consistent and reliable, but largely mundane in comparison to the sidearms. The big bad ballistzooka from the first game returns in all its glory, but is basic in comparison to some of the new options, like the haunted skeleton of a baby in a cage that radiates evil or a magical lute that can confuse foes. I found that these had more specific uses than melee weapons - the crossbow was for picking off weak enemies on the fringes or stacking debuffs on an enemy while the aforementioned options were for starting fights with a bang.

Like shells, both ranged and melee weapons can be enhanced, and those enhancements can be refunded to reapply on a different set of weapons. This refund isn't completely free, though. You’ll get the materials used to upgrade that weapon back, but the gold that was spent is lost. This does mean you need to be willing to commit more to the weapons you invest in unless you’re willing to grind a lot of gold. It also sort of discouraged me from too much experimentation late-game, even as I was still finding new weapons, knowing that it would be an expensive waste of time if I didn’t love one.

On top of all that, Tarstones that add additional stats and features to your gameplan can be slotted into your weapons and shells. They come in all sorts, as simple as raising damage or crit rate passively, or adding the ability to infuse elemental properties to your attacks for limited periods of time. But some even go as far as adding new abilities to your arsenal, like a big sword spin or a bullet rain for area damage. Tarstones are fickle, though; many of them can only be attached to certain weapons, making the war tool you invest in even more important. I found some of the most useful ones pretty early, and being cool and flashy aside, I went most of the game opting to spend my Resolve elsewhere.

It's the combination of weapons and shells that really creates the playstyles, and those configurations felt endless. While I'm sure there is some min-maxing to be done between melee, ranged, and shell combos, I found that I could make anything work in some capacity, which actually had the unexpected effect of staying more within the lines when it came to gearing up. Each shell has a signature weapon, and though nothing about them changes in their hands, some of these pairings do feel uniquely matched. The minigun is slow to startup and leaves you stationary while you rain bullets downrange, but Proxima’s ability to mitigate incoming damage passively makes her the perfect person to fire it. Gragu’s axe whirls with sometimes wild abandon to do good damage but not much stun, leaving you open for attacks pretty regularly, but Gruga’s ability to refill his healing item by killing enemies adds some reward to the risks.

There are a dizzying amount of paths to get sidetracked down.

These shells, weapons, and Tarstones are scattered through a dense and dangerous reimagining of Fallgrim. In the first game, a central hub zone sprawled into three directions, each path narrowing into a dungeon with a boss waiting eagerly at the end. Mortal Shell 2 takes that concept to its limit, with the “central hub” zone being a huge pangea of twisted flora, bizarrely bleached mountains, and dilapidated kingdoms. You have to fight your way to the six gates lingering at the fringes of the land, each the threshold of their own dungeons with evil to cleanse on the other side.

There are a dizzying amount of paths to get sidetracked down on your journey. Around every corner felt like another pair of corners to turn. Fallgrim is perfectly designed to engross you. Each angle reveals just enough of a thing on a horizon or a path fading into a dark cave that you just to know what’s going on over there. There's a map this time around to help keep your bearings, but I do still wish it had a more robust pinning system or a note option, because you are so often forced to leave a point of interest behind to explore something else… and then something else, and then something else, and before you know it you forgot about that first thing you meant to come back to. It also doesn’t help solve how confusing the world can be to navigate at first. Things start to look very samey until you get some significant travel time logged. It's better at landmarking locations with unique features than the first game was, at least.

Of the many things you can expect to find out in the wild, like altars that produce mini combat gauntlets for a prize or gates that sling you across the map towards faraway lands, it's the many little dungeons littering the world that were always the most curious. Each one of the misty doorways reveals a self-contained mini-adventure. Sometimes these are just snaking tunnels or rundown mines with puzzles to solve or doors to unlock that hold some sort of valuable treasures in their depths. Sometimes its just an arena where you need to outlast the enemies for your prize. These bite-sized encounters are also in beacons, jagged spikes that jut through the soil like rotting teeth that serve as your bonfire-style checkpoints. What you do in them isn't necessarily different, but when you walk down one’s narrow corridors and out the door to reveal a cloudy night sky above, the strange nature of this world is most apparent in them. They weren’t Breath of the Wild levels of clever, but they really broke up the main adventure well.

I got pretty used to seeing these beacons because the monsters lurking around Fallgrim can be real nightmares. Almost any group of enemies can be lethal if you’re not on your game. I can tell you how many times I didn’t take a lowly group of miners seriously, missed an attack, and got jumped nearly to death as punishment. Foes come in many different forms, from surly, iron-clad knights and crazed cultists, to noodle-armed slendermen, to exploding bats - everything is more cursed than you first expect it to be. The spiders have human faces. There are dog sized creatures whose bodies are just bearded skulls. These are the weirdest bad guys I’ve seen in quite some time. It's also refreshing to see a game so clearly inspired by Dark Souls - and a developer who historically was the best at capturing and evolving the sort of dark wonder of FromSoftware’s signature series - so gleefully go above and beyond in creep factor. Bosses are the culmination of this inspired aesthetic, mothman knight and a crazed bog witch in a fiery chariot of a wheelchair among my favorite, even if they aren’t always the most interesting combat scenarios in game.

items.title: Wingspan Pocket Card Game Review
items.author: Chris Reed
items.content:
You’ve probably heard of Wingspan, the multi-million selling game of bird ecology that introduced a whole new audience to the strategic delight of . But however widely appealing the theme of the game might be, it presented a significant barrier to new players in the form of rules overhead.
