There’s a lot to learn in the game, and a lot more to master.

This new game, from Elizabeth Hargrave, the same designer as the original, aims to slash that barrier down by presenting many of the same mechanics in a convenient, bite-sized box. As we saw in our recent review of Diplomacy: The Golden Blade, however cleverly you cut down a game, there’s a risk you’ll lose what made it special.

Half of the box is taken up with a stash of resin eggs which will be instantly familiar to fans of the original game. These are all one base color but they compensate with a variety of freckles and speckles of pattern, making them look surprisingly realistic. Rooting around in the eggs, you’ll also find a packet of wooden feathers, one color for each player.

The other half is filled with cards. Mostly this is one giant deck of bird cards which will, again, look very familiar to Wingspan veterans, featuring a similar layout and, in many cases, the same bird with the same artwork, although the mechanical details are different. Some cards do have all-new art, and there are also some birds that are entirely new to this edition. Whatever the provenance, the bird pictures remain a delight, full of detail, life and movement.

In addition to the bird cards there are some player aids, a nest card for each player, and some smaller decks. One is an automaton for solo play, another, of smaller, fiddly cards, has a series of goals players try to complete during the game.

Cards in Wingspan Pocket are double-sided. On one side there’s a food symbol for things birds like to eat; on the other is a bird itself. Players get dealt six cards and get to decide which two of them they’re going to hold as birds, with the remainder being kept to play as food. The rest of the cards are divided into four and the top card flipped off each stack and kept face up. There’s thus a selection of four different birds and four possible foods to choose from.

Each player also gets a nest card with an egg token on it and the card details one of three actions they can take on their turn: play a bird from your hand, take cards, or place eggs. Each bird has a cost in specific foods and, sometimes, eggs as well, and you’ll need to have these available to pay if you want to take the first action, after which you lay the bird to the right of your nest. Otherwise, picking up cards lets you choose any two from the selection of food or birds as you like, while the egg action lets you place eggs on three different cards.

Most birds have some kind of special power which is often related to their real-life behavior or ecology. The nefarious common Cuckoo lets you place an egg on another of your birds. The ghostlike Snowy Owl lets you draw a bird at random and tuck it under the owl, becoming a prey item, if its wingspan is under 100cm. The extravagantly named Turquoise-Browed Motmot gives every player the chance to blind draw a food card. Once you have any birds in play you use a feather token on your turn, moving from your cards from left to right and instituting that effect in sequence. First the nest with its choice of actions, then each bird’s special power.

In this way you are essentially creating an engine, like a much simplified version of the three-habitat engines that characterize the original Wingspan. Once you have birds in play that provide food or eggs then you need to take those actions from your nest less often, meaning you can put birds into play faster. It’s an optimization exercise, but there’s a surprising amount of nuance from this simple setup. In your initial selection, for example, it’s helpful if you can have one of the birds you’ve kept provide a resource that helps you play the second. And it’s strangely satisfying when your bird line-up clicks into gear.

What you’re really aiming for is some kind of combo between the bird powers in your line up. The Kookaburra, for instance, lets you pick a fish or mouse food type for free so it combines brilliantly with the Inca Tern or Secretarybird which let you discard those food types respectively to gain two cards of your choice, meaning you’ll never have to waste nest actions taking cards again.

There’s a surprising amount of nuance from this simple setup.

You can try and specialize in particular resources, or go for a broad base. And as your hand of available bird and food cards change, you’ll need to be constantly revisiting your strategies to keep things in line. Waiting to see if the food or birds you want to extend your strategy are going to be available in the selection when your turn rolls around is surprisingly exciting.

The game ends when one player gets six birds in their row, at which point you flip your nest card over and it becomes a handy track to tally your points. Each bird card has a points value printed on it, with more expensive or less useful birds being worth more points. You also get a point for each egg and each tucked card. In the advanced version of the game, which you’ll want to use after your initial grapple with the rules, there are also two goal cards in play which reward you with additional points for having eggs on birds that meet their printed criteria. Worth three or fewer points, say, or having a wingspan over 66cm. The whole game takes just 10-15 minutes per player.

Goal cards are important because they significantly enrich the strategic decisions in building your engine. Birds that meet one or both criteria are obviously more valuable and you have to balance the need to acquire and play them with the utility of special powers on birds that don’t fit the bill. Given that you only get six birds maximum in a game, the margins on these decisions can be wafer thin. It can also sometimes be frustratingly random if you just never get the chance to grab good or high-scoring birds when they’re available, or find complementary powers to create a good engine. Them’s the breaks, but it’s far less annoying in this half-hour package than it would be in a longer game.

The whole game takes just 10-15 minutes per player.

If you’re familiar with the original, the truly striking thing about Wingspan Pocket is how successfully it recreates the feel and basic strategies of the original in a fraction of the complexity and play time. It’s a masterclass in trimming fat, from the clever way cards act as both food and birds, removing all the rules around the original’s food dice while retaining the seed or randomness, to the way birds synergize effectively in one row instead of three habitats. Sure it’s less strategic and skillful overall, but the improvement in convenience and accessibility is so huge that it’s easily a worthwhile price to pay.

items.title: Lanterns Series Premiere Review: Restoring Faith in James Gunn's DCU
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
This is a spoiler-free review of the first episode of Lanterns Season 1. The series debuts on HBO and HBO Max

It’s safe to say that a lot is riding on the first season of . This is one of the first key pieces of James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DCU that isn’t directly steered by Gunn himself. We’ve seen enough by now to know that Gunn himself has a solid handle on the DC brand. Creature Commandos, Superman, and Peacemaker have all been enjoyable. But can this fledgling cinematic universe thrive when he hands the reins over to other creators? Supergirl certainly calls that into question, casting doubt on Gunn’s lofty claims about strong scripts and clear artistic visions being the driving force of this line. The DCU needs a win right about now, and I’m happy to say that Lanterns is ready and able to deliver in its first episode.

Granted, it’s been tough to know what exactly to make of this series. For a franchise as fundamentally fantastical as this one, the prospect of focusing on an Earth-based murder mystery and downplaying the actual Green Lantern elements wasn’t necessarily appealing to all fans. The initial Lanterns trailer did little to assuage the fears of those concerned by that premise. And then co-creator Damon Lindelof really stepped in it with some of his comments, to the point where no less a DC authority than Grant Morrison felt compelled to clap back. Suffice it to say, DC and Warners didn’t really do themselves any favors with the marketing of Lanterns, but the proof is ultimately in the pudding.

Yes, Lanterns is essentially what the trailers and early previews have made it out to be. It’s as much a True Detective and Slow Horses-style murder mystery as it is a superhero drama (and, in fact, features veterans of both shows among its creative team). It’s not necessarily going to appeal to viewers intent on seeing the cosmic side of the Green Lantern mythos on full display. We rarely even see Kyle Chandler’s Hal Jordan put on the costume. And given how ugly and clunky this live-action rendition of the suit really is, that’s probably a good thing. The series generally looks good, but more in that quietly stylized, more grounded True Detective way than because of any budget-busting special effects. In short, Green Lantern purists who want unadulterated, comic book-accurate, ring-slinging cosmic spectacle are setting themselves up for disappointment with this show.

But for those willing to abandon preconceived notions and take Lanterns for what it is, this strange combination of superhero adventure and terrestrial murder mystery works surprisingly well. A lot of that comes down to the chemistry between Chandler’s Hal and his trainee, Aaron Pierre’s John Stewart. Hal has never been portrayed as the nicest or most well-adjusted member of the Justice League in various DC media, but here he’s downright hostile and standoffish to his young charge. As much as the first episode lays the foundation for an urgent investigation in the remote town of Rushville, Nebraska, it makes it clear that the real conflict is between Hal and John. One is a cocky, grizzled veteran suspicious that his space cop handlers are trying to replace him. The other is a former Marine with a deep desire for the ring but limited tolerance for shenanigans. To say the two butt heads in the first episode is putting it mildly indeed.

The series leans a lot on that core dynamic, making it crucial that it finds the right actors for the job. That’s one area where Lanterns succeeds unequivocally. Both actors are pitch-perfect in their portrayals of these iconic (if sometimes barely recognizable) characters. Chandler probably isn’t the first name to pop up on anyone’s list of dream Hal Jordan actors. He wasn’t even DC’s original choice for the part, it seems. And were the series striving for a more traditional, youthful take on the character, Chandler would obviously be a poor fit. But that’s not the goal here. This is a version of Hal who’s been active in the DCU for decades and truly feels the weight of those years. Chandler expertly captures that unique blend of exasperation, paranoia, and deep-seated overconfidence that define the DCU’s Hal Jordan. The last thing he feels like doing is training the guy who’s trying to steal his job, and he makes that clear in every interaction with John.

As for John, Pierre brings a quiet, no-nonsense charisma to the screen that contrasts nicely with Hal’s fiery bravado. John is quiet, composed, and stoic, qualities that could make for a very boring role in the wrong hands. Fortunately, Pierre is able to bring enough subtle nuance to the screen that his character never comes across as dull or underdeveloped. He’s reserved, but underneath it all he burns with desire. We see how badly he wants the ring, even if it means putting up with an endless stream of nonsense from his superior officer.

It’s also nice to see the first episode dig a little bit into the racial undertones of this Training Day-esque dynamic. In one scene, a seething John calls his father for advice and is reminded that white men like Hal Jordan have the privilege of being eccentric and difficult. Not so for a Black man trying to prove his worthiness for the most exclusive law enforcement gig in the entire universe. At least at this early stage, it doesn’t appear that Lanterns is going to be steeped in the racial tensions of modern America to the same degree that Lindelof’s previous DC series was, but it’s still satisfying to have that element acknowledged – especially given how important John Stewart was to the early diversification of DC’s comic book universe decades ago.

On the subject of John Stewart, Sr. (played as a young man by J. Alphonse Nicholson and an older man by Sherman Augustus), the premiere teases a very intriguing dynamic there that’s sure to be explored in future episodes. It’s such a common trope for superhero media to paint their protagonists as orphans yearning for a lost father figure. That’s even baked into Hal’s origin story. But Lanterns is clearly striving for something much different with John’s family background, adding in new layers and details that aren’t necessarily taken from the comics. It’s a useful reminder that while the series isn’t afraid to alter the source material in sometimes profound ways, those alterations are about more than simply making Green Lantern practical in a small-screen format.

Once the Hal/John dynamic is firmly established, the premiere sets about laying the groundwork for the murder mystery that looks to be fueling the conflict in Season 1. To be frank, said mystery isn’t the reason to tune into the series, at least at this early stage. It gets the job done in terms of moving the plot from A to B, but for now the conflict is pretty small in scope. It’s mostly about Hal’s uphill battle to convince everyone around him (John included) that the dead bodies in front of them have extraterrestrial ties.

Here again, the various characters and their interpersonal clashes are what make the series shine. Early in the episode, viewers are introduced to another major character in Kelly Macdonald’s Kerry, the no-nonsense sheriff in charge of keeping the peace in the formerly quiet town of Rushville. As much as Chandler and Pierre’s icy dynamic fuels the series in its first episode, there’s also plenty of fun to be had in the equally standoffish relationship between Hal and Sheriff Kerry. There’s all the bickering over jurisdiction and one-sided flirtation you’d expect. Kerry quickly develops into a very fun, likable character who’s every bit the effective foil to Hal that John is.

Rounding out the notable cast members introduced in Episode 1 are Garret Dillahunt as local cowboy/ranch tycoon William Macon and Poorna Jagannathan as another Rushville native named Zoe. Macon serves his purpose as a charming but quietly unsettling antagonist figure with murky ties to the town’s murder mystery. Zoe, meanwhile, quickly strikes up a close bond with John, allowing the series to explore shades of the character that aren’t possible through Hal alone. Rushville is a small town full of interesting personalities, offering plenty of room for growth in the coming seven episodes.

Again, the murder mystery itself gets the job done in terms of plot catalysts, but it’s the characters who tend to shine more than the plot in Episode 1. It is worth noting, however, that the premiere keeps one big reveal under its hat until the final moments. This twist is sure to be as controversial as anything the show has to offer in its debut chapter. But as far as throwing viewers off-guard and hinting at a larger, more ambitious scope for the series, it delivers just what’s needed. If the prospect of plainclothes Green Lanterns loudly squabbling and rubbing elbows with cowboys isn’t enough to lure you in, this twist might just do the trick.

items.title: The Brink of War Review: Jeff Daniels and Jared Harris Lock Horns in Talky Cold War Drama
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
Writer-director Michael Russell Gunn’s well-meaning feature film debut, The Brink of War, takes a wordy, academic approach to chronicling the two momentous days in October 1986 when US President Ronald Reagan (Jeff Daniels) and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev (Jared Harris) sat across a table in a house in Reykjavik, Iceland hoping to strike a landmark nuclear disarmament deal designed to keep the Cold War from finally turning into a hot one. (Impressively, the film was shot at the actual location and in the same rooms where the leaders spoke.)

As thoughtful and earnest as the drama is, it’s also pretty chill for a movie about trying to prevent nuclear war. The events may take place at the peak of the Cold War, and the movie reiterates that this meeting is the last chance for such a deal to happen, but The Brink of War lacks the urgency that any film about, say, the Cuban Missile Crisis (e.g., ) possesses, where the viewer truly feels the global stakes and intense pressure the President is under.

The Brink of War is very stagebound, often feeling like a play adapted for the screen, but it is just as reminiscent of those solid, actor-driven that dutifully covered biographical or then-topical subjects. (Angel Studios’ other recent Presidential pic, , at least offered cinemagoers some flintlock-firin’, tomahawk-throwin’ action scenes to keep it from feeling like TV movie fare.) Still, if this was made as an HBO movie in the ‘90s, it probably would’ve won an Emmy or two.

The Brink of War is most alive whenever Reagan and Gorbachev are negotiating one on one, challenging each other’s positions and calling out each country’s hypocrisies. Things get heated between them — as issues ranging from human rights, religion, and the US’s Strategic Defense Initiative are raised — with each leader standing their political and philosophical ground. These are two men trying to find a way to connect with one another, each knowing this is their chance to make history and accomplish something great and lasting. But they each possess their fair share of pride, stubbornness and mistrust.

Jeff Daniels and Jared Harris solidly handle the material as if they were onstage together in a two-hander, their characters each probing the other for weakness or advantage. Daniels doesn’t quite capture the specificities of Reagan’s voice and mannerisms, but he ably conveys the 40th President’s convictions.

The closest the film comes to trying to get to explore Reagan as a human being is seeing him still troubled, physically and mentally, from an assassination attempt a few years earlier. While not outright hagiography, The Brink of War is not out to paint the Gipper in a critical light. This film is pro-American values even as, in the moments where Gorbachev goes off on Reagan, it acknowledges the US’s flaws.

Harris is even better as Gorbachev, his standout scene being where he castigates the US policy that prevents farming and cow-milking equipment to be sold to the Soviet Union so they could feed their children. This Gorbachev isn’t pro-West but he understands the USSR needs to change. He hopes this nuclear deal — a risky, almost fantastical proposition for either ruler to try to sell to various factions back home — will give him the political capital needed to mold the USSR in his vision even as he suspects his own KGB is spying on him at this event.

The film’s most successful and amusing subplot involves the gamesmanship between First Lady Nancy Reagan (Hope Davis) and Raisa Gorbacheva (standout Branka Katić). Nancy didn’t go to Iceland but Raisa did, and she uses the press to throw shade at her US counterpart. What results is a passive-aggressive proxy war where each savvily uses the media to knock the other. It’s all very deliciously petty.

This subplot, however, also involves a kinda sorta ongoing flirtation between two reporters (Aya Cash and Guy Burnet) that doesn’t really go anywhere and left me wanting the movie to get back to the more pressing matters at hand.

Able support is provided throughout by J.K. Simmons as US Secretary of State George Schultz, to whom the film is dedicated. At this point, the Oscar winner can play Badass Bald Man in Charge in his sleep, but he nevertheless provides Daniels’ Reagan with someone else to open up to besides Nancy. The end of The Brink of War, though, doesn’t help make it not feel like a filmed play by abruptly having Schultz break the fourth wall to explain the outcome of the summit just as a character might on stage.

Forty years later, it’s amazing to see a depiction of US and Russian leaders engaged in thoughtful dialogue. It’s impossible to divorce this period piece from current events or to take politics out of it. The biggest takeaway from The Brink of War is how vital it is for world leaders, even foes, to be intelligent in their approach to vital issues facing their peoples and empathetic enough to acknowledge their shared humanity.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto 2 – The Legacy Review
items.author: Luke Reilly
items.content:
Over the next few months, I’m going to be taking a look back at each of the core Grand Theft Auto games and replaying them in the lead-up to the arrival of Grand Theft Auto 6. What we’ll be putting together won’t be traditional re-reviews, and they won’t carry IGN’s typical score out of 10, because it really wouldn’t be at all fair to simply pick apart old games published multiple hardware generations ago and make them sweat under the harsher standards of 2026. What we will be doing, however, is re-examining what made each GTA remarkable upon the time of its release, digging into what they achieved and the legacies they established, and rediscovering how much fun each of them remain today. We’ll also be identifying both the parts of the GTA experience that have seen the most evolution and growth, as well as the parts that remain fascinating, commendable, and timelessly impressive. At the end of the project, using GTA’s previously six-star wanted level, you should be able to get an idea of where each of these games roughly sit in my long-term love for this series.

Next in the queue? GTA 2.

Grand Theft Auto 2 arrived right at the tail end of the 20th century, sticking with the same brand of top-down turmoil that previously propelled its predecessor to great success. It’s a noticeable refinement of the original in some fundamental ways – slightly more forgiving thanks to the ability to save, and also a bit smoother to drive around in. It didn’t, however, replace its antiquated, tank-like on-foot controls for something that better exploited the dual-analogue controllers that had rapidly reinvented the status quo in the late ’90s. What it shed was the original GTA’s recognisable, contemporary setting. It instead opted to set its action at an unspecified point in the near future, in a stylised, retro-futuristic backdrop called Anywhere City, USA – a place overrun by gangs, ruled by a megacorporation, and featuring the highest rate of Elvis Presley’s per capita this side of Graceland. Did it work? Well, the answer – unlike Anywhere City’s proliferation of Elvis impersonators – requires a little more conversation.

GTA 2 immediately comes off as a game with a bit of an identity crisis. Even if you ignore the fact that it sports a totally different look and vibe to the original, it also completely clashes with its box art, and even its own intro movie – which features contemporaneous ’90s cars and an obvious New York setting. At the time of its release, I actually bounced off GTA 2 rather quickly, and this was absolutely a major reason. As soon as it began it just felt like an entirely unrelated product to everything that had come before – up to and including the tone-setting FMV intro it just served me. That’s a really weird problem to have. As a result, I don’t feel like I stuck around anywhere near long enough back in 1999 to get a feel for how much slicker it actually is to play.

I don’t feel like I stuck around anywhere near long enough back in 1999 to get a feel for how much slicker it actually is to play. 

Despite the fact it costs in-game currency to use, the addition of a save function represents a clear improvement over the original. Just head to the nearest church, and the good lord above will remember your progress for you. Jesus indeed saves in Anywhere City, albeit for a fee. Straight away GTA 2 appears a little more aware it’s a PC and home console product. By the late ’90s, hefty, mission-oriented action games had largely moved on from the ruthless arcade philosophy of starting from scratch every session with a tiny set of lives. Developer DMA Design adjusted its format accordingly, albeit only slightly. That is, GTA 2 retains score-based progression, still operates with strictly limited lives, and is hard as hell – but saving is nonetheless a crutch the original did not have.

A newly added health bar addresses another major frustration from the original GTA. If you’re trying to avoid cheating just to get through the missions, the boosted health is an even more useful fix than saving. Health in GTA 2 works on a 10-point scale (with five hearts that can be halved). This is in stark contrast to the first GTA, which essentially operates with your character on his or her final sliver of life at all times – where you’re instantly wasted after sustaining just a single hit. The tank controls make dodging incoming fire hideously difficult in both games, but the challenge is at least tempered here by the very sensible addition of that extra padding. It doesn’t make it easy, by any means, but it’s certainly less annoying.

The improvements don’t stop there. GTA 2’s camera is considerably less janky and, while it still shimmies around a little as you drive, it does a way better job of tracking cars smoothly. Cars also self-straighten when blazing along the streets, so it’s far less finicky to line up within a lane – or indeed change lanes – with less furious tapping of the d-pad.

There are also far fewer obstacles for cars to get hung up on than there were in the original. With the top-down perspective, it can be challenging to tell what objects are rooted into the ground and will cause a crash, because depth can be a difficult thing to effectively communicate from directly above. GTA 2 skirts this by having skinny things like light poles not even register to cars at all. It's not a particularly realistic approach, but it cuts down on the constant collisions which bogged down the pace of the original.

Cars can now be fitted out with weapons and gadgets, like machine guns, mines, and oil slick traps, and the amount of handheld weapons has been more than doubled. GTA 2 adds tossable explosives like grenades and Molotovs, a suppressed SMG that won’t alert other nearby NPCs, a shotgun for more devastating close quarters damage, dual pistols to dial up the John Woo factor, and a futuristic electro gun that will saute suckers into skeletons. The electro gun is particularly nifty considering it can lock onto multiple targets at once, but a mild auto-aim function (an assist sorely missed in GTA 1) makes for less frustrating combat all around, regardless of what weapon you’re using.

Despite the more polished gameplay, GTA 2 still leaves me indifferent in a number of ways. I know that merging the aesthetic of ’40s and ’50s vehicles with a crime-ridden, near-future corporate dystopia is a stylistic choice, but it just doesn’t really grab me. It’s not that I don’t find this era of automotive history interesting – I love skidding around in games like Mafia and LA Noire – but they just look silly in this setting and don’t sync with it at all.

It’s really easy to tell cars apart in the original GTA, because they resemble real cars and they all look quite distinct. In GTA 2, there are more than 60 different vehicles, but there are far too many that look too similar to each other – and none that really resemble anything particularly iconic. They just look like caricatures of cars, and I vastly prefer the realism of the original GTA’s vehicles.

I also prefer the original’s maps over the three districts of Anywhere City (the Downtown Sector, the Residential Sector, and the Industrial Sector). Now, GTA 2 boasts sharper graphics than its slightly murkier predecessor, and the effect of this cleaner image arguably makes it the more timeless-looking of the two. On PC there are even day and night versions of each area. However, with the possible exception of the Residential Sector (which is the most varied), there’s a plainness to Anywhere City that I don’t think the cities in the original GTA shared.

I do enjoy how much more alive and dangerous Anywhere City feels – with muggers, carjackers, and gang members scurrying the sidewalks everywhere as an omnipresent threat.

I do enjoy how much more alive and dangerous Anywhere City feels – with muggers, carjackers, and gang members scurrying the sidewalks everywhere as an omnipresent threat. However, I don’t think it has the charm of Liberty City, San Andreas, or Vice City – as primitive as their renditions were by modern standards.

I’m willing to concede my preference here may simply be because the amount of time I sunk into those maps dwarfs the moments I’ve spent in Anywhere City, but there is also something bigger at play. The 3,500 pound, 350-horsepower elephant in the room here is Driver, which was released on PlayStation in European territories about five months GTA 2, in June 1999. Now, the original Driver has no on-foot component – so it’s not an entirely like-for-like comparison – but it a fully 3D, open-world car chase classic that rapidly cemented itself as more or less my favourite game of all time at that moment. I’d seen the future, and GTA 2 couldn’t lure me back.

The dawn of 3D action-driving games was upon us. Prior to Driver we’d already seen Midtown Madness on PC, from future Midnight Club, Smuggler’s Run, and Red Dead Redemption developers Angel Studios. Following Driver came Mucky Foot’s ambitious but janky Urban Chaos in late 1999 on PC and early 2000 on PlayStation, which boasted a primitive brand of driving and third-person action. A PlayStation-exclusive Driver sequel followed in late 2000, where you could exit cars to steal another. June 2001’s World’s Scariest Police Chases sank with little trace after arriving on PS1 after the PS2 had launched, but it was actually a surprisingly decent open-world driving game of its own considering the totally outmoded hardware it was running on.

Any way you slice it, GTA 2 was a buck late and a dimension short to be a part of the first wave of 3D action-driving games.

Of course, the series wouldn’t be the bridesmaid for long – but that’s a discussion for next time.

Playing Grand Theft Auto 2 again in 2026, I’ve definitely found myself with a stronger appreciation for its technical improvements over the original. Certainly much greater than I gave it credit for back as a teenager in 1999. The driving is better, the shooting is better – and those are important and welcome gains. However, I just cannot muster any true enthusiasm for its retro-futuristic setting. I don’t know that I’d go so far as to call it aggravating but, in the words of the king of rock and roll, it just ain’t satisfactioning me.

Luke is a Senior Editor on the IGN reviews team. You can track him down on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.

items.title: Diplomacy: The Golden Blade Card Game Review
items.author: Chris Reed
items.content:
There are few more storied titles in the annals of board gaming than Allan B. Calhamer’s Diplomacy. Reputedly the favorite game of John F. Kennedy and Henry Kissinger, it sees players taking control of one of the great powers of Europe on a map of the continent and fighting it out for military supremacy. Its genius is a 1:1 combat system where pieces simply eliminate other pieces, making it impossible to gain an edge over rivals without an alliance. And it’s in these negotiations and inevitable betrayals that the thrill of the game lies.

The trouble with Diplomacy is that it runs long: with the optimal full complement of seven players, it can easily take up most of a day. Diplomacy: The Golden Blade makes the unlikely claim of retaining all the stab-in-the-dark charm of the original while cutting out the board and slashing the play time to around 15 minutes per player.

Without a board or unit pieces, there’s not a lot to talk about in terms of the box contents. Most of the components are cards, in two different sizes. The smaller ones are unit cards, representing your military forces. The larger ones are order cards that you’ll be playing to enact your decisions against opponents and these have both a picture and a text description of the order. There’s nothing special about the cards, artwork or icons, everything is clear and functional.

More curious of all are a series of punch-out cardboard tags that you use to delineate three rows and seven columns for your play area into which you place your unit cards. They show you what “level” you’ve reached in each row as you fill it with cards. These are fiddly, easily moved during play and, strictly speaking, unnecessary, although they do help all the players read the game state at a glance rather than card-counting.

Each player has a grid outlined by cardboard markers into which they play units cards from their hand. There’s a row for each of the three unit types: army, political and navy. One or two cards gives you level 1 in that unit type, three to six cards gives you level 2 and seven wins you the game. Most turns you’ll only get to play one card into your grid, although the randomly drawn selection in your hand may mean you can’t always play what you want.

However, this being diplomacy, these cards are tangential to the meat of the play, which is order cards. Every player gets an identical set of 12 of these, from which they’ll secretly select two each turn, one for each neighboring player. There are four kinds, one matching each type of unit which you can only choose if you have an equal or higher level in that unit type than that neighbor, and a fourth, “promises”, that you can play anywhere and which generally rely on your neighbor selecting a particular card.

In a turn, you’ll start by drawing a unit card, then there’s a timed five-minute negotiation period where you can make deals with other players – none of which are binding, of course. After that you play your order cards face-down before everyone reveals them all and you go around the table, working out the impact of each pairing. Finally, everyone plays a new unit card to their grid. It’s a simple core loop, easily taught, but the complexity is in the text on the order cards themselves.

Each kind has the potential to achieve different aims. Army orders let you interfere with your target’s units, allowing you to swap cards from your hand with theirs, or even removing played units from their grid. Political cards can give you a leg-up by letting you play an extra unit card or blocking enemy orders that interfere with the cards in your hand. Your naval choices include drawing extra cards, or blocking the most powerful army and political orders. This, then, is a cunningly varied game of rock, paper, scissors in which you get the chance to persuade your foes of your intentions, honorable or otherwise, before selecting an option.

However, it’s the promise cards that really give the game its flavor. Two of them, coalition and accord, give both players vital benefits if they both select a matching card. The former lets you block the order of your other neighbor, while the latter gives you two extra unit cards to draw. Alliance, on the other hand, allows that neighbor to resolve their chosen order against your other neighbor, and it can never be blocked. Critically the card says “may” ... so it leaves you very vulnerable to a sudden stab in the back.

Because you can’t play orders on an opponent unless you match or exceed their level in the matching unit type, players are caught between wanting to try and race towards the seven units needed to win and diversifying to protect themselves. Sometimes that decision is made for you by a lack of unit cards of the desired type, others by what your neighbors are choosing to collect. Either way, picking what to play each turn can be made part of both your ongoing strategy and your ongoing negotiations, bluffing about what you’re holding and might choose to play.

This network of options is, frankly, brilliant. Although it’s initially overwhelming, when you understand the effects of each card you’ll see how they interlock to create a framework of delineated decisions that feel like the free form of maneuvering and fighting in a map. Just like full-fat Diplomacy you can make and break alliances, broker deals, lie, cheat, and backstab to your heart’s content. And because your unit cards are visible to everyone, also just like classic Diplomacy, you’ll certainly have to betray one or both of your neighbors in order to win, because once you reach five or six units cards in a row, everyone will band together to stop you.

So it’s kind of a shame that, while you can still do all the things that drive the original game in this slimmed-down version, it turns out that the real draw of that game is in the cream that’s been lost.

It turns out that racing to seven cards simply isn’t enough time to establish the interpersonal relationships with the other players to really make it feel worthwhile. And it doesn’t matter if your opponents are friends or strangers: you still need time to build up a sense of trust, or develop a really festering feud, within the context of a single game. Without that, the inevitable twists of the knife just aren’t as painful, or as satisfying. Often, in games, the epic feel that players long for can only be delivered by devoting epic amounts of play time to deliver it.

Also, because the game is so short, and there’s a tendency for some players to race ahead in their favored unit type, it’s often a good idea to start getting those stabs in early. Accord is powerful if you pull it off because a bigger selection of cards means it’s more likely you’ll have what you need to push towards your goal. And everyone knows it, so you tend to get a round or two of that before such niceties give way to brutal warfare. Things pick up again towards the end of the game where alliance cards, suggested in the spirit of stopping the leader from getting over the line, can be exploited to give the betrayer a quick leg-up, but backstabbing is so commonplace at this point that it’s rarely the surprise it should be.

items.title: Wild Blue Skies Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
I remember where I was the first time my friends and I beat Andross in Star Fox 64. We’d been trading controllers all day, but Brian was the one who pulled it off. I remember the light streaming through the big windows of his media room, the way it flanked his TV. I remember the way we cheered. I was eight years old. I also remember introducing it to my then-girlfriend-now-wife more than a decade later, and I remember watching my friends play through it for the first time earlier this year. Normally, I try not to compare one piece of art to another when I’m writing a review. It’s bad practice and poor criticism. But Wild Blue Skies invites nostalgic comparisons like this at every turn, and is lesser for them. It often pulls directly from Star Fox 64, and the stuff it gets wrong shows that it doesn’t always understand what makes that game great. It’s at its best when it has the courage to be itself, to take inspiration from Star Fox 64 rather than copy it outright. Unfortunately, those moments are rare. I don’t enjoy writing reviews like this; Wild Blue Skies has left me no choice.

Stop me if you’ve heard this one before: Long ago, the evil Grimclaw, once chief engineer of the army, declared war on the world. With the help of the Blue Bombers, General Harding exiled Grimclaw to the volcanic regions to the north. Now, Grimclaw has returned, and it’s up to a new generation of pilots to liberate the world and stop him once again. A lot of the characters map one-to-one to Star Fox’s cast: Bowie Stray is a dog whose skills and leadership make him an admirable but unoriginal replacement for Fox. Chuck Barbacoa fills in for Peppy as the team’s mentor who may or may not have served with the original Blue Bombers. (It’s implied, but never confirmed.) Thorne is an overprepared lizard whose pilot skills aren’t quite a match for his mouth and most clearly maps to Slippy. The highlight, though, is Roe Whitetail (wonderfully voiced by Suzie Yeung), a deer; she’s Falco if he was quieter and an even better pilot. She’s a great addition and by far my favorite member of the Bombers.

Okay, so the characters are eerily similar, and the plot is… basically the same, but that’s not necessarily a dealbreaker for a game clearly paying homage to a classic, right? Well, then you play the damn thing. When I tell you that Wild Blue Skies is essentially just Star Fox 64, I’m not kidding. Like its inspiration, this is a rail shooter that sees you pilot a ship through a branching series of six levels (out of a total pool of 13) and chase high scores. You can pick up bombs (and hold nine, just like Star Fox 64), find power ups for your blasters that level them up, and use charge shots to take out groups of enemies for a score multiplier. Certain levels even have All Range Mode segments that place you in an arena and give you full control over your aircraft. There are three paths on the world map – hard, medium, and easy, if you’re going left to right – and completing optional objectives in certain levels (or failing to) can move you up or down in difficulty. All of this, to be clear, is fine. Star Fox’s general structure is wonderful and provides near-infinite replayability.

But play Wild Blue Skies for a minute and it becomes clear that it doesn’t always understand what made Star Fox work. Fox’s Arwing is a nimble beast capable of whatever you ask of it, while Bowie’s Cloudcutter handles like a racing yacht. It’s fast, sure, but it don’t turn so good unless you tilt in a direction, or barrel roll. You get used to it, but it never feels as good as the Arwing does. Star Fox’s bombs explode in a star pattern that makes it easy to line them up with enemy formations. Wild Blue Skies’ are just big circles that never feel accurate, and you can’t compensate for that by locking on with a charge shot and then firing them the way you can in Star Fox. These might sound like small changes, but the net result is that nothing ever feels quite right, or is as satisfying as you want it to be.

Wild Blue Skies doesn’t always understand what made Star Fox work.

Even the laser upgrades come with unfortunate caveats. You lose them once your health drops below a certain threshold, but you’re never told what that threshold is, and it doesn’t seem consistent. I’ve lost lasers at 75% health and 25% health, and seemingly everything in between. If it was predictable, fine. But it’s not. On top of that, the starting blaster is so bad that you’re often better off restarting certain levels entirely if you lose your upgrades. In Star Fox, you can get through losing your lasers by using charge shots, and Wild Blue Skies does smartly map charge shots and lasers to different buttons, which means you have more control over your blasters and can hold down the button to fire continuously. But it doesn’t matter when they’re this weak. Against tough enemies, it feels like you’re throwing rocks.

That’s the other big problem with Wild Blue Skies: it’s intent on punishing you for making mistakes. You can see it most clearly in how it handles your health during and between missions. Healing items are rare; even something like a checkpoint doesn’t give you any health. You also don’t get lives for hitting score milestones (they’re pickups in levels) or getting three gold rings to expand your health bar. In fact, there is no way to expand your health bar at all. What you start with is what you get, and while you and your team do heal between missions, Bowie’s ship isn’t fully repaired, just fixed by a set amount. Combine that with fewer health pickups overall and blaster upgrades that just… arbitrarily go away in a game where they’re already rare, and a single bad sequence can end your entire run.

I respect that Wild Blue Skies wants to be challenging. I like challenging games. But Star Fox isn’t brilliant because it’s hard (though it absolutely can be if you’re score chasing on Expert). It’s brilliant in part because it gives you room to mess up and still make a triumphant comeback. I’ve beaten Andross without either of my wingmates, lost my lasers in Area 6 and defeated Star Wolf anyway, and been down to my last pixel of life and pulled out the win because I was able to play well enough to clutch it out. You can clutch it out in Wild Blue Skies, but it’s more dependent on your knowledge of the current level and less on moment-to-moment skill.

To its credit, Wild Blue Skies does do some neat score chasing things. You can get commendations if you perform well, but they are split into two parts: medals and ribbons. You get the former by finding letters – WILD – scattered throughout each level, whether out in the open or hidden inside crates or enemies, and finding them is fun. Ribbons come from getting a high score, so landing charge shot combos and knowing the levels is important, but you also get score bonuses for things like finding all the letters, keeping your team alive, finishing a level at full health, and taking out a boss quickly. When you nail all of them in a single run, it feels pretty great.

But even here, Wild Blue Skies stumbles. The WILD pickups are a good idea, but once you know where they are, maxing your score becomes an act of rote memorization. Go this way, kill this thing, etc. And again, losing your blaster upgrades can often lock you out of them entirely. It’s nice that you can restart a level at any time or replay one after you finish it (with all your lasers and bombs, too) at the cost of a life, but it still feels restrictive and it’s easy to spend too many lives and handicap yourself for the rest of a run if you’re not careful.

Many of these levels are essentially just reskins of existing Star Fox stages.

I could live with all of that, though. I don’t expect perfection. Where Wild Blue Skies loses me is in its level design. It’s not even that the levels are bad; it’s that many of them are essentially just reskins of existing Star Fox levels. Mines is just Fortuna. It’s literally the same level. You fly around, kill some enemies, and then the Prowlers show up. They come in low out of the rising sun, just like Star Wolf does in Fortuna, and you fight them on a time limit, just like in Fortuna. The difference between them is entirely in the visual design and the fact that your team planted the bomb instead of disarming it. It is, in every way that matters, the same level – to the point where I wouldn’t be surprised if Nintendo’s kennel of attack lawyers is already frothing at the mouth.

In so directly copying Star Fox, Wild Blue Skies’ blemishes come into clear view. It’s not inherently a problem that you can’t U-turn or somersault here, but when you’re going to recreate entire levels where those things are part of what makes them fun, their omission is a real issue. I can’t somersault, but the Prowlers can’t either, so once I get behind them, it’s over – even if they can also somehow magically phase through solid objects. At least Star Wolf has the decency to take damage when they run into something.

It might be cute if Wild Blue Skies pulled this trick once, as a loving nod, but it happens several times. Iceberg is just Zoness, complete with the searchlights, and it’s not nearly as good. Temple is just Katina, which was itself a reference to Independence Day, but now there is no mothership – instead, the temple is attacked by walkers you have to destroy and enemy ships, * come out of the temple you’re trying to protect, because makes sense. (I don’t know how you reference a reference without including the reference that makes the reference cool in the first place, but Wild Blue Skies found a way.) Foundry is literally just Bolse, with the rotating arena, enemy placement, and Prowler fight toward the end all near exact copies, minus the lasers.

Shall I keep going? Because I can. The first level, Archipelago, is Corneria, down to the placement of its opening enemies, the All Range Mode fight against a walker at the end, and even the optional hard path that requires you to follow Thorne through some waterfalls. Channel is just a worse version of the legendary Area 6, complete with a fleet for you to blow up, just in the ocean instead of space. If you take the easy path, Volcano is very clearly the easier version of Venom. Even the final boss fight against the easy path version of Andross – sorry, Grimclaw – is a mech with many of the exact same attacks and a fakeout twist (spoilers: you will).

The worst part of this is that by blatantly pulling from and overly referencing these levels, Wild Blue Skies cheapens their best moments. For example, the searchlights in Zoness are a core part of that mission’s design. You’re sneaking through it, and shooting them before they see you keeps Andross’s forces from knowing you’re there – miss one, and you not only get knocked down in difficulty, you raise the alarm. In its equivalent, Iceberg, there are only searchlights because there were searchlights in Zoness. There’s no story to it and nothing cool happens if you miss them. You can shoot them, but there’s no reason to do so besides score chasing, and I often wondered why they were there at all.

Wild Blue Skies can soar when it’s not openly aping Star Fox.

I want to shoot down Pigma during the Star Wolf fights because he betrayed the original team and is directly responsible for James McCloud’s death. He throws that in your face every chance he gets, and comes gunning for Peppy because he’s looking to finish the job. Playing Star Fox 64 will make you that guy. Meanwhile, I shoot down Wartle in Wild Blue Skies because he’s there. Yeah, he has some kind of relationship with Chuck and it’s implied that he might have been a former Bomber, but it’s never confirmed and the only reason that part of the story even exists at all is because it’s in Star Fox 64. When I cut down Pigma, I’m smirking. When my blasters sear through Wartle’s cockpit and I listen to him scream on the way to hell, I feel nothing.

Wild Blue Skies can soar when it’s not openly aping Star Fox. Canyons is my favorite level; not just because it’s gorgeous and it doesn’t have an obvious Star Fox reference behind it, but because there’s a point where you come to a waterfall, the camera pans behind you, and you fly straight up, shooting down enemies and boulders that fall from the sky. It’s an awesome and novel sequence that never happens again. Canyons’ boss is a chicken with a Kentucky-fried accent who trades fowl puns with your team! It’s great! Cloudtop’s “the boss is a part of the level” gimmick recalls Sector X’s, but it’s different enough that it doesn’t feel cheap, and lighting up Grimclaw’s forces while you’re skimming clouds rules. Grottos’ increasingly tight spaces are intense, and while I see parts of Meteo and Sector X in Hurricane, it’s still visually stunning and doesn’t feel like a direct copy of either.

But then I’m back playing a level I’ve been playing since I was eight years old again, and all I see are the ways it doesn’t measure up, from the story to the enemy placement to the flying itself. In Star Fox 64, score chasing is a kind of zen; I’m not shooting for a number. I’m performing a dance, building a beautiful pattern I’ll repeat again and again. I’m trying, for a few seconds, to be perfect. In Wild Blue Skies, I’m doing the same things, but the magic is gone. There are multiple paths, but the levels always end the same way; there’s no extra bosses, no warps, no feeling that I’ve actually changed an outcome beyond picking a route. And with every copied voice line and sequence that doesn’t quite live up to the original, I am reminded of the game this isn’t.

I have a theory: We – everyone really into video games – are all chasing the way we felt when we were younger and things were new. I’ve been chasing Star Fox 64 for as long as I can remember. So has Nintendo. That’s why it's been so hard to recapture Star Fox 64’s lightning in a bottle, and why they’ve remade it so many times. It’s a near perfect video game. But the thing about chasing a feeling, an experience, is you never get there just by doing the same thing again. No Zelda ever made me feel the way Ocarina of Time did until Breath of the Wild threw out the rules and dared to try something else. I have gotten the ribbon on every level in Wild Blue Skies and the medal on most of them. The magic is only there when it’s bold enough to be different.

On the final run of my six and a half hours with Wild Blue Skies, I stuck to the hard path. After rolling through Legally Distinct Area 6, I hoped, I prayed, that the final level wouldn’t just be Dollar Store Star Wolf again. I wanted to feel something, to be surprised. And then there they were, just like I remembered them. The same camera framing, more or less the same arena – just with lava this time, and letters to collect. Wild Blue Skies’ true ending even copies Star Fox 64’s final sequence. You know the one. It has none of the emotional impact because it never earns it. It’s not enough to simply retrace the footprints of giants. You have to take the final steps yourself.

items.title: Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4, Episode 4 Recap and Review - (Please Don’t) Play It Again, Sam
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Alright, here’s the thing about Strange New Worlds. For whatever reason, at some point showrunners Akiva Goldsman and Henry Alonso Myers decided that gimmick episodes were what this show needed. After of adventure-of-the-week episodes, Season 2 featured occasional segments like “Those Old Scientists,” a crossover with the animated series , and “Subspace Rhapsody,” a musical episode, which lit a fire under the notion of what a modern episode of Star Trek could be. And that was great.

But somewhere along the way, the gimmicks became the focus, and frankly, they’ve grown kind of tiresome. I was really hoping with Season 4 that we’d just get back to regular weekly adventures. So when this week’s episode, “A Case of Chiaroscuro,” began and everything was in black and white, my mind immediately went to Yellow Alert. By the time we were on Mat'aar XII, the planet of the week (which is a kind of throwback to a film noir and/or Casablanca world), my inner Red Alert was in full effect. IT’S ANOTHER GIMMICK EPISODE.

When a newly promoted Commander Una Chin-Riley (Rebecca Romijn) leads an away team of Dr. M'Benga (Babs Olusanmokun) and Ensign Uhura (Celia Rose Gooding) to retrieve a probe that’s strayed into Klingon space, the group find themselves stuck on Mat'aar XII, where not only does everything appear to be black and white to our heroes (due to the infrared something something radiation of the system), but also you have to dress up like knock-off Humphrey Bogarts and Carmen Sandiegos in order to fit in.

Look, it’s a cute enough idea I suppose. did go to a gangster planet after all. And the visuals of the episode are pretty cool. But as “A Case of Chiaroscuro” labors through its beats to hit the tropes of the genre(s) it’s working to imitate, the hour just winds up feeling like a Cinema Studies 101 midterm paper: High-contrast and shadowy black and white photography? Check. Doppelgänger characters? Check. A central bar/cafe where conspirators and their foes can congregate? Check. Corrupt local authorities? Check. And so on and so on. The thing is, like that middling paper from the kid who only half paid attention in class, the episode really gets its film noir chocolate mixed up in its wartime/romance film peanut butter.

But whatever, let’s not quibble about that. The real problem here is that Una’s struggle isn’t really fleshed out enough. I understand that she’s torn between wanting to help the local resistance fighters who are pushing against the Klingon occupation they are enduring, and I also understand that this is a particularly personal issue for her due to her own childhood when it was the Federation who were seen as the occupiers by some of her fellow Illyrians. And yet, there’s little here that makes me feel much for Una’s current (or past) situation.

Indeed, it’s Olusanmokun’s M'Benga who once again steals the show, even though he’s depicted here as more of an advisor to both Una and Uhura rather than given his own plotline. The idea of the kindly physician who is also a skilled warrior an adept spy is so darned cool as the good doctor counsels the young Uhura in how to navigate this strange (new) world while also reminding Una that she can’t let her responsibility to the resistance movement overtake her oath to Starfleet. He even gets the best line of the hour: “My calling is medicine, healing people. It's the great mystery of my life that some of my strongest skills lie in opposition to that calling.”

The B story involves Christina Chong’s La’an, who’s been flirting with going over to the dark side all season, obsessing over what she thinks might be clues that there’s a traitor onboard the Enterprise. The thing is, nobody else buys her theories, not even her friend-with-benefits-but-actually-her-boyfriend Spock (Ethan Peck). Again, it’s a fairly low-impact plotline that culminates in the revelation that, whew, La’an is not crazy, but also, whoa, she just lied to Captain Pike (Anson Mount) to cover up the truth. Pike seems to maybe know there’s more going on here, and trusts La’an to do the right thing, but still…

Questions and Notes from the Q Continuum:

  • So if Una’s next step up the promotion ladder is captain, how long until she gets her own ship and leaves the Enterprise for good? (Never to be mentioned or seen again, by the way.)
  • In her opening log, Una says that they’re at risk of “re-starting a very Cold War,” but shouldn’t that be “re-starting a shooting war”? The Klingons and the Federation are in a state of Cold War by the time Kirk is in command of the Enterprise, and presumably that’s been the situation since the end of the war depicted in …
  • The chief Klingon here is Kor, who I guess is supposed to be from The Original Series and Deep Space Nine who was played by the late, great John Colicos. Fine, I guess? (The House of Kor was also depicted in Star Trek: Discovery, although Kor himself was not.)
  • Speaking of Discovery, the shuttle Una and the gang take in this episode is the Cervantes, which according to is a Stamets-type vessel. It’s gotta be named after either the Discovery’s Paul Stamets (who is considered lost and MIA at this point in the timeline) or possibly the real-life mycologist Paul Stamets who the character is named after. Right?

items.title: The Miskatonic Tales: Journey to Innsmouth Board Game Plays Like a Tabletop RPG Without a GM
items.author: Chris Reed
items.content:
If there’s one board game theme that rivals pleasing Renaissance-era nobles in popularity, it’s the works of H. P. Lovecraft. There’s just something about those tentacled horrors from outer space that seems to keep on appealing to tabletop adaptations. Just look at the ongoing acclaim heaped on Arkham Horror: The Card Game.

Miskatonic Tales: Journey to Innsmouth is the latest game to join this crowded lineage. But it’s attempting to stand out by taking a different route to the majority of its sticky, ichorous peers. A leaflet in the box suggests that you might want to go buy not another Lovecraftian board game but the role-playing game based on his works: Call of Cthulhu. This is more of a storytelling game than a strategy game.

The box is so hefty that you might worry it could actually contain an avatar of Nyarthatolep, but you can lift the lid in safety: the weight comes from the inclusion of three big spiral-bound books that contain the text paragraphs you’ll be referring to during the game. They’re good quality and will absolutely stand to be bent and flipped through time and time again. What’s less inspiring is the sheets of errata stickers you’ll need to paste onto various entries to ensure you have all the options the designers intended.

The remainder of the weight is mostly from several decks of cards. There are square location cards that are used to build the map, tarot-sized encounter cards for the bad guys you can meet on your adventures, and several standard playing-card sized decks. These include condition cards to track the bad – and occasionally beneficial – things that can happen to your character and a ton of skill cards that you’ll play to meet challenges. Most of these cards are purely informational, with solid graphic design that favors function over form but the location cards are graced with darkly evocative artwork.

It’s a similar story for the selection of character boards and their accompanying punch-out standees, representing an excellent variety of character types in every sense of the word, brought to life nicely in all their 1920s glory. There are lots of other, more workmanlike tokens to punch out, too, for tracking various actions and statuses during play.

Alongside the weighty components is an innocuous-looking, lightweight rulebook that you’ll quickly find is poorly laid out and worded. Everything you need to play is in there, but you’ll need repeated puzzled flip-throughs during setup and the first few turns before everyone is comfortable with what’s going on.

Broadly, your group will choose one of three missions, which are best played in order, and which you’ll work together to complete. You place a starting location and objective card and read an introductory paragraph of text which explains the various options that you have in that location. Most of them require you to discard one of your character’s skill cards to do something, while others require you to pass a skill check. This involves characters, often more than one if working together, to discard cards either of the skill type required for one automatic “success” towards the target number, or a card of a similar type to get a dice to roll which may, or may not, generate a success. You need enough successes to pass the target number in order to succeed.

In addition to the dice you get by generating cards you will also always roll a red dice in these checks. This can give you an extra success, but it can also roll scary-looking symbols like skulls or tentacles. These cause the matching track to increment and, often, to cause you to flip to a paragraph in the book, triggering an event in the in-game narrative, usually an undesirable one.

Running out of cards also causes a time track to increment with similar paragraphs along the route, putting you under a bit of pressure to hurry along and achieve your objectives. It’s a neat way of giving your adventures a sense of time and dynamism as you move through the locations.

You’ll spend a lot of your time in Miskatonic Tales reading paragraphs, not only from the tracks but when you enter a new location and in describing the results of your actions, pass or fail. You can appoint one person to read these out to the group, or take turns, or there’s a free app to download which will do it for you with very questionable voice acting. The writing is fine: it’s not overloaded with the obscure adjectives that Lovecraft was fond of, nor is it lifeless, but it’s not especially inspiring, either. It’s just about enough to set the scene and keep you engaged.

Where the paragraphs really shine is in giving you options. The choose your own adventure books this style of play derives from often leave players feeling as though they’d like to do things that aren’t offered as choices. That rarely happens here: there are paragraphs to interact in different ways with pretty much everything described. Indeed there are too many options to explore them all without running down your time track dangerously fast. You’ll need to pick and choose what you do based on your curiosity and your objectives.

The trouble is that you don’t have very much else beyond those two things to guide your picks. Again, like the gamebooks it evokes, most of the decision-making happens in the dark as you have very little information on which to guess which options are better than others. You can’t even really strategize around the skill check system beyond a bit of risk-reward analysis. The closest the game comes to giving you meaningful decisions are your use of when to spend magic points which give you re-rolls, and when to use each character’s special abilities. As a result, this feels less like a board game and more like a particularly fancy way to run a role-playing game without a GM.

This feels less like a board game and more like a fancy way to run a role-playing game without a GM.

You don’t even get much strategy or tactics when it comes to combat. Encounters can either be fought with weapons, if you have them, or via a different skill, either of which is resolved with the standard dice-rolling skill check mechanism. That’s pretty much the only choice you get. Damage is taken off your character’s health or sanity values and you can also take hits to these tracks from accumulating status cards like panic or injury that are given out by in-game events. If either track runs down to zero, that investigator is out of the game.

Win or lose, one thing the plethora of exploration options gives you is a decent amount of replay value. There’s a ton of stuff to do in Miksatonic Tales and a second attempt at a scenario can work out very differently from the first. The game has a neat keyword system that tracks how past decisions can impact future situations although, as per most of the game, you have no way of knowing how this will play out. Many of the choices lead to blind alleys or horrible punishments you cannot anticipate, which can feel frustrating but it suits the source material well enough. What it lacks in strategy, it makes up for in anticipation. However, whether you’ll want to replay a scenario is a moot point as game times run long, much of which is taken up by players reading out text. You can “save” your game to stretch it across multiple sessions if needs be.

items.title: Reacher Season 4 Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
premieres Wednesday, August 12, on Prime with the first three episodes; subsequent episodes debut each Wednesday until September 16.

Adapting Lee Child’s 13th Jack Reacher novel, Gone Tomorrow, was never going to be an entirely straightforward exercise in 2026. Obviously, I can’t quite explain why; if I did, non-readers would still be able to connect enough dots to ruin at least one of the twists in the latest live-action adventure of Prime’s premier skull-pounding ex-MP. Broadly, however, the backgrounds and motivations of Gone Tomorrow’s villains simply weren’t going to work in the present day, with 17 years having passed since the book’s publication.

As such, Reacher Season 4 takes more creative liberties than ever before while unfurling its eight-episode story. However, it doesn’t just change the entire aforementioned backstory and motivations of the core bad guys; it also weaves in a far grander ultimate threat as well as entire stretches of plot that are completely unique to the TV adaptation. The upshot is that this is perhaps the least predictable season yet for entrenched fans who’ve already devoured the novels. However, it’s also arguably the most frustrating, seeing as these alterations have resulted in the show sidelining at least a couple crucial components of the Reacher formula.

Season 4 finds Alan Ritchson’s always-wandering Jack Reacher in Philadelphia. The novel was set in New York, but Philadelphia seems similar enough; besides, Season 2 already did New York (despite the source novel for being set in California). The long-running book series has seen Reacher in the Big Apple on multiple occasions, but it certainly wouldn’t make sense for the city to suddenly be the primary setting for half the Prime Video series aired to date.

At any rate, I will say that the “small town, big city, small town, and back again” cadence definitely doesn’t feel coincidental at this point, especially since we know that Season 5’s source novel — 2015’s Make Me — has already been locked in and will again return Reacher to small-town America. I continue to believe that it’s the right play to swing between backdrops; it makes the series feel like it’s truly shifting gears between seasons.

As Season 4’s story begins, Reacher finds himself drawn into a random encounter in a sparsely filled subway carriage, as his training compels him to approach a visibly distressed woman named Anna Merrick. She’s showcasing a number of signs that Reacher immediately finds impossible to ignore, but while his instincts initially steer him towards an incorrect assumption, Anna’s next move drags Reacher into a police investigation. This quickly widens into a twisted and wide-reaching conspiracy, with a shady government agency, hired mercenaries, a pair of foreign nationals, and a former special forces operator-turned-US congressman clashing with Reacher as they work to track down a USB drive Anna is purported to have had in her possession. This MacGuffin drives the bedlam (and the body count) for some time, until the season quickly mashes the throttle for an escalation that leaves the original novel in the rearview mirror. I can concede it makes for a more traditionally explosive television finale, but I’d argue that it arrives as a pretty worn out crescendo we’ve seen a hundred times before.

As with previous seasons, Reacher picks up a number of new allies, including Philly detective Tamara Green (GLOW’s Sydelle Noel) and Anna’s brother Jacob (Christopher Rodriguez-Marquette), who is a small-town cop himself. They’re actually a lot more present in this season than I’d expected considering Gone Tomorrow the novel is a slightly more solitary affair that sees Reacher slogging his way through most of the story’s encounters solo.

It’s a competent supporting cast, and their characters carry credibility as investigators thanks to their law enforcement background, but the only memorable standout is Tamara’s partner Docherty, played by veteran character actor Kevin Corrigan (True Romance, Superbad, The Pineapple Express). Corrigan absolutely nails his role as an exhausted veteran detective with limited patience for Reacher’s schtick. He doesn’t get a ton of screen time, but what he receive is actually a little more in line with what I’d expected for the side characters this season.

Unfortunately, Season 4’s villains are far less convincing. They’re ruthless and awful — the perfect combination for a Jack Reacher death sentence — but they’re thinly drawn. It takes a while to wheel them out, but this is admittedly in line with the Gone Tomorrow novel. They don’t have much in the way of great dialogue; in fact, some of it is quite poor, with one particularly exposition-heavy exchange coming across as unnecessarily detailed and rather forced considering how long they’ve apparently known each other.

Reacher’s remarks are at their very best when he loads the promise of a dramatically shortened lifetime of pain into a single word.

They also seem to have survived way longer than their decision-making skills should have allowed. At one stage, they bring literal knives to a gunfight, and only live because the script lets them monologue when the novel Reacher would have just made sure they were each shot in the face. Ritchson’s TV Reacher definitely also began life as an uncompromising force that doesn’t fight fair and never waits until the count of three, so scenes like this continue to play as disappointingly off-brand. I’m sorry, but knives do move faster than bullets.

Fortunately, Season 4 still regularly lets its man mountain off the leash, and the best thing about the series unambiguously remains Ritchson’s Reacher himself and the crunching fight scenes he finds himself in. Reacher is still a principled yet completely remorseless killer when the situation requires, and I live for his largely emotionless pre- and post-action ultimatums. These quips are always delivered unironically with a mix of ice-cold military sternness and almost child-like honesty: “I’m good at not letting people get away with things,” he says early on. While his expressions are typically blank, they always leave me grinning, and I commend the show’s habit of wheeling them out at the perfect moments and not overusing them to the point of parody. Frankly, I love how uncomplicated they tend to be too; hell, Reacher’s remarks are at their very best when he loads the promise of a dramatically shortened lifetime of pain into a single word.

“What’s the signal?” asks one of Reacher’s allies as Reacher prepares to split from the group and attack an encroaching group of goons from behind. His reply is one, deeply satisfying word: “Screaming.”

items.title: The One Piece: Escape from Egghead Board Game Is Runny and Undercooked
items.author: Scott White
items.content:
Escape from Egghead reminds me a lot of the games I played growing up, where there wasn’t much player interaction and the games would sort of play themselves. Leaning heavily into randomness, nearly every aspect of Egghead, from where you can go, if you succeed, and even what help you may get, is largely out of your hands. It all comes down to a roll of the dice or what card gets drawn. This won’t be the game for folks who enjoy much strategy in their board games.

The board is split up into six paths, composed of three spaces, each leading to a boss. During setup, you shuffle and place facedown the bosses and the route’s tiles, before flipping over the first tile. Then on your turn, you roll two or three dice whose values will determine which routes Luffy and Bonney can take, with the remaining die adding to your food total – a resource that you can spend to boost your rolls during the following “Rush” phase.

This second phase is where a majority of the “action” takes place, which really just amounts to rolling dice and seeing if you surpass a number. Each of the route tiles features an enemy for your character and an associated challenge rating for you to get past. Passing just involves rolling a die and spending food to beat the route's challenge number; doing so gives you some sort of reward like additional food or a reroll token. From there, you either repeat the process or set your flag down, which lets you start your future rushes down that route further along, in future turns.

The bosses at the end of each path play out the same, except there is usually some sort of restriction or challenge. St. Saturn for instance has an increased challenge rating of 11 if you enter his space with an odd amount, whereas if you face him with an even amount, it’s only 9. Why is that the case? I have no idea. A quick read through from the character’s page on the One Piece Wiki did not share insight as to why this man has an aversion to odd numbers, and it makes me curious how much thought was put into best representing the characters and their quirks.

Once you have escaped a route’s boss, you place a marker on one of the rewards and return to base. Each boss only has so many open spots to be claimed, meaning if there is no reward to be claimed, the rules state “you can no longer escape from the route”. The rulebook doesn’t clarify whether the route becomes permanently closed or if the boss can still be defeated but you simply wouldn’t get a reward.

This sort of ambiguity underlines my biggest issue with Egghead: the whole thing just feels a bit runny and undercooked. From typos in the instruction manual, missing rule clarifications and examples, even down to the board’s design, it’s hard not to feel like this was pushed out the door too soon without getting a final pass through.

Escape from Egghead reminds me of the games I played growing up, where there wasn’t much player interaction

As for the board itself, its outward expanding routes are visually interesting and catch the eye, but this leads to two unnecessary problems. First, it results in a larger table footprint than the board really needs. Worse, it causes an unfortunate situation where the closest tiles to the players are all upside down. Unless you intend to play this on a large rotating lazy-susan or your players all love to read upside down, Egghead will require you to move around the table just to read the tiles you’re landing on.

I frequently found myself asking why couldn’t this game simply have six horizontal lines with the tiles connecting on their sides instead of tops and bottoms? This would serve the same function, and allow everything to be facing the players, making it take up far less space, and allow everything to be readable from a single direction.

Another rather odd aspect to Egghead is that, at least using the rules as written, playing at two players inadvertently removes the countdown timer from the equation. There are six Vegapunks that must all be flipped before the countdown timer starts, which can result in everyone losing. The game ends when the first player escapes three bosses. Put those two systems together and have yourself a situation where it is impossible to trigger that losing scenario. This doesn’t feel intentional either, and comes off more as “we didn’t test the game enough” since the stated objective in the instructions reads “Be the first player to escape from three different Bosses and leave Egghead Island before the Vegapunk Timer runs out.” Playing with two players basically erases everything after “and”.

The stated goal the game gives players is not only to escape three boss but ALSO to do so before the timer runs out. If the timer never starts, then half of the challenge is meaningless. As a homebrew rule, I would recommend adjusting the Vegapunk count per player counter (2 players / 4 punks, 3 players / 5 punks, 4 players / 6) just to keep that little bit of tension in the game.

One Piece: Escape from Egghead feels tailored toward the more casual general consumer crowd rather than the board game hobbyist. This is a “push your luck” dice rolling game that leans heavy into randomness and away from giving you much in the way of meaningful choices. Your only real choices come down to whether you want to roll more dice or not and which reward spot you take on the bosses. Everything else is out of your control.

I have enjoyed Kess’s other One Piece offerings like Luffy’s Bento Panic, and I'm excited for the full release of their big Dawn of Liberation game. Even here, I see the value in a good ol’ dice chucker game that you can just turn off your brain and enjoy. If that is what you’re looking for and you consider yourself a big One Piece fan, you may find some fun here with Egghead. That being said, it’s also hard to overlook the stumbles and some of the odd design choices the game makes, knocking it down a peg. While some homebrew fixes and adjustments can help patch the holes, Escape from Egghead is still a leaky ship.

Scott White is a freelance contributor to IGN, assisting with tabletop games and guide coverage. Follow him on

items.title: Coyote vs. Acme Review
items.author: Clint Gage
items.content:
