Looney Tunes have been around since the ’30s. That’s almost 100 years, so it’s safe to say they’ve seen it all. That creators are still finding a way to make Bugs, Daffy and the rest continually fun and relevant is frankly pretty wild.

With Coyote vs. Acme, writer Samy Burch and director Dave Green have figured out a way to do it again. Tired of being exploded, bludgeoned and stranded in mid-air at high altitudes with nothing but the canyon floor distantly beneath him, Wile E. Coyote decides to sue Acme, the iconic company behind all the insane products he uses to catch the Road Runner.

It’s a premise built on pain, suffering and pathological repetition that generations of humanity have found hilarious… myself included.

When he tracks down Will Forte’s Kevin Avery, a billboard-famous personal injury lawyer looking to do the bare minimum to get by in life relatively undetected,the movie turns into equal parts courtroom drama, corporate intrigue and dry absurdist comedy. It’s A Few Good Men by way of Who Framed Roger Rabbit and it works on just about every level.

Everything from the products themselves – from Acme brand canned lions to dehydrated boulders to the old reliable metal pellets mixed in with bird seed and a book titled How to Wait Around Dramatically, – to the characters named in honor of original Looney Tunes creatives Tex Avery, Chuck Jones and Michael Maltese, the details in the film are on point. The film is a mix of classic Looney Tunes gags with a more modern comedic sensibility, and it proves not only that Looney Tunes have always had that going for them, the filmmakers behind Coyote vs. Acme understand this and can add to it.

But Coyote and Road Runner are a very short form tradition. Stacking a narrative on top of a popular but story-less property is a phenomenon that The LEGO Movie perfected and plenty of would-be franchises have tried to imitate in the years since. Pianos being dropped on heads is all well and good for a few minutes at a time, but the real challenge with making a feature-length version is figuring out what can be interesting for an hour and a half. The answer for Coyote vs. Acme isn’t just the legal backdrop; it’s the weird psychological motivation behind Wile E. Coyote’s decades-long determination to catch Road Runner.

It's a story about becoming the best version of yourself... and also pantsless modeling gigs.

The film treats Coyote with no small amount of sadness. There’s a genuine obsession to what the Tune is doing with his life in the desert. Living in a cave, surrounded by blueprints of all his failed plans, Wile E. Coyote is the Joker to Road Runner’s Batman. Or vice versa, depending on who you’re rooting for. Ultimately, however, this is Will Forte’s movie as well, and as a two-hander with an animated coyote, the pair of them form a legitimately engaging emotional core. They both grow and learn and all that junk, but before you start thinking that a Looney Tunes movie is taking itself too seriously, I can assure you it does not. In the balancing act of adding enough heart to hang a whole story from while not shoving something so gauche as a “theme” down our throats, Coyote vs. Acme nails it.

Yes, it’s a story about becoming the best version of yourself, about trying over and over again in the face of failure, pain and rejection because you know it’s the right thing to do. There’s a mystery to solve in a fight against a heartless corporation. But also Porky Pig is “here for the pyuh-p-pyuh-pyuh-p-pantsless modeling gig.”

The comedic timing at play is also excellent. The movie is not afraid of an awkward pause or rapid-fire sight gags. Every joke is treated with exactly what it needs. This is due in large part to the supporting cast. John Cena as Acme’s shameless in-house counsel Buddy Crane does exactly what he needs to. Ditto Lana Condor as Avery’s idealistic, recent law school grad. They’re both very good and carry their scenes with humor weight as needed, but the funniest non-animated cast members have way fewer lines than either of them.

Luis Guzman as the trial judge who doesn’t want any silliness in his courtroom, Martha Kelly as an employee of Avery’s law firm who might not make it back from her mini-golf tournament this weekend, and P.J. Byrne as an Acme stooge and Cena sycophant all bring a ton to this movie in small doses. For me, those are the types of characters to keep an eye on. They’re the ones that speak to how effective a movie like this is. When there are entire moments built around the supporting cast members that survive the editing process, it means the filmmakers knew what they were doing during casting, production and post.

We also have to talk about the meta narrative at play with this movie. Coyote vs. Acme famously slipped the noose when Warner Bros. boss David Zaslav tried to kill the movie to take a tax break. Thanks to the cast and crew and, frankly, most of us shouting about how dumb and tragic that would be, WB rethought the decision and Ketchup Entertainment stepped in to release the movie.

The film wasn’t written about that in the first place, but it is hilariously appropriate that a Looney Tunes movie about corporate shenanigans would fall victim to corporate shenanigans itself. There were a few touches most likely added in the aftermath of the Warner Bros. near-miss, like the “Based on a True Story” title card at the beginning of the film, and the jokes about WB being a wholly owned subsidiary of the Acme Corporation.

It’s a testament to the filmmakers trying over and over again, in the face of failure and rejection and corporate overreach, like the film’s central characters. Coyote vs. Acme is ironically the perfect movie to have survived that ordeal. It’s so perfect, the cynical side of me wonders if WB didn’t stage the whole thing as a publicity stunt. Who knows? Either way, it’s a layer of intrigue to this movie that fell on their heads like an anvil from the sky and the film does not waste the opportunity.

items.title: The End of Oak Street Review
items.author: Clint Gage
items.content:
The End of Oak Street follows a family, led by Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor, as their neighborhood mysteriously teleports from an early ‘80s suburban landscape into the swampy age of dinosaurs, leaving them to fight for survival against a crew of beasts that look a little more like what passes for “scientifically accurate” these days. (They’ve got feathers and fur and everything.) It’s really a blank canvas of a science-fiction conceit. As specific as it may sound, “family must survive dinosaurs” can go a million different ways. It’s an engaging premise no matter which direction the filmmakers choose, but it’s also one that’s pretty familiar. The dangers lurking in the swamp of a family-forward dinosaur adventure are the impossible to avoid comparisons to Jurassic Park. That’s the bar The End of Oak Street, intentionally or not, fair or otherwise, has set for itself.

So, how does a dinosaur movie set itself apart from such obvious influences? The answer for The End of Oak Street seems to be, don’t. Instead, lean into them.

First, I have to say this movie might have been created in a lab just for me. I’m an ’80s kid, so the setting hits all the right heartstrings. I’m always here for a good, warmhearted adventure yarn, an energy the trailer for this film has piles of. On top of that, I love indie movies, and David Robert Mitchell, whose It Follows is a creepy experiment in creating eeriness, is making his first film in eight years and bringing dinosaurs along for as Spielbergian a ride as any you’ve seen in recent memory. These are all good things.

The End of Oak Street delivers on all the expectations I had for this movie. By the time the dinosaurs show up, the movie turns into a fun little creature feature pretty quickly. The dinosaurs don’t look quite the way we’re used to seeing them on screen, which effectively modernizes them in a way Jurassic Park never really has. They can be scary and campy in equal measure. There’s a sequence that includes a memorably goofy photo op followed immediately by a harrowing escape. It’s a combination that works when the movie is in its stride.

But I say Oak Street delivers because the film is walking a fine line where loving and effective homage is on the right and “I’ve just seen this before” is on the left. It’s those influences and those sleeves David Robert Mitchell is wearing them on. He clearly loves adventure films of the ‘80s, you can even hear it in the score from the production logos on. This film would have been right at home 40 years ago. But the audience isn’t mysteriously teleported to 40 years ago, and there are moments in the film that left me trying to outrun some outdated cheese.

For example, the film can be incredibly sweet and earnest. There’s an honest love for the setting, the ’80s in suburbia, that’s evident in every frame of the film’s first act. But that sweetness borders on saccharine at times, feeling like an affectation that’s not totally earned. In parts, it's a script that’s being read to me, admittedly with a lot of heart, but there’s a stiffness to it nonetheless.

No matter how many feathered dinosaurs appear on screen, this movie is all about the family.

Among all of that sticky sweetness, though, there are genuinely terrific moments, including one that I even found legitimately shocking. I would, were I a cooler person, describe my state in the aftermath of that scene as “shook.” But the key to all of the moments that worked is a decision David Robert Mitchell clearly made early in the development of The End of Oak Street – that no matter how many feathered dinosaurs appear on screen, this movie is about the family.

Putting a family dynamic front and center is a staple of all the Spielberg sci-fi Oak Street is borrowing from. Whether it’s the harsh light and wind blowing through the curtains calling up Close Encounters of the Third Kind or all the dinosaurs (and their poop) giving Jurassic Park in sometimes very literal, one-to-one ways, family dynamics are always the more important thing happening on screen. And so, while this is a movie about a wormhole blipping an entire neighborhood into dino-times, it’s really always about navigating difficult times in a marriage. And not only from the couple’s perspective, but the children’s as well.

That a wonky science-fiction trope leading to what could easily have been a spec script for Jurassic Park 8 that was rejected for being too weird is turned into a capable metaphor for a crumbling marriage is no small task. While the writer/director deserves the prehistoric flowers for pulling that off, I do think the bulk of the credit goes to Anne Hathaway. She’s having a pretty great year, and The End of Oak Street is coasting right along on that streak. As the mother of the pack, she’s strong and fiercely protective, but also frayed at the edges in all the right ways. She’s barely holding it together as the brutally realistic yin to Ewan McGregor’s relentlessly positive “it’s just all gonna be alright” yang. She’s grounded in a way that’s crucial to pulling off the metaphor-asaurus that David Robert Mitchell is aiming for.

Another thing that can’t be overlooked is the runtime. It’s about 90 minutes, and while this may be an unfair claim to make, I bet there’s a 105-minute version of this movie that just doesn’t work as well. An obvious thing that’s missing from that runtime is an explanation. And that is great. How the neighborhood actually transports somewhere else remains a mystery that the film never even thinks about unravelling. There’s some vague talk with some science-y words, and a touch of exposition from a radio broadcast heard from off-camera, but to incorporate more of an expertise or a character that could offer a definitive scientific explanation for the mysterious events, would’ve been a film-destroying mistake. Keeping the film to 90 minutes avoids that urge to explain stuff that does not need explaining, or over-complicating what is a straightforward survival tale to the detriment of what the movie is really about, which again, is about Anne Hathaway weathering a rough patch in what to everybody else appears to be the picture of happiness.

The other thing I really like about this movie is the visual set-up and payoff. One way David Robert Mitchell pulls this off is something my film nerd side is excited to talk about, which is the use of a split diopter lens. To get technical for a moment, a split diopter is an arrangement of glass on the lens that allows for two focal lengths in the same shot so that subjects in the very near foreground can be in focus while the background is in focus as well. But it’s not like everything is just in focus, there’s also a visible line in the frame separating the two subjects, so the audience’s attention is drawn to both in a much more distinct way.

Anyway, I love seeing split diopters because you don’t use them. They’re representative of a clear choice being made. Sometimes there’s just information on screen because we need to get from one scene to the next, but when you can tell a bag of tricks is being opened, I generally appreciate the effort. So where does a split diopter relate to the visual set-ups and payoffs in this movie? To me it seems the moments where the focus is split are when a character is hiding something. There are some uncomfortably framed split focus shots seen in the trailers, which take place during a tense and important moment for the family. They happen in a few other places as well, in spots where what’s being discussed in the foreground isn’t quite jiving with what’s happening in the background. Pay attention to which moments are framed at a distance as well. Instead of just a standard two-shot, there are conversations we see through a window, or over a hedge, or in the reflection of a mirror. This is a movie that’s undeniably thoughtful in its visuals.

There’s also some great, eerie blocking at play that sets up the world our characters start in to juxtapose the world they find themselves in later. This is something that David Robert Mitchell did really well in It Follows, and he excels at it again here in The End of Oak Street. The movie’s opening act is admittedly a little slow; in spite of the brisk 90-minute runtime, there’s a methodical pace to the stretch of film leading up to the first dinosaurs on screen. But what’s happening in those lingering shots of a treeline, the edits that feel a beat too slow after a character leaves frame… they’re all set-ups. Later in the film, those treelines that the film took great pains to establish as a safe part of ’80s suburbia are no longer empty, but instead are hiding something dangerous. Those edits that take an extra beat after the kids exit the shot suddenly feel like maybe we’re waiting to see something else show up.

The high-water mark for this technique is in a oner in the middle of the movie. The family is running away from a T. rex (a chunk of this shot is seen in the trailer) and it starts with near misses and ends with, as Dr. Malcolm said in The Lost World, running and screaming. The shot is a great little microcosm for what works about this movie. It’s also admittedly a little hokey, making it a microcosm of the things that don’t work about this movie as well.

But ultimately, the movie is like an old friend. There aren’t a lot of surprises, but you still enjoy their company. Maybe you haven’t seen each other in eight years or so, but there doesn’t need to be any explanation when you get back together. You know their secrets, warts and all, so maybe they don’t impress you like they used to but damn if it isn’t nice to see them again anyway. In spite of being a little under the influence of nostalgic sci-fi adventures, David Robert Mitchell and Anne Hathaway in particular add enough plumage to the familiar so that The End of Oak Street… finds a way.

items.title: X-Men '97 Season 2 Finale Review & Recap: "Survival of the Fittest"
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for X-Men '97 Season 2, Episode 9!

At this point, it's officially safe to say that X-Men '97 Season 2 doesn't live up to the standard set by the first. The highs are just as high, as we saw in the stellar first half. But the whole thing fails to come together in a cohesive package. These final two episodes have really lost the plot where Apocalypse (Ross Marquand) is concerned, resulting in a finale that hits some of the right notes yet ultimately still fails to bring the season home.

It's tough to make sense of the handling of the Apocalypse storyline post-Episode 4. The character was such a driving force of the first four episodes, but he faded into the background after that point. Not that every installment needed Apocalypse as its focal point, but the series has really started to suffer from the lack of attention paid to the character in recent weeks. So much about his motivations and actions is unclear. That entire backstory regarding his love affair with Candra was treated as an afterthought in Episode 8.

So it is that when Apocalypse finally resurfaces to confront Professor Xavier (Marquand) and the X-Men in the finale, that reunion falls a little flat. All the momentum Season 2 built up around Apocalypse in those first four episodes has faded.

When we finally see the reborn Apocalypse square off against the X-Men here, it's a very brief and anticlimactic battle between good and evil. No sooner does Apocalypse get to stretch his new Cajun-y legs than the power-boosted Rogue (Lenore Zann) shows up to save the day. This is the payoff to the entire season? Compared to the epic spectacle that was the "Beyond Good and Evil" storyline from the original series, this feels pretty bland and small potatoes in comparison. It's just bizarre that Apocalypse's grand, millennia-spanning master plan boiled down to stealing Gambit's (A. J. LoCascio) body and hassling the X-Men for a few minutes.

It's really in the build-up to that final showdown where "Survival of the Fittest" actually shines. There we get an actual epic throwdown between the reunited X-Men on one side and the combined forces of X-Force and X-Factor on the other. The action flows hot and heavy here, but the real joy is in how this conflict pays off on a season's worth of buildup for characters like Cable (Chris Potter) and Polaris (Carolina Ravassa). Their conflicted loyalties add a nice, extra touch of tragedy to the entire battle. At a time when human/mutant relations have really soured, it's a terrible thing to see the X-Men and their ilk fighting amongst themselves. Awesome in that Staurday morning cartoon way, but terrible.

I'll also say that, as much as I was underwhelmed by Rogue becoming the deus ex machina that quickly resolves the Apocalypse conflict, this episode does tug at the heartstrings when it comes to the Nightcrawler (Adrian Hough) twist. We're at first left to assume that Rogue and Remy will be torn apart once more, only to realize that Kurt sacrificed himself for the sake of his beloved sister. The writers of this series clearly love this character deeply, and his last and greatest sacrifice feels like a fitting end to his deeply emotional journey. Assuming it is the end, anyway. Based on how the Celestials operate, I would think that they're less interested in acquiring one little death than they are a replacement for Apocalypse in his role as cosmic gardener.

Ultimately, I find myself wishing that Season 2 retained the 10-episode structure of the first, which could have allowed this episode to focus on the X-Men vs. X-Force & X-Factor conflict and the finale to better flesh out the Apocalypse side of things. Former head writer Beau DeMayo has offered some insight into what the original plans for Episode 10 involved, though, to be frank, it sounds like that would have compounded the problem rather than addressed it. Perhaps it's best that the series simply wipe its hands of Apocalypse and try to start fresh in Season 3. The post-credits scene certainly gives us some idea of what's coming, but that's a topic for another article.

items.title: The X-Files: I Want to Believe - Vrach Frankenshteyn Review
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
No one is ever going to accuse The X-Files: I Want to Believe of being the better of the two X-Files films, but time has been fairly kind to this overly maligned 2008 release. It hasn't hurt that the two revival seasons now exist, and I Want to Believe no longer shoulders the burden of being the last word on the story of intrepid FBI agents Fox Mulder (David Duchovny) and Dana Scully (Gillian Anderson). And now the film is due for a whole new reappraisal thanks to the release of Chris Carter's director's cut, subtitled "Vrach Frankenshteyn." Just don't come into this version expecting a dramatically different or improved experience.

As far as contemporary director's cuts go, Vrach Frankenshteyn is no Kingdom of Heaven or Doctor Sleep. Carter isn't dusting off entire reels of lost footage or significantly recutting and reworking the final product. In fact, this version of the film is actually a bit shorter than the original. The goal isn't to fundamentally transform the experience, but to lightly streamline the picture and amp up the horror elements that were somewhat lost in the studio's pursuit of a PG-13 rating.

The result is a very minor overhaul of I Want to Believe, to the point where I felt compelled to pull up the original cut and skim through it just to get a sense of what had actually been changed. As the new subtitle suggests, Carter wants this version to be a more direct homage to Mary Shelley's Frankenstein. But aside from a bit more gore and body horror elements in the climactic surgical sequence, I can't say that this version really has the intended effect. The villain characters are still too thinly drawn and little-seen to leave much of a lasting impression.

So it is that we're left with a film that still boasts the same strengths and suffers from the same weaknesses as the original. I Want to Believe has always been a middle-of-the-road procedural X-Files episode masquerading as something bigger. Apart from resolving the cliffhanger ending of the series (rather abruptly and anticlimactically, I might add), it lacks the ties to the franchise's larger mythology that make 1998's The X-Files: Fight the Future such a thrilling and necessary piece of the canon. It's a strangely unambitious spinoff, asking fans to settle in and simply watch Mulder and Scully embark on a new case. Nor does it boast the terrifying creatures or wonderfully quirky sense of humor that defines many of the show's best monster-of-the-week installments.

That all being said, there's a fundamental appeal to the Mulder/Scully dynamic that can't be downplayed. Even in a case like this, where the monsters in question are of the purely terrestrial variety and the plot feels cribbed from any number of murder mystery thrillers, these two characters are never not compelling to watch. The intense personal chemistry that Duchovny and Anderson spent years honing on the main series remains in full force here. It's enough simply to sit back and savor their bickering and the eternal clash between Mulder's lofty theories and Scully's dogged rationality.

In either version, I Want to Believe is best appreciated as a Scully-focused story. Mulder doesn't have much of an arc here, even with this being his first big case since becoming a pariah and fugitive from the government. As usual, he jumps to conclusions and finds his belief in the paranormal amply rewarded. But with Scully, the film becomes an exploration of faith tested and faith rewarded. Can she do right by her terminally ill young patient? Can she put aside her innate revulsion to Billy Connolly's disgraced priest, Father Joe, and accept his psychic visions for what they are? Scully is the one who struggles and grows the most in the film, and Anderson makes the most of that material with a suitably fraught and emotional performance.

Connolly himself deserves special mention, as he also turns in a strong performance amid a sea of mostly forgettable supporting actors. It's easy for the audience to despise Father Joe as quickly and deeply as Scully does, given his terrible crimes, but Connolly is able to find a warmth and humanity to the character despite all that.

Again, it's easier to look back on The X-Files: I Want to Believe with kinder eyes now that the two revival seasons exist. It's not a great film, but for anyone who simply wants to kick back for an hour-and-a-half and watch Mulder and Scully do their thing while Mark Snow's haunting score plays in the background, it does the trick. Vrach Frankenshteyn does nothing to alter that equation for good or for ill. It's a very minor update that nonetheless serves as a handy excuse to give this sequel another look after all these years.

items.title: Fields of Mistria Review So Far
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
I’m at the point in Fields of Mistria where I’ve started talking to my dragon statue, Caldarus, and telling my pink dog to do chores. If that interests you, even without context, then you probably have a lot to look forward to. Fields of Mistria is the type of farming sim I wish I had in my youth – it resembles early 2000s cozy classics from Harvest Moon to Animal Crossing, all mixed together into an anime-coded concoction. The world of Mistria is brimming with lore and its villagers have distinct personalities that shine through in their dialogue. I can tell I still have a while before I’ve seen everything its newly released 1.0 update has to offer, but I already can’t wait to learn more about my new home and neighbors.

This fantasy farming sim takes place in a pastel pixel art world where mythical creatures and magic exist, but not in a way that dominates the otherwise down to earth tasks that are asked of you. I sometimes forget I’m in a magical world when I’m just farming and talking to villagers, and those humble tasks are plenty amusing as is. However, when I walk into the bathhouse and see a giant witch’s cauldron bubbling in the open, it sets me straight. It feels like a farming sim with a fantasy RPG skin over it – similar to Rune Factory, but less overt – so most of my attention goes to the actual farming loop.

Fields of Mistria about the farming first and foremost, asking you to care for crops, till soil, chop wood, and so on. It’s neat that you can also catch fish and insects and donate them to a local museum like in Animal Crossing, as well play with enticing cooking and crafting systems that I have yet to dig into. While a lot of this might sound fairly standard, you can also improve your capabilities by giving spiritual currency to Caldarus for power-ups, like the ability to sometimes get seeds back when you harvest plants or replenish energy when watering.

I saw these activities as a way to speed toward my goals: to revitalize Mistria and grow my farm. However, I couldn’t rush toward that target immediately, and I’m glad that's the case. I had the urge to start grinding for gold right away, but I was too broke to buy seeds and didn’t have the equipment to clear sticks and rocks from my farm. Instead of having access to all tools and skills from the beginning, I unlocked them one by one, and I appreciated how that forced me to slow down and really take notice of the town and its inhabitants.

Simple quests impress with the little stories that sometimes come with them.

A day in Mistria can last as little as 12 minutes and 30 seconds in real-world time. My average day took at least 20 minutes, though, because I talked to every single person I passed and often paused to flip through menus (inventory, relationship journal, etc). I spent my first few days completing requests for villagers and ended up getting to know many of them, even ones I wasn’t particularly interested in. These requests, which seemed like simple fetch quests at first, impressed me with the little stories that sometimes came with them. Need some lilacs? Well, you may have just signed up to be a lab experiment.

Some farming sims make me feel like I’m watching a performance, where the characters only exist in my personal bubble and don’t do anything outside of that. Fields of Mistria does the opposite. Seeing characters interact based on a shared history with each other made me feel like an actual newcomer who had a lot to learn about the relationships and unique quirks that this town had to offer. I especially appreciated Friday nights at the Sleeping Dragon Inn, which gather every villager into one spot for what feels like the whole day. It’s those moments that convinced me these people actually do talk to each other and have lives when I’m not actively witnessing them.

Their personalities stand out the most. Even for characters who are based on anime stereotypes (like March, who is unapologetically a tsundere), developer NPC Studio finds a way to enhance them through effective dialogue. Even when I’m mad at March because he insinuated that I’m a leech for accepting a free pickaxe from his brother, I can show up to the bar on Friday and he’s suddenly buddy-buddy with me after a few drinks. Meanwhile, the little girl at the inn told me that she would put the local Blackfire lookalike in jail for making stinky potions. Sometimes, their words just make me laugh, and it’s worth mentioning when a game like this actually makes me want to read all the dialogue and not just skip it.

Another interesting quirk: the villagers actually react to you. For example, someone may go out of their way to tell you where to find a particular item for your fetch quest, or mention something that happened in the past. I haven’t seen anything mindboggling yet, but it’s still a nice touch to add immersiveness to the world.

I’ve had more than enough time to know I really like what I’ve seen so far

I do have a few gripes with Fields of Mistria so far, but they are mostly tied to my current progress in the storyline. It can sometimes feel like a chore to run back and forth between my farm, especially when I haven’t upgraded my inventory yet and my tools take up half the space. Also, for some reason, my character will occasionally swap to an awkwardly slow pace while moving. As far as I know, that’s a bug that pops up under uncertain circumstances, and I haven’t found the right sweet spot for my setup yet.

I’ve played a lot of farming sims, even bad ones, for hours. At this point, I have faith that I’m still climbing towards the peak of what Fields of Mistria has to offer, especially since the completion of the Town Repair Storyline and marriage were just added with the 1.0 update. It’s so early that I have yet to fill up a heart for any character, let alone a love interest. And yet, I’ve had more than enough time to know I really like what I’ve seen so far, and I’m eager to keep going until I'm ready for my final review.

items.title: House of the Dragon Season 3 Finale Recap and Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
In King’s Landing, Rhaenyra (Emma D’Arcy) continues to make one unforced error after another. Driven to near hysteria by the news that Aegon (Tom Glynn-Carney) has survived, she exiles one of her more clear-eyed advisers, Mysaria (Sonoya Mizuno) and baffles her subjects, speaking to them about prophecies – occasionally in High Valyrian – when they’re worried about putting food on the table.

More troublingly, she makes a classic Henry II of England error and has the head of her church assassinated in his cathedral. That didn’t go well for Henry, who sparked widespread unrest and had to make significant concessions to the Pope to settle things down, and doesn’t seem likely to go well for Rhaenyra either. Perhaps significantly, Rhaenyra has the generally likeable Alyn (Abubakar Salim) strike the fatal blow. His brother Addam (Clinton Liberty) accused him of being overly ambitious and under Rhaenyra’s thumb; he may have had a point. Rhaenyra is no longer as hesitant as she once was, but fear has also made her vicious. The woman who hisses commands to Alyn in the Sept is not the same one who wrung her hands over violence last season. Something has broken in her; she may no longer be one of the Targaryens capable of greatness.

We also bade farewell this week to Queen Helaena (Phia Saban), who has given one of the most quietly and consistently compelling performances this season as a woman who knows how tragically it’s all going to play out. The manner of her death – she threw herself out a window – was the same as the book, but there are some differences: her youngest son, Maelor, was born before her death on the page, and met his own tragic end. This is less horrible than the murder of an infant might have been, but it’s plenty disturbing. Her final scenes with Rhaenyra are also superbly done: watch how Viserys’ older daughter, when she tries to force Helaena to eat, impatiently puts aside the very tapestry that might have given her the answers she so desperately sought.

At Harrenhal, Aegon arrives on Sunfyre and resolves to work together with his wayward brother Aemond (Ewan Mitchell) for maybe the first time in their lives – albeit not before slapping him around a bit and threatening to kill him for, in fairness, his attempt on Aegon’s life. But Aemond’s obvious guilt and true repentance saves him; the pair set off to find the and take the fight to Rhaenyra. We also learn, by the way, that Alys Rivers (Gayle Rankin) is the former Lady of Harrenhal. She was the wife of Black Harren, its builder, and was cursed to remain in the limits of its lands and never die when she sought dark powers in the forest to save the life of her badly-burned son. Alys’ background was never established fully in the book, so this is a new and potentially pretty potent wrinkle. In fact, Aegon and Aemond’s reconciliation is also new territory, and it’s going to be interesting to see how much trouble that terrible twosome get into as a united front.

The majority of the episode, however, concerns the attack on Tumbleton. Despite the efforts of the late Ser Criston Cole (Fabien Frankel), the Rivermen have arrived en masse and Daemon Targaryen (Matt Smith) has flown down on Caraxes to take command and, oh yes, flame anyone who needs flamed. Ser Gwayne Hightower (Freddie Fox), one of the most likeable characters on the board and therefore probably doomed, tries to make peace by offering the return of the imprisoned Corlys Velaryon (Steve Toussaint), but no dice. He and Daeron (Benjamin Evan Ainsworth) are left trying to survive in the besieged city; it’s not clear by the end of the episode that Daeron is OK.

The Battle of Tumbleton is – at best – a draw for the Blacks, and if it’s a victory for the Greens it might prove to be a Pyrrhic one.

Meanwhile, Ormund is searching desperately for his ace in the hole, the dragonrider Ulf (Tom Bennett), who is so excited about his heel turn that he’s drunk himself into a stupor. Here, Ormund makes an ultimately fatal mistake. He’s so overcome by the stink of the privy where he finally discovers Ulf that he entirely loses his temper and whales on the other man. Ulf still does his bidding long enough to flame half the army of Rivermen – but he then turns his fury, and Silverwing, on Tumbleton itself and Ormund in particular. So long, you prissy little manbaby bully.

Ulf is not the only dragonrider who’s in trouble this week: Hugh (Kieran Bew) also left his post in King’s Landing to look for his wife in Tumbleton, running in with the ground forces, while Baela (Bethany Antonia) is grounded in the Keep after daring to criticise Rhaenyra. As for the episode’s title, there are any number of candidates. Ulf obviously, but Hugh also disobeys orders to go to Tumbleton. Daeron and Gwayne both betray Ormund in attempting to sue for peace; Ormund has arguably betrayed Aegon in elevating Daeron. And Daemon accuses Corlys of treachery when he argues for peace. There’s a lot of it going around.

The end result is shellshocked troops stumbling around a charred battlefield, trying to collect corpses, while Caraxes and Hugh’s Vermithor chase off Ulf’s Silverwing. The Battle of Tumbleton is – at best – a draw for the Blacks, and if it’s a victory for the Greens it might prove to be a Pyrrhic one, what with the loss of Ormund, their best strategist, and the uncertain fate of Ulf and Silverwing afterwards.

At this point it’s a positive disadvantage to have read the books; some of us have been waiting for one face-off for nearly half a decade now, since that could plausibly have happened at the end of Season 1 or the start of Season 2. Now we will have to wait two more years it’s even going to happen as written. The overall shape of the show is also becoming more evident, and something that I wrote about last season seems to be taking shape (read that here if you’re not scared of major spoilers). Whether showrunner Ryan Condal and his team can stick the landing for the finale better than Game of Thrones did remains to be seen, but they have made a great foundation for it this year.

items.title: Asus ROG XReal R1 XR Glasses Review
items.author: Jacqueline Thomas
items.content:
Sometimes it feels like XR glasses are the next frontier when it comes to gaming accessories. And it makes sense, with the rise of handheld gaming PCs – at least before RAM prices started making them nigh unaffordable – these glasses are a great way to get something like the Steam Deck a bigger screen while you’re away from home.

So, it makes sense that Asus would team up with XReal to make a bespoke pair of gaming glasses, especially off the back of the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X. And when the glasses are plugged straight into a handheld, the ROG XReal R1 is awesome, with a clear picture and some nice RGB lighting. But, these glasses cost $849, and at least part of that goes to the dock, which allows you to connect multiple devices through HDMI and DisplayPort. That’s a cool concept, but it ends up being the worst part of the entire package.

Out of all the XR gaming glasses I’ve tried so far, none of them look especially . Just due to the fact that there needs to be displays, mirrors and whatever else built into the glasses themselves, the format lends itself to bulky, garish designs. The ROG XReal R1s are no different.

The little hood that houses the displays measures about an inch thick, which naturally makes the glasses protrude a bit from your face. The outward-facing lenses, then, have this angular design that does look a bit more attractive than something like the Viture Beast, but not by much.

The ROG XReal R1 does hide the little camera that powers head tracking a bit better than most of its contemporaries, though. The entire front of the glasses is one piece of dark plastic, with a small section kind of boxed off in the center. The 3DoF sensor lies in that little boxed off section, and if I didn’t know that these kinds of glasses a camera sensor to function, I wouldn’t have even guessed that it was there.

There are plenty of these kinds of glasses out there that try to at least maintain an air of professionalism. The Viture Beast, for example, prides itself as being great for productivity. But the temples of the ROG XReal R1 are about as ROG as you can get. In the middle of each temple are nine RGB lighting zones, arranged in little diagonal lines. By default they have the standard cycling rainbow effect we’ve all seen a million times, but you can change the lighting by messing with the settings.

Most of the time, you’ll do that through the buttons found on the left temple. On the bottom, you have a button that either centers the screen in your field of view, or opens the settings if you double tap it. Behind that button is what you’d expect to just be a volume rocker, but instead pressing it in either direction will bring up a little menu with which you can adjust things like tint, screen size, and, well, the volume.

The speakers are also in the temples, and they’re fine. They’re loud enough that you’ll be able to clearly hear the game you’re playing, but they’re not great at drowning out everything around. That’ll be fine for most people, but if you really want to get immersed in your game, or you just don’t want people around you to hear what you’re playing or watching, you should probably use some headphones.

I don’t think I’ve ever used a pair of XR glasses where the menu setup was intuitive, and the ROG XReal R1 follows that trend. After fiddling around with it for a couple of hours, everything did kind of click – but there’s a definite learning curve.

Everything changes once you plug the glasses into the dock though. The dock itself looks even more like a generic ROG accessory than the glasses do. It’s essentially a gemstone-shaped hunk of plastic with angular lines engraved into it. Shockingly, though, despite the need for dedicated power in the back of it, there is no RGB. The only lighting to speak of are indicator lights that tell you whether or not connected devices are on.

Above those lights are two triangular buttons and a little control stick. The button on the left is the power, and the triangle on the right turns on fps boost. This essentially lowers the resolution and ups the refresh rate from 120Hz to 240Hz. That sounds cool, but in practice it ended up with a glitchy picture where looking at text instantly gave me a headache.

The little control stick is how you’ll usually mess with the settings. There are shortcuts, where pushing to the right, for example, will switch the glasses between Anchor mode – where the display is held in one space – and Follow mode, where, you guessed it, the display follows you wherever you look. Most of these controls work fine, even though it is easier to use the buttons on the glasses. After all, when you’re using the glasses your vision is going to be a bit obscured, so it’s a bit awkward to try and look at what you’re doing down on your desk.

On the back of the dock, you’ll find two USB-C ports, one of which supplies power, along with two HDMI ports and a DisplayPort. Then, on the front is another USB-C port, which is meant for the glasses themselves.

However, the biggest problem with the dock was that when you push the stick upwards, it’s supposed to toggle between different visual profiles. That’s pretty standard for monitors these days, but for some reason, it simply didn’t work on the unit I reviewed. Even after updating the firmware and trying several different devices, the ROG XReal R1 was stuck on “Racing” mode the entire time I was reviewing it.

That mode didn’t necessarily look but, it’s always a bit of a red flag when a button just doesn’t do what it’s supposed to.

The dock being mediocre would be one thing if it was just an added accessory, but you can’t buy these glasses without it. And given that XReal and Asus are asking $849, when the XReal 1S is just $449 for a pretty similar experience, it does make you wonder how much extra you’re paying for the dock.

By itself, the Asus ROG XReal R1 is a 1080p display with a 120Hz refresh rate that sits on your face. Asus and XReal talk a big game about the actual display too, claiming brightness of up to 700 nits, and that it's 106% of the sRGB color gamut. I can’t actually test that, because the display is too small for a colorimeter. However, at its best, the display is quite colorful, though it is a little washed out and dim most of the time – but that might be the visual profile that the glasses were stuck on.

When the glasses are plugged into something like the Xbox Ally X, they’re pretty solid. Games look great, and XReal has done a lot of work to make text less of a pain to read. However, it’s important to keep in mind that this is still a 1080p display. You can stretch the display out to the equivalent of a 171-inch display, but when you do, the image can start to look a little pixel-y. The sweet spot, then, is having a smaller display in follow mode. That way, you can see the entire display without moving your head, and it’s not so blown up that you start to see the imperfections of the 1080p image.

I spent quite a bit of time laying in bed and replaying Final Fantasy XIII on the Lenovo Legion Go 2 with these glasses, and the game looked great – if a little dated. But one of the cool features on these glasses is an instant 3D mode. For some reason, that just wouldn’t work when plugged into the dock, but when plugged straight into the handheld it used the X1 chip built into the glasses to transform FFXIII into a 3D game.

That wasn’t perfect, obviously, but it kind of made it look like I was playing the game on a very large 3DS. But, because it was strapped to my face, rather than held awkwardly in front of me, the 3D effect didn’t give me a headache as soon as I moved my head a little bit. I don’t know if I’d use the ‘Instant 3D’ mode all the time, but it is a cool little effect that adds, well, another dimension to whichever game you’re playing.

The big selling point of this ROG and XReal crossover, though, is plugging in a gaming PC or console and playing via the dock. After fighting with a firmware update, this worked fine enough. The display doesn’t change all that much when it's plugged into the dock, so it was still a good 1080p image, just with the same weird text shimmer that all XR glasses have right now.

But as soon as I enabled the 240Hz mode, everything went downhill. Motion is smoother with this mode turned on, there’s no doubt about that, but pixels that aren’t supposed to be moving start wiggling around a little bit. There’s this strange shimmer to the glasses when the 240Hz mode is turned on that makes subtitles actually painful to read and makes the rest of the image look downright strange, like static elements of the scene are moving somehow.

This problem goes away as soon as you push the little triangle button to swap the refresh rate back to 120Hz. I’m not sure what’s causing the problem, or even if I’m just particularly sensitive to it, but I’ve used of regular 240Hz monitors without seeing that weird behavior.

It’s just another point against the dock, though. Really, the benefit of the dock is just the ability to easily plug in a gaming PC or a PS5. That’s a neat feature, to be sure, and I loved playing a bit of Beast of Reincarnation on these glasses through my gaming PC. But that’s not worth twice the added cost over the $449 XReal 1S or the $549 Viture Beast.

Jackie Thomas is the Hardware and Buying Guides Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. You can follow her

items.title: Madden NFL 27 Review
items.author: jon Burgess
items.content:
From the first pregame animation I watched, Madden NFL 27 had a presence I haven't felt in this series a while. The expressions of the players, the roar of the crowd, and even the coaching staff on the sidelines felt right, as if I was watching Week 1 six weeks early. That good first impression only grew as I dug into each mode, finding tweaks to the passing game and an improved Franchise mode that make it a noticeable improvement on its predecessor. It's not at Hall of Fame status yet, with some noticeable technical hiccups and an Ultimate Team in need of a shakeup, but Madden 27 is definitely trending in the right direction. EA Sports may be on to something here.

For starters, the reworked passing game is instantly impactful thanks to a new Timing-Based Catch mechanic. After passing the ball to a receiver, when I hold down the catch button, a meter will appear over my receiver's head. If I release the button in the meter's green zone, the receiver gains an advantage over the defender, which usually results in a completed pass. Conversely, if I hold the button too long or release it too quickly, I run the risk of dropping the pass, or worse, deflecting it to a defender.

This is an ingenious system that emphasizes how the quarterback and receiver should work in tandem on every pass play. I've been able to aim my passes and adjust the strength of the throw, but now I can also give my receiver the chance to make a spectacular play with clear and direct inputs, which makes it feel more like I was the one who brought the big catch to fruition. When that meter turns green, and the pass is completed, it's a genuine rush.

However, this new system takes a minute to lock down, as the timing can be very precise. Bullet passes are difficult to land with this method, simply because the ball is coming at the receiver quickly and my window for holding the catch button is smaller. Additionally, in modes like Quick Play where I control both the quarterback throwing the pass and the receiver catching it, it starts to feel like I'm entering fighting game move sequences with all of the button presses and directions that are required.

The new Timing-Based Catch mechanic is an ingenious system.

Thank goodness for the Skills Trainer, then, which returns from last year's game and once again conveniently groups all of Madden 27's changes into one tutorial mode on the main menu, which I can try as many times as I need. This is a great place to work out the timing on both the throws and the catches, along with other changes like a new tackling system that adds Conservative and Dive tackles to the mix, as well as new pass rush moves designed to get past the offensive line and into the quarterback's face.

This year's Madden looks as impressive as ever, with players, coaches, and fans that are closer to the real thing with each passing year. There are still immersion-breaking issues, however, like the time Devonta Smith celebrated a touchdown and the camera was placed inside of his body, or another time when an entire celebration was blocked by what I assume to be a fan's brown pants. Moments like this mostly just made me laugh and immediately moved on, but they still break the authentic NFL feel Madden strives for.

The in-game menus, meanwhile, are some of Madden 27's biggest struggles. Loading times cripple the experience, with even something as simple as "pressing X to proceed" resulting in a noticeable delay. God help you if you press the wrong button in Ultimate Team, especially after opening a pack, as you'll have time for a full sip of your coffee before you can get back to looking at the cards you pulled. The menus are an unavoidable, and highly noticeable, nuisance, and they will inevitably get in the way of your experience at some point.

The marquee change to Madden 27 is the Persona Engine, a new approach to Franchise mode that gives every player on your team motivations, goals, and desires. Pay your top stars well, and they'll be happy; neglect them, and you'll begin to hear words like "trade" and "holdout." Zack Baun, a starting linebacker for my beloved Philadelphia Eagles, was the first to start talking about a new contract, followed by Jalen Carter, and negotiating both was so stressful, I delegated both tasks. It ended up working out, even if the cap hit was more than I expected.

The marquee change to Madden 27 is the Persona Engine.

Another major factor in Franchise mode is training; I can work with individual players in minigames in order to raise their stats. These minigames range from "hey, this is fun," to "hey, this is total BS." Each position offers a range of minigames designed to focus on a particular skill, which makes sense; a lineman will have different priorities than, say, a free safety. This means the team has to cook up six or seven minigames per position, and the strain of that challenge becomes apparent pretty quickly.

Take the Wide Receiver position, for example: one minigame asks me to run around for as long as I can without getting tackled, using padded walls and a rotating obstacle positioned around the field. This is a really fun time, as trying to avoid three defenders barreling down on me by forcing them to get wrecked by the rotating obstacle got some genuine laughs.

But another requires me to evade a defender and catch passes in marked zones, in an attempt to score as many points as possible. This defender is, apparently, the greatest cornerback to ever play the game of football, because he stuck to me like glue and either broke up or straight up picked off the majority of my reps. I get that these are supposed to be challenging, but there's a fine line between "challenge" and "hair-ripping frustration," and some of these minigames inch toward making me more bald than I already am.

I ran into a similar, albeit isolated, incident in Superstar mode. As Jason Fanelli, the standout Temple Owl running back, was participating in the Combine, I was dropped into a few passing drills in order to gauge my performance. I was supposed to catch a pass in the intended zone, but more often than not, the quarterback didn't throw the ball any where near the zone. When I made the catch outside that zone, it counted negatively toward my performance, and I don't quite understand what I could have done better.

That said, once I was drafted by the Pittsburgh Steelers in the second round, Superstar mode became the same fun option I've enjoyed in years past. I like slowly getting mo re playing time as the season progresses, becoming a bigger part of the offense as I improve, and eventually turning into one of the top players on the team. The little vignettes in between, where I speak at press conferences or meet with my agent about sponsorship deals with brands like Oakley (product placement!), are fine enough, but the important part, the on-field stuff, is fun.

Ultimate Team continues to follow a simple pattern: open packs, complete challenges, get more packs, repeat.

Madden Ultimate Team also returns for another season, and of course it would as one of Madden's most popular modes. My Philadelphia Cream Cheeses have become a juggernaut thanks to some choice pack openings, welcoming legendary defender Luke Kuechley, current Eagles star Cooper DeJean, and Madden cover star Caleb Williams to the squad. Williams is even my , so I know I'm doing alright.

However, the MUT experience continues to be distilled into a simple pattern: open packs, complete challenges, get more packs, repeat. I can take my team online against other MUTers, but other than the unique roster I've fostered, it's just the core Madden 27 gameplay again. Granted, "don't fix what isn't broken" certainly applies to a mode that many people enjoy, but after opening pack after pack, it just doesn't stand out from previous years. I'm not sure how you improve on MUT, but it needs something to breathe some fresh air into it.

To its credit, however, the controversial microtransaction push that caused a stir in the College Football 27 community doesn’t make it to the big leagues. I see ads for new MUT packs, of course, but the Cream Cheeses squad I've built so far has been constructed without me spending a single extra dollar, and I'm happy with the results.

items.title: Big Walk Review
items.author: Tom Marks
items.content:
To know something's name is to understand it — at least just a little, be it the thing itself, or the world around it. In Big Walk, there are lots of things yet unnamed. You will certainly recognize trees, mountains, that dang cowbell. But there are plenty of things you won’t: the red, peanut-shaped objects my group calls a bean, which makes the structures they must be delivered to the bean towers. To us, the underground tunnel system is the backrooms, and the glowing medicine balls that light paths throughout the world are simply orbs – but not to be confused with the Big Orb, a mysterious and ominous structure looming in the distance. Big Walk is a co-op-only puzzle adventure that relies heavily on shared experience, shared language. Its genius lies in how it pushes you to decipher the logic behind the clever puzzles spread around its open world in a way that only you and your companions will understand. With all the twists and limitations it imposes, it’s unlike any other multiplayer game out there.

Big Walk is a puzzle game, and the puzzle is communication. Everyone is initially dropped into a playground of sorts with some colorful, blocklike structures to climb on, light switches to flip, and your controls pinned up as posters. I call this place home. Crucially, you are given no objective. We fiddle about with the buttons, obnoxiously clang the cowbell. We test out our movement options – mostly arm gestures – by looking at our shadows. Eventually, we head out into a lifelike world with lush foliage and waves breaking on the beach; it's a direct contrast to our charming, goofy characters, who are, essentially, a stack of three colored balls with googly eyes, stick arms, and twig legs (and a nose that moves like a mouth as we speak in-game).

When someone asked what we're supposed to do, what the objective of this game was, I couldn’t really answer that. And so we walked. But here's what I knew at this point: Big Walk has walking and puzzles. That, and outside of arm flailing or typing out written messages, we can only communicate through proximity-based voice chat. This means your voice is muffled when you're behind a wall, and echoes when you're in a vast tunnel. If someone wanders too far off, I can no longer hear them, and as a game that can only be played with others, it’s “cooperative” in the very sense of the term. There's no way to play Big Walk alone, and it supports up to 12 players with different settings for different sized groups: two, three, or four-plus, which adjusts puzzles slightly to suit the number of people in a session. Big Walk cleverly takes advantage of the essential limitation of proximity chat, and it wouldn't be the same without it.

Venturing out, my group of three walks together along desert terrain and up a cliffside until we find a button on a platform. We originally think nothing happens when it's pushed, but someone notices a faint red light flashing in the distance. It illuminates each time it's pressed, so we send someone in its direction to see what’s out there. There's a red bean in a box, which opens when the button is pushed. He grabs it and rushes back. No one knows what to do with it but it seems important, so we hold onto it (or try our best until someone drops it while falling off a cliff). Through that simple opening task, we start to get it: This puzzle, this bean, they’re teaching us something about the world and what we need to do within it. We're starting to create our own language.

The map is cleverly designed to nudge your group to build something together.

Each piece of this map is cleverly designed to nudge your group to build something together, forms of communication that feel like only you understand. We keep walking, keep exploring and finding puzzles that require real teamwork, and continue to build our language. My group played in several sessions across a few days: a core group of three, with some stragglers jumping in here and there. We spent nearly 20 delightful hours romping around. It's easy for people to jump in and out of the session, popping in to adventure for a bit. There is a kink in this system, though. The save file is tied to the player who originally hosted the game. For my group, that was me. If my companions wanted to play when I wasn't there, they'd have to start a new save file—and a new big walk. This may very well be by design; developer House House wants a group to stick together. But I felt bad when someone wanted to play, but I couldn't.

Big Walk's world runs on a day-night cycle, with sun-soaked days and pitch-dark nights. And in the latter, a different kind of communication is built. Early on, my friend Riley dropped our only flashlight off a cliff, immediately after I accidentally kicked our walkie-talkie down the same one. We spent a not-insignificant amount of time looking for our tools because, without them, we could easily lose each other in the dead of night. (Even more so when looking for Riley, who got stuck in a hole while searching for our gear). Perhaps in another game, losing your tools or falling in a ditch would be frustrating. Not so here. While movement can be finicky at times, and you will briefly get stuck in spots, Big Walk often felt even more impactful when things were going very, very wrong.

We spent plenty of time doing Big Walk's actual puzzles, which are scattered around the map and usually embedded in big, brightly colored structures: a green horror movie house, an orange colosseum, a blue sound stage. Some of them are relatively easy, like throwing an orb into a basketball hoop multiple times, or playing a game of telephone to identify a specific sequence of shapes or buttons to push. But there are mechanical challenges as well, ones that require platforming and precise movement or throws. There's an entertaining puzzle that requires one person to put on a blindfold (which is actually a big, weird gold head that blocks their view) and navigate through an obstacle course. The others then have to yell instructions at them about where to go and what to do; the scariest part of this was figuring out how to time a jump over a gap. These challenges don't necessarily get progressively harder, because you're free to do whichever puzzle in whatever order you discover them. Some are certainly difficult, but never cruelly so. Big Walk always gives you the tools you need to solve them, so there's no danger of a dramatic learning curve.

One particularly inventive puzzle had my friend Chris locked in a soundproof room trying to relay little musical jingles to us so we could match that to stereos playing the corresponding melodies. Another forced us to split up onto three platforms that were pretty far away from each other and correctly time a synchronized button push. There are a couple puzzles with similar ideas, and the problem was often that we only had two walkie-talkies amongst us. So, we used our laser pointer to signify a countdown or our arms to send a silent message. Little by little, we created a sort of body language cipher to help solve matching puzzles and timing-based challenges alike, and it was a thrill to naturally develop our own system of visual cues.

Big Walk's puzzles are always sharp, and always fun.

Each of these puzzles rewards us with another red bean we have to take care of as we bring it back to a bean tower for deposit. Once you've found enough beans for a given tower, you get a special key to unlock something new and helpful: stuff you otherwise couldn't figure out how to operate, like a stalled train or an island-spanning chair lift. And in this progression, Big Walk further embeds the ethos that these discoveries are yours to make.

Big Walk's puzzles are always sharp, and always fun. The use of proximity chat makes the process of solving them feel special in a way I haven’t experienced in a game for a long time. Despite the recent wave of co-op games with an emphasis on hanging out with your friends, it feels so new to play in this particular way, as if we were all physically in this virtual space together. Video games often make us feel like superheroes, like the world revolves around our individual characters. In Big Walk, relationships and language are that superpower. The world doesn't revolve around me, but .

So much of Big Walk's fun is found in the spaces between the puzzles, too. One of my favorite moments was this time Riley and I wandered away from Chris to go gallivanting in nature without care. This would not have been a big deal… if Riley and I did not have both walkie-talkies. Notoriously bad at navigating, we got wildly lost, even more so after we tumbled down the mountains once again. We were lost for nearly an hour, maybe longer. We went to the train to honk its horn. We tried to follow the coastline, then the train line itself, to make our way back to the place where we first realized we'd lost Chris. Then, a flare shot up in the distance. We walked toward the sound and eventually the direction of the green hue the blast gave off. That's where we found him, at a bean puzzle, firing off flares. Eventually, we sent Chris off to follow the curve of the flare and the bean was waiting at the end of it, like a pot of gold at the end of a rainbow. Riley and I certainly couldn't have been trusted to go find it.

I spent a lot of time playing Big Walk over the last week, but I also spent a lot of time thinking about it, and talking about it with the folks I played with. I'm thinking a lot about names, and the power they hold. In the book Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge, and the Teachings of Plants, author and scientist Robin Wall Kimmerer writes that names are how we, as humans, build relationships with each other and "the living world." She muses on what it might be like to know the names of things around you. Kimmerer writes, "I think it would be a little scary and disorienting – like being lost in a foreign city where you can’t read the street signs." Big Walk's opening feels a little bit like that. Its island is not yet a place with which we've built a relationship, or developed a language. The moment you understand this, Big Walk changes. And what a special thing it is to name this world with friends.

items.title: The Last House Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
A chamber piece with no consistency, Louis Leterrier’s The Last House plays tonal hopscotch with reckless abandon. Following a family of four who find themselves suddenly trapped indoors, the movie jumps not just between scenes but entire genres, with a head-spinning edit that makes things move at a million miles an hour while, paradoxically, very little actually happens.

Assisted by voiceover befitting children’s folklore, the story opens with Jason Delgado (Wagner Moura) fishing off the coast of Seattle. Rain bears down as the seemingly glum patriarch laments his sparse catch before heading back to his sprawling suburban home. However, any potential drama offered by Jason’s mood (or environmental commentary, by his spoken lines to no one in particular) is quickly brushed aside when he returns to what seems like a happy marriage to Riley (Greta Lee), with whom he has two kids: an elder son, Graham (Noah Alexander Sosnowski), and a younger daughter, Ruth (Riley Chung).

The strange premise rears its head before long as the family suddenly finds that their doors and windows won’t open and their neighbors are in a similar jam. The details are best discovered while watching The Last House — they involve a sudden downpour and mysterious shapes fluttering in the distance — but the film features no sense of buildup or gradual discovery. Perhaps to move things along, the family’s very first assumption is some supernatural occurrence or lurking evil, though this is just one of many instances where they behave more like plot delivery mechanisms than actual human beings.

The days turn into weeks as the Delgados learn more about their conundrum. The movie begins to resemble something born from COVID lockdowns, then adopts the hues of a survivalist thriller before eventually zig-zagging into something else entirely. However, few dramatic beats are allowed to breathe along the way, making this metamorphosis feel especially awkward. Despite its nearly two-hour runtime (which seems endless on occasion), The Last House feels cut within an inch of its life, moving suddenly and jaggedly between conversations and events.

It’s grating to watch, even before the movie swings in its umpteenth different direction, widening to include Lovecraftian concepts without the requisite, eerie atmosphere. 

More time goes by than you’d expect, which the evolving production design of the family’s home helps track. However, you might not feel these changes intuitively based on how anyone behaves. Moura and Lee are two of their generation’s finest actors, but The Last House turns them into cheap sideshows who burst with anger and melodrama practically at random. It’s a perfect example of how to build bad performances from presumably serviceable footage; both Jason and Riley go from passive to hysterical at the drop of a hat. It’s grating to watch, even before the movie swings in its umpteenth different direction, widening to include Lovecraftian concepts without the requisite, eerie atmosphere.

There’s some heavy-handed moralizing about humanity’s place in this world, but it ends up taking the form of either clunky narration or ethical dilemmas spun from thin air via flashbacks to scenes shown just minutes prior. Leterrier has never been the most interesting storyteller — The Incredible Hulk and Clash of the Titans are hardly vulgar auteur classics — but his previous works have at least held together as coherent mainstream fare. Whether he’s to blame, or it’s the powers that be at Netflix, The Last House feels cobbled together from disparate footage and ideas, resulting in hastily-changing story modes and emotions you can barely track. The individual images all look right, but when strung together, everything feels wrong.

items.title: Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4, Episode 3 Recap and Review - Humor. It Is a Difficult Concept
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Ortegas and Scotty (Melissa Navia and Martin Quinn, respectively) get the spotlight this week, as their long-simmering (well, two-episode long) dislike for one another comes to a head in an attempt at a comedy episode that’s not necessarily , but is at least kind of fun at times thanks to game performances from some of the cast.

With the crew burning the warp core intermix chamber at both ends lately, and a key peace negotiation pending, Captain Pike (Anson Mount) and First Officer Una Chin-Riley (Rebecca Romijn) decide Alpha Shift needs a vacation. So a quick trip is planned to a resort planet where the unique atmosphere causes a type of inebriation for all who land there… and, of course, a lot of silliness too.

Look, Star Trek has been doing comedy episodes practically since the very beginning, and sometimes quite well, but there’s a trick to it. You can’t really make fun of your characters or break the logic of how they fit into the Star Trek world, and I’m afraid that “Human Best Friend” skirts dangerously close to both of those no-nos on occasion.

Again, it’s a fine line. When a sober Ortegas and not-so-sober Scotty visit an apparently wasted Spock (Ethan Peck), he’s still very Spock-like. “I apologize for the mess,” he says as he adjusts a chess piece’s placement on the board by about one centimeter. It’s subtle and one of the funniest moments in all of “Human Best Friend,” but later, when the pair visit Pike as he’s getting a tattoo, it feels like the entire Strange New Worlds universe is cracking around us thanks to Mount’s over-the-top take on an inebriated Pike. It’s like seeing your boss drunk at the office holiday party, or even worse… your dad at a family gathering! Get it together, man.

Yes, I understand that Christopher Pike is capable of getting drunk (or whatever we’re calling this state), and yes, I also understand that he deserves some R&R like anyone else does. I also recognize that Mount is doing a swell job with the performance. But for the captain of the Enterprise to allow himself to be seen in such a state by his crew… I’m sorry. Maybe I’ve just spent too much time with Captain Picard in my life, but that sort of cheap gag breaks the show.

So each character gets their own bit to play: Workaholic Uhura (Celia Rose Gooding), so unwilling to relax, becomes the ultimate relaxer and relaxation host; Una sings Klingon karaoke power ballads; Dr. M’Benga (Babs Olusanmokun) does his best Cocktail impression; La’an (Christina Chong) is in commando mode (again); Chapel (Jess Bush) becomes a win-or-die Bingo player; and so on. Some of these bits are cute, some are a bit eye-rolley, but none really pop.

If the episode works at all, it’s because of Navia and Quinn, who have good chemistry and whose characters actually get to grow a bit through these shenanigans, as they’re forced to work together first to deliver a letter to the captain (“A piece of paper!?” says an amazed Scotty) and then to find their missing shuttle. That the two realize they’ve likely been butting heads because they’re, as Scotty puts it, “not so different after all,” is a nice enough thread for “Human Best Friend,” and sweetly played.

But again, the logic of the episode is flawed. By the time Pike and the crew are trying to fake their way through the negotiations back on the ship while still drunk – negotiations involving a civil war, mind you – it’s pretty clear that Alpha Shift really shoulda called in Beta Shift not just for the negotiations, but for the episode itself.

Questions and Notes from the Q Continuum:

  • Dave Foley is mostly wasted as one of those annoying Star Trek alien salesmen types, but he does get a line or two that are worth a chuckle.
  • I guess Ortegas keeps the gaffer tape handy.
  • We don’t usually hear about duty shifts (Alpha, etc.) on Starfleet ships. No doubt Captain Jellico would be pleased by all the mentions here (while simultaneously disappointed that it’s only a three-shift rotation).
  • The animated sequence in the planet’s advertisement is cute, but did you notice the woman wearing the same outfit that Andrea has on in TOS’ “What Are Little Girls Made of?”
  • So now we know that Scotty has six brothers. And this doesn’t include the at least one sister he has, who will one day have a son – the ill-fated from Wrath of Khan.

items.title: Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls Review
items.author: Aimee Carr
items.content:
It’s a very rare feat when a fighting game manages to tick virtually every box across the board: Excellent fighting mechanics, fantastic teaching tools, great netcode, and both hardcore extras like Replay Takeover alongside more casual treats like a worthwhile story and ancillary modes. Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls is about as close as a game has gotten to checking all of those boxes since Street Fighter 6. This is a gorgeous and innovative fighting game that can appeal to players of all skill levels, with characters that are easy and satisfying to just mash some buttons with, but equally fun to dive deep into and tinker with in the lab. The albatross that used to hang around its neck was the poor performance of the PC version at launch, but thanks to a recent patch that seems to have fixed most of those issues, Tokon is now a recommendation I can make wholeheartedly without any caveats.

Let’s start with the fundamentals: Tokon is a 4v4 tag fighter with a of unique rules that attempt to control the inherent chaos of having eight swappable characters in a single match. For example, all characters on a team share the same lifebar, removing one of the core elements of traditional tag fighting games, which typically let you swap in a fresh fighter so the damaged one can restore health while they sit on the sidelines. It’s a smart adjustment that allows for a much cleaner UI, avoids the pitfall of 4v4 matches that would otherwise run too long, and removes one of the big barriers of entry to any traditional tag fighter: the need to learn multiple characters in order to have a competitive team.

But what’s especially cool is that while you be very strong by knowing how to play just one character, there’s still a ton of value in crafting a well-synergized team. For instance, if you know that your main struggles in a particular match up, like maybe your opponent plays Magneto and you would have trouble against his strong zoning, you could have a better option waiting in the wings. Or maybe you have a character that you really like but have trouble opening opponents up with, like in my case, Blade – you could lead with a more mix-up-heavy character, and once you land the hit, swap to continue the combo and deal more damage than the mix-up character might have been able to get on their own.

What I really love about this system is that you can add new elements to your gameplan piece-by-piece rather than feeling like you need to have everything on lock right from the start. When I first started playing, all I needed to do was get competent with Spider-Man. I learned some high/low mix-up options, some bread and butter combos, got a basic understanding of how to use his web-zip to maneuver around the screen, and I felt ready to start playing against other people online. When I started to feel like I hit the ceiling of what I could do with just Spider-Man, I went back into training mode to learn more about Blade, and was able to add new layers to my gameplan. After that, I added in Magneto as an assist to help me convert more damage off of the low part of my high/low mix-up. Now I’m experimenting with the fourth position to try to find someone else with an assist that adds extra value to my team. This process of being able to start with a small foundation and build upon it is the ideal way to learn a fighting game, and Tokon feels designed specifically for it.

I love that you can add new elements to your gameplan piece-by-piece.

Those assists are where things start to get a little strange. You see, Tokon doesn’t begin as a 4v4 fighter. Instead, every match starts with just two of the characters on each team available, with the remaining fighters needing to be unlocked by either landing a light auto-combo, hitting the opponent with a move near the corner that causes a stage transition or wallsplat, or losing a round. Unlocking these characters is important, because each one increases your overall health and adds another bar to your Assemble meter, which governs the ability to call assists during specific moments.

Tokon has a lot of hyper specific rules surrounding its assists, which leads to a system that can be fairly overwhelming for newcomers – it was certainly a lot to take in for me, even as someone who’s played many tag fighters like Marvel vs Capcom, Dragon Ball FighterZ, 2XKO, and more. Before a match begins, you place your four characters into various positions: Leader, Shooter, Vertical, and Assault. These placements determine what kind of assist is used when you call them out in neutral (meaning when you’re just standing still or walking without pressing a button or blocking). Leader is whoever the current point character is, Shooters will use a projectile, Verticals predictably cover a vertical hit box, and the Assault spot is generally reserved for each character’s most powerful assist.

These neutral assists don’t cost any meter, but if you try to call an assist after landing an attack to pick up a combo or to cover your recovery after a blocked move, you’ll instead get a universal dash-attack assist that costs one bar of the Assemble meter. What’s finicky about this system is that you have to be very precise with your assist call, because if it happens too early (or too late) the assist won’t come out. This extends to the active tag system, which allows you to switch control to your assist character for a brief period while they’re on the screen. It’s very similar to 2XKO, but here it feels much more restrained. In 2XKO, you can basically swap to your assist character at any point, enabling some really tricky mix-up opportunities. Tokon, on the other hand, seems to be much more hesitant to allow these kinds of unrestrained mix-ups. That isn’t to say that you can’t do gnarly things with the active tag system once you lock your opponent down in blockstun, just that the rules that govern the system are a little more rigid than what I’m used to.
