And you know what, that’s probably for a good reason – given how cluttered the screen can get with four characters throwing nonsense out all at once, I think the amount of chaos that Tokon allows is already more than enough. Especially when you’ve got characters like Peni Parker, who takes up a huge portion of the screen can send out a bunch of random drones; Magneto, who can fill the screen with literal garbage that can enhance his attacks; Magik, who can summon fire pillars that cover a fourth of the field. It can be very easy to lose track of what’s going on.

ArcSys has gone above and beyond in making each character feel authentic.

There are some cool nuances to the tag system as well: The raw tag outs have a bit of delay to them, so you can do cool stuff like tag, perform a move during the delay, and when you take control of the incoming character, the previous character’s move will cover your approach without needing to spend a bar of the assemble meter. It’s touches like these that really add that extra layer of depth that makes learning Tokon on a deeper level so much fun.

The characters themselves are Tokon’s greatest strength. We’re no stranger to seeing a lot of these faces in fighting games before, but ArcSystem Works has gone above and beyond in terms of making them feel authentic to their comic book counterparts, while also ensuring they are each a blast to play in their own particular way. Spidey is able to zip all across the stage, baiting anti-airs by hanging and then jumping off his webs; Storm can manipulate the weather to push and pull objects and enemies (or even snatch her opponent in a command grab from half-a-screen away with a gust of wind that pushes her forward); Deadpool is a walking love letter to the FGC with a kit that is almost entirely comprised of memes and special moves from Street Fighter, Mortal Kombat, King of Fighters, Tekken, Guilty Gear, and much, much more.

It’s an impressive roster of 21, and while there are certainly some notable omissions (especially on the X-Men front) and curious inclusions (), the characters who did make the cut do a good job of justifying their spot with very unique playstyles that add something special to the roster. I can’t imagine Green Goblin being at the top of anyone’s list of characters to include in a Marvel fighting game, but he has ended up being one of the most interesting thanks to his unique ability to fight both on and off his glider.

The most delightful surprise about Tokon is that its story mode is actually pretty dang good! It’s broken up into five episodes, with each episode essentially being its own graphic novel centered around one of the five canonical teams of four: The Fighting Avengers, The Unbreakable X-Men, The Amazing Guardians, Samurai Outriders, and Knights of Doom.

The set up for all of this in-fighting between Marvel heroes and anti-heroes (and a few straight up villains) is the same throughout each of the episodes: an otherworldly being known as The Champion has challenged five of the Earth’s mightiest warriors to compete in a tournament, with the winners getting the opportunity to do battle with him – and, should they win, he will grant them any wish they desire. So it’s basically a Marvel version of Mortal Kombat meets Twisted Metal, and while that concept doesn’t win any points for creativity, it does for execution.

The episodes themselves are presented like motion comics, each illustrated by a different famous manga or comic book artist. This gives each story its own distinct art style, and I loved seeing all the different takes on these iconic characters. It’s especially cool as a big anime fan to see famous mangaka like Hiro Mashima of Fairy Tail fame and Betten Court, the creator of My Hero Academia: Vigilantes, each apply their very distinctive art styles to classic Marvel characters like Captain America and Spider-Man.

The most delightful surprise is that the story mode is pretty dang good!

It’s not just the art though, the writing is strong as well. Kieron Gillen, the writer of all five mini-stories, does a great job of tailoring each one to the strengths of the characters involved. The Amazing Guardians focuses on Peter Parker struggling with the need to be a leader and reluctant mentor to Ms. Marvel, while also trying to rein in the added chaos of having a wildcard like Peter Quill on his team. Meanwhile, the Unbreakable X-Men episode deals with the familiar conflict of Storm, Magik, and Wolverine being heroes to a population that reviles them purely because they’re mutants. There’s not a lot of time to explore these themes beyond anything but a surface level, but the fact that there’s at least something to chew on at all is a step in the right direction for fighting game stories.

These episodes aren’t the end of Tokon’s ancillary modes either. There’s a survival mode that challenges you to take on 100 fights against steadily more difficult foes, giving you a variety of stat boosts to choose from as you increase your power level every five rounds. Your progress is saved at those five-round milestones as well, so it isn’t a true survival mode, since you get to restart without losing much progress, but it’s still a nice diversion for people who want another challenge to conquer before taking the fight online.

And then there’s Arcadia Rumble, which is entirely its own beast. It’s almost structured like a fighting game version of the City Trial mode from , in that it’s split up into two phases that alternate for a total of five rounds, with the first phase being all about powering up your characters, and the second phase being about taking your powered up characters and competing against other juiced up fighters. Up to eight players and their customizable avatars roam around Tokon’s gigantic lobby with the goal of collecting stars. Stars can be obtained by beating up other players and knocking them out, participating in limited time events that pop up around the map, or defeating other players in the second phase, which are the traditional 4v4 battles. It’s actually pretty fun, and while I don’t see myself personally spending a ton of time with it beyond what I’ve played for this review, I can definitely see its value as a mode where players of all skill levels can play together and still have a chance to win.

This whole package is rounded out with some of the best teaching tools I’ve seen in a fighting game: General mechanics breakdown with playable lessons, character guides that explain the basics of each kit, practical combo explainers that cover things like how to convert a combo off of a unique skill, and my favorite feature, free-form combo challenges that simply give you a move you need to include in the combo and a damage threshold you need to hit.

I love this much, because it really encourages people to actually experiment and the characters rather than just memorize a string of buttons. The prompts you’re given are often very practical as well, teaching me how I should combo off of Spider-Man’s overhead, or what I should do when I land a hit but don’t have any assemble meter, or what my big cashout combo is when I land a hit and have full resources. Not to mention the excellent training mode, replay searching, replay takeovers, training presets, and so on. It’s everything I could ask for when it comes to learning tools, and Tokon has it all right out of the gate.

PC Performance and Online Play

I’d be remiss not to mention the PC performance woes that many people have had since launch, and even in the beta before it. Personally, I didn’t actually have any notable issues on my rig, but I say that as someone running a GeForce RTX 5090 and AMD Ryzen 9 16-Core processor with 32 GBs of RAM, so I would certainly hope that’s the case.

That said, on several occasions while I was playing online this past weekend, I’d be in a match where everything moved at a fraction of the normal speed. These games always were against other PC players who had green network connections when I accepted the match, and they felt very different from the standard experience of playing someone on a poor connection. My guess is that these opponents were having performance issues, and that those problems were affecting my game even if I wasn’t personally experiencing them.

A post-launch patch has fixed many of the issues that were being reported on PC.

But wait! Good news arrived just as I was finishing up this review: A patch dropped only a few days after release that has seemingly fixed many of the PC issues that were being reported. True enough, since then I haven’t seen any matches like what I just described. I haven’t done a ton of testing myself yet, so I’ll continue to play on PC and will update this review should any issues arise, but it seems like the Tokon team may have managed to narrowly avert disaster.

However, the one minor complaint I do still have regarding online play is the fact that matchmaking has been quite slow considering how many players Tokon has. The speed of getting in and out of matches is the one place Tokon pales in comparison to other modern fighters, which is a bit of a bummer. But since you can mess around in training mode during a queue, it’s at least more time that I get to spend working on my combos, and I certainly need the practice.

items.title: Star Wars: Visions Presents - The Ninth Jedi Season 1 Review
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
This is a spoiler-free review of all eight episodes of Star Wars: Visions Presents - The Ninth Jedi. The entire series is live now on Disney+ and Hulu.

The Star Wars franchise is definitely in a bit of a slump lately. The Sequel Trilogy ended poorly, and Lucasfilm is still in the process of figuring out how to move forward in that era. Meanwhile, the mediocre performance of The Mandalorian and Grogu shows that even that once dependable pillar of the franchise is hemorrhaging support. But one thing fans can generally count on is that Star Wars will always deliver when it comes to new animated projects. Star Wars: Visions Presents - The Ninth Jedi does nothing to change that fact.

As the title implies, The Ninth Jedi is a spinoff of the two short films included in Seasons 1 and 3 of the Star Wars: Visions anthology series. As such, it's best to watch those first and get a feel for this futuristic setting and cast of characters before diving into the new series. Building on those shorts, this new series follows up-and-coming Jedi Lah Kara (Chinatsu Akasaki/Kimiko Glenn) and her allies as they search for Kara's father, Lah Zhima (Shin-ichiro Miki/Simu Liu), and battle the tyrannical Nawaam (Nao Omori/Young Mazino).

The core appeal of The Ninth Jedi is and always has been the blank canvas it offers. Many argue the best thing Lucasfilm can do for the franchise in its currently troubled state is to carve out a new storytelling era completely free of the baggage that is the Skywalker Saga. Well, that's precisely what you get with The Ninth Jedi. The series is set centuries after the films, establishing a completely new blank canvas on which to paint.

Mind you, the picture it paints isn't always that dramatically different from what's come before. Despite the massive time jump, this is a series that deals in a lot of familiar elements. You have the wide-eyed neophyte Jedi coming of age under the watchful eyes of a grizzled Jedi Master. You have a galaxy plagued by war after the Jedi have been all but wiped out. You have an evil empire that trades in planet-destroying super-weapons and is ruled by a foreboding, lightsaber-wielding villain in black armor.

The Ninth Jedi walks a fine line between celebrating the tropes of the franchise and becoming bogged down by them. Early on, the series tends to fall on the wrong side of that divide. It gets off to a fairly sluggish start in the early episodes, which tend to highlight just how little has really changed in this galaxy after all this time. If you took umbrage with the Sequels and the idea that the ending of Return of the Jedi wasn't a permanent victory over evil but merely a temporary reprieve in a neverending conflict, you may have a similarly hard time swallowing what this series has to offer.

But, eventually, The Ninth Jedi does find its groove, and with it, opportunities to take advantage of this wide-open new era. The show builds steam as it pivots away from simply focusing on the ragtag rebels fighting the evil empire and more into the motivations of figures like Zhima and Nawaam. With time, they become more than simply recycled archetypes, but fascinating characters with their own, unique views on the Force and the dichotomy between Light and Dark. Kara herself develops into a compelling protagonist whose journey doesn't simply mirror that of Luke and Rey Skywalker. One caveat, though - definitely watch the show in subtitled Japanese language form, as the English dubbed voices are mostly flat and bland by comparison.

Technically, The Ninth Jedi is a non-canon series (not that this distinction matters much when the setting is so far removed from the rest of the franchise). Regardless, it manages to hit on and develop some of the same ideas and themes that have been slowly percolating in other contemporary Star Wars projects. There's the notion of democratizing the Force. Here, being a Jedi is less a question of innate ability than courage and a willingness to fight in defense of others. There's also the concept of lightsaber blades changing colors and serving as a window into the wielder's psychology and moral compass.

Most interestingly, The Ninth Jedi dabbles with the concept of Gray Jedi in a more direct way than we've seen anywhere else in the Disney Star Wars era. In that sense, the lack of canonicity may actually be a boon, because it gives the writers and animators room to dig into an idea that the Lucasfilm Story Group still seems hesitant to embrace. This series is very interested in exploring that struggle to achieve a state of enlightenment beyond good or evil. There's power in embracing both the Light Side and Dark Side together. But is that the true endgame for a Force user? Is pure detachment a desirable state, or must it be tempered with compassion? All of these questions are explored over the course of the season. For a show that initially starts out on such familiar turf, it's satisfying to discover that The Ninth Jedi has so much on its mind.

And even when the show is at its most predictable, it does have the benefit of not looking like any of Lucasfilm's more traditional Star Wars projects. The Ninth Jedi is once again animated by Production I.G, and they bring a very distinct look and feel to the franchise. The ships and droids are very different. The general vibe is more purely fantasy-oriented. Heck, there's an entire group of characters that are basically Tolkien-style dwarf space miners. Compare this to something like the MMORPG Star Wars: The Old Republic, where many of the character and ship designs feel right out of the movies despite the game being set thousands of years beforehand. This fresh take is greatly appreciated.

It's also worth pointing out how much the score adds to the whole endeavor. Composers Nobuko Toda & Kazuma Jinnouchi manage to capture the majesty and scope of the classic John Williams music without actually recycling any of Williams' leitmotifs. The music is both fresh and unique and deeply Star Wars-y, which is ultimately a solid metaphor for the show as a whole.

items.title: X-Men '97 Season 2, Episode 8 Review & Recap: "Dead Man's Hand"
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for X-Men '97 Season 2, Episode 8!

I have to wonder if it was the smartest idea for the X-Men '97 crew to telegraph the resurrection of Gambit (A.J. LoCascio). At the time, that stinger scene was a great way to cap off Season 1 and tease what was to come. But now that we've finally arrived at Season 2, is having that knowledge working against the show as it actually brings Gambit back into play? All I can say for sure is that something is missing in Episode 8. Gambit's resurrection doesn't pack quite the emotional punch his death did back in 2024.

Maybe part of the problem is that we don't get a great sense of what Apocalypse's (Ross Marquand) larger goals are here. The obvious assumption was that he was assembling his latest and greatest team of Horsemen with which to dominate the world, and Gambit was his Death. But there's no indication that En Sabah Nur has been gathering other minions. He simply revived Gambit and then turned into a desiccated monkey corpse for some reason. I suppose we're meant to assume his spirit now resides within Gambit? Whatever the case, now back among the living, that simply leaves Gambit to assemble his old posse of thieves and assassins and do... whatever it is Apocalypse wanted him to do.

Part of that seems to involve punishing Candra, the X-Ternal to whom the two guilds have been paying their tithes for all these years. In what is easily the most disappointing element of Episode 8, we learn that Apocalypse and Candra were former lovers, and the latter stole a piece of his power before forsaking him. That all of this backstory is conveyed through a brief, matter-of-fact flashback sequence does this episode no favors at all. The Apocalypse/Candra dynamic needed to be a lot more fleshed out than it is, particularly with the previous foreshadowing in Episode 4.

Not to mention that, if the series really wants to dig into the concept of Apocalypse having a long-lost lover, the character Genesis holds far more storytelling potential. We can only hope this show sticks around long enough to tackle a proper House of X/Krakoa adaptation.

None of this is to say that Episode 8 doesn't sink its emotional hooks at times. While the long-awaited reunion between Rogue (Lenore Zann) and Gambit isn't quite what I hoped for, the two characters do have some strong scenes together. Rogue's opening nightmare is a strong start to the episode, and her entrance into Gambit and Xavier's (Marquand) psychic battle also stands out as one of the better moments of the episode. But again, too often throughout "Dead Man's Hand," I was left with the feeling that something is missing.

It's telling that I wound up finding more weight in the Summers family drama than Gambit's return. Episode 8 makes the most of the fleeting alliance between the X-Men and Cable's (Chris Potter) team, along with all the awkwardness that comes from father and mother being reunited with their now much older son. That plays right into Cable's more ruthless nature and his struggle to still be the man his parents (briefly) raised him to be. The Summers family tree is so stupid and so convoluted, but somehow this series makes us care about all of it.

It's also fun seeing the X-Men fully reunited after spending nearly all the season split into different camps. There's a small part of my fanboy brain that dislikes seeing the team simultaneously decked out in a mixture of classic '80s costumes and more modern New X-Men suits, but I'll allow it. In what is definitely the highlight of Episode 8, we see the combined might of the X-Men and X-Force take on Gambit's forces, only to get absolutely wrecked by Nightcrawler (Adrian Hough). It's a blast seeing what happens when this normally benevolent hero finally cuts loose.

"Dead Man's Hand" certainly has its moments, but this episode doesn't come together as well as I would've liked. And that's a little worrisome now that we only have one chapter left in Season 2. The show has an awful lot of ground to cover in terms of reestablishing Apocalypse in the present and orchestrating this final showdown between rival mutant teams. As strong as Season 2 has generally been, it would be a huge shame for it to collapse at the finish line.

items.title: Ted Lasso Season 4 Premiere Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Three years after a Season 3 finale that sure did feel like a finale at the time, Ted Lasso is back for a fourth season after all. In the modern streaming world, it’s become far too typical for a three-year gap between seasons to become something of a norm. At least Ted Lasso is accounting for this prolonged break in a bigger way, with a semi-reboot approach that feels more akin to a show being revived 10-15 years later rather than one we last saw the same year Oppenheimer was in movie theaters.

The third season ended with Ted (Jason Sudeikis) returning home to America and realizing it was time to stop being the semi-deadbeat dad he’d become, given his young son was back in Kansas City while Ted had been overseas coaching AFC Richmond. Season 4’s premiere is notable, because it’s actually entirely set in Kansas City. Ted is surprised when Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham), Leslie (Jeremy Swift), and Keeley (Juno Temple) show up on his doorstep, hoping to recruit him to return to London to coach the new AFC Richmond women’s division team.

The premiere was shot on location in Kansas City, giving it a markedly different visual landscape than your typical Ted Lasso episode, and it makes the most of it. And there’s plenty of comic mileage drawn from making Rebecca, Leslie, and Keeley the fish out of water for once, as they take in these new sights and sounds. The cast all slip very comfortably back into their characters, whether it be the sweet and funny sisterly connection Waddingham and Temple exude, or the lovably dorky demeanor of Swift’s Leslie.

As for the title character, series co-creator and EP Sudeikis still wears the smile and stache of Ted like he was born for it. Ted’s gotten through the mental health issues that plagued him early on, but we find him at a restless point of his life, working as an assistant manager at a supermarket. He’s still maintaining his usual sunny disposition, but clearly without a true sense of fulfillment. Of course, there’s not a lot of dramatic tension as to whether he’ll accept the offer to coach again — there’s a whole season’s worth of episodes to fill, and we’ve seen the trailers — but the premiere does a solid job of showing how Ted gets to the point where he can admit that’s what he wants to do.

Pushing things on the credibility side though is how the premiere deals with the fact that Ted not only wouldn’t want to leave his son Henry (now played by Grant Feely) again, but wouldn’t want to ask to separate Henry from his mother, Ted’s ex-wife Michelle (Andrea Anders). The solution feels far too easy and convenient, awkwardly handwaving what would likely be a very difficult conversation in real life.

Given the nature of the premiere and how focused it is — no other series regulars appear beyond the four mentioned above, and we never actually see London — it’s hard to be sure how much it will reflect the remainder of the season. But the approach it takes is promising as far as its willingness to lock in on just a few characters and interconnected situations.

While Ted Lasso never lost its kindhearted center, Season 3 was notably overindulgent and often felt lacking in form after EP/co-creator Bill Lawrence stepped back as showrunner. This was demonstrated by its incredibly overlong episode runtimes, which frequently hit a full hour or more in the midst of a show that began with half-hour installments. The amount of subplots and side stories got out of control to the point that we somehow were following the inner workings of two different restaurants at one point on a series that was meant to be about a soccer team.

The premiere does give hope that Sudeikis and new co-showrunner Jack Burditt have learned that less can be more. 

As we prep to meet AFC Richmond's women's team, it’s definitely going to be odd adjusting to saying goodbye to the entire team we’ve spent the last three seasons invested in, and I do worry that it will feel even more difficult to move on thanks to the show still being set in the same location as before with most of the same support staff in place. It likely would have been an easier transition to send Ted and a few key players to an all new part of the world for a cleaner break from what came before, but even as we prep for these big changes, the premiere does give hope that Sudeikis and new co-showrunner Jack Burditt have learned that less can be more. Ted Lasso needed to feel more reined in again… albeit with a 47-minute runtime. Hey, that’s still short by Season 3’s standards! And while we have yet to meet the new team, the prospect of returning to the Season 1 feel of Ted and his team getting to know each other and once more starting from a true underdog perspective is a welcome one.

items.title: Motorola Razr Fold Review
items.author: Bo Moore
items.content:
The Motorola Razr Fold takes the Razr family to a new dimension. While earlier foldables from Motorola followed in the footsteps of the original Razr, offering a flip-phone style footprint, the Razr Fold opts for a hotdog fold, akin to what Samsung has offered from its Galaxy Z Fold lineup. Motorola hasn’t taken generations of iterations on this design to get to a very solid point, though. The Razr Fold is impressively thin and looks like all the experience gained from the earlier Razr foldables is paying off big. At $1,899, it’s not a cheap option, but it may still have what it takes to earn your money or at least due consideration.

Motorola Razr Fold – Design and Features

As mentioned, the Razr Fold opens like a book rather than an old school flip phone. Where Samsung’s early folders were normal-size while open and double the thickness of a typical smartphone while closed, the Razr Fold has jumped straight to ultra-thin dimensions.

Closed up, it looks almost like any other smartphone, and it’s a pretty one with a textured, rubberized back. It’s a little thicker than most, and the camera bump adds quite a bit of depth (that’ll prove worthwhile), but it doesn’t feel unusually large. Unfolded, it becomes impressively thin at 0.19 inches to edge out even the or – camera bumps aside. The hints that it’s a foldable are the asymmetry and the seem running around the perimeter of the phone. It a bit on the heavy side at 8.6 ounces, but that’s not so crazy next to the 8 ounce .

Folded shut, the 21:9 exterior display is a large 6.6-inch, 1080x2520 panel, and it opens up to reveal an even larger, nearly square 8.1-inch, 2232x2484 internal display. Both screens are sharp and bright LTPO pOLED displays with the internal reaching 120Hz and the external hitting 165Hz. For ultra-wide cinema, the external display will probably be the one to go with, and then it won’t really stand out from the crowd of bigger flagship phone displays. But for the wealth of 16:9 content out there (or even squarer formats like 4:3 or ), the internal display can provide a larger surface for viewing than the competition. That inner seam where the phone folds remains a minor nuisance. It shows glare readily, and it’s all the more apparent when displaying dark content or viewed at an off angle. You can also easily feel it when swiping across. That said, when the screen is lit up and you face it head-on, the seam mostly vanishes.

Either way, both screens can look gorgeous in the right conditions, and even though they love to show finger oils and glare on the interior folding seam is apparent, they push out enough brightness to easily get past that glare. You won’t want to treat the two displays the same, though. The exterior has Gorilla Glass Ceramic 3 that should withstand drops and scrapes a lot better than the internal display’s Ultra Thin Glass.

While you’ll want to be gentle with the phone, it’s still tougher than early foldables. It has an IP49 rating to keep a good deal of dust and debris out (just don’t fold it closed with a bunch of crud inside. It can also withstand submersion in freshwater and water jets.

It’s truly a shame we as a body of consumers let smartphone makers get away with killing the microSD card slot, because the Razr Fold likely could have had one. The SIM try in the phone is extra long, with easily enough space to accommodate two SIMs or a SIM and a microSD card, yet it only holds one SIM card. I might have accepted space constraints as an excuse if the SIM tray didn’t just have dead space built in.

Motorola includes facial recognition for sign-in. It also has a fingerprint scanner built into the power button, which makes it conveniently accessible whether using the phone folded open or closed.

Motorola has a bonus for creatives and handwriting enthusiasts. The Razr Fold supports a pressure-sensitive active stylus, and it worked quite well in my brief testing with it. I’d be careful about pushing too hard on the internal display, though. It’s also an accessory (i.e., even more money out of your pocket), and it doesn’t attach to the phone or charge from it either. It has its own separate charging sleeve that it inserts into for storage and recharging.

The speakers on the Razr Fold are decent, offering loud stereo sound that’s a decent match for the display.

Motorola has fitted a 5Gbps USB-C port with DisplayPort 1.2 output, letting the Razr Fold connect to an external display and work as something of a portable computer.

Motorola Razr Fold – Software

The Razr Fold is pricey, so it’s good to see that Motorola isn’t holding back on long-term support. The company is promising seven years of Android OS and security updates, which helps keep it competitive with Samsung and Google on those fronts.

The software itself is a tame implementation of Android. The phone came running Android 16, and it’s not heavy handed about AI features or bloated with unwanted software, though there is a button dedicated to recording notes, making images and quickly tapping into other AI features. The OS is fairly flexible with customization as well. I found the default quick setting buttons a little large, but the OS let me shrink some of them down. I could also go from a 4x6 home screen app grid to a 5x7 to get more apps just a tap away.

Motorola Razr Fold – Gaming and Performance

The Razr Fold doesn’t feature Qualcomm’s top-of-the-line chip, but it comes close with the Snapdragon 8 Gen 5, which gets 16GB of memory and 512GB of storage. This is a chip I saw in the , which mustered solid performance, and though the Razr Fold is wielding this chip in a much thinner chassis, it nearly keeps up. It’s not quite up to or speeds, but it’s no slouch. The sustain is also impressive.

The phone performed surprisingly well for how thin it is. I played over a half hour of Neverness to Everness with the graphics settings at their max cinematic level, and though there was the occasional stutter, the game generally ran smoothly at 60FPS. At the end of my session, the phone wasn't even noticeably warm. It even managed 70% consistency in 3DMark’s Steel Nomad Light stress test.

The Razr Fold’s performance is enough to rival the and even the new despite the latter’s more advanced Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip. In my colleague Jackie’s review, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra could struggle under sustained loads. It started the Steel Nomad Light stress test with a high score of 1641 and sank down to 1,296 by the end of the 20-run gauntlet. That may have been more stable technically, but the Razr Fold started out higher at 2289 and finished with a low of 1600 points. It had also settled into a groove after 5 runs, so it seemed unlikely to ever sink as low as Samsung’s fold in the test.

The fact that Jackie found the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra uncomfortably warm to the touch after gaming while the Razr Fold was chilling puts the Razr in a great position to be the better gaming device.

The phone has a sizable 6,000mAh battery despite its thinness, and it’s even willing to take some pretty fast charging. It can juice back up at 80W from a wired connection of 50W from a wireless one. Sadly, even with some magnetism going on at the back of the phone, it doesn’t support Qi2. While battery life can vary dramatically from person to person, I was easily able to get through the day even while squeezing in some time gaming on the big screen.

Motorola Razr Fold – Cameras

Motorola didn’t skimp on the cameras included in the Razr Fold. It decked out the rear with a triple-sensor setup to rival Samsung, OnePlus, and Google, and it even has a couple of sharp selfie shooters. Here’s a quick rundown of what’s on deck:

  • 50MP wide, f/1.6, 2.44-micron, 1/1.28”, OIS
  • 50MP ultrawide, f/2.0, 1.28-micron, 1/2.76”
  • 50MP telephoto, 3x optical zoom, f/2.4, 1.6-micron, 1/1.95, OIS
  • 20MP exterior selfie, f/2.4, 1.22-micron, 90-degree FOV
  • 32MP interior selfie, f/2.4, 1.28-micron, 88.5-degree FOV

I can’t say that the camera system is faultless, as it occasionally exhibits some oversharpening on the telephoto sensor, and it can get a bit soft and noisy in dimmer settings, but beyond those fairly common faults, it is excellent.

The cameras blend together well, matching one another’s color and dynamic range for a great consistency between shots. The sensors capture vivid color, bringing life to nature shots and street scenes alike. The cameras also snap sharp photos for loads of detail even when zooming in on them a bit. It’s just a bonus that the internal display’s squarer aspect ratio is all the better for previewing and reviewing the 3:2 photos that cameras will take.

The zoom is actually exceedingly strong. Though it has just a 3x optical, the 50MP sensor is happy to keep cropping in a bit further, and it has some impressive results. I could snap photos of details well beyond what I could see with my own eyes.

The sensors also do a great job handling macro shots, letting me get much closer to small subjects than I’m used to. The selfie sensors are no slouches either, snapping crisp photos with natural exposure. All of this combines to make the Razr Fold a rather excellent all around shooter for big and small subjects near and far.

The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra may have added in some higher-end cameras for this generation, but it will likely have its work cut out for it beating the Razr Fold. Motorola included a bigger, higher-res telephoto sensor than the Z Fold 8 Ultra’s 10 megapixels, and the main sensor here may be lower resolution, but it’s offering a slightly wider aperture, bigger sensor, and bigger pixels.

items.title: Ice Cream Man Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Eli Roth is no stranger to violence. Over the course of his career, from directing unrelentingly gruesome films like and the darkly fun yet forgettable recent to playing a brief yet memorable part in , he’s made blood and viscera the materials with which he paints. Sometimes, this has yielded results you can’t help but be begrudgingly captivated by, where the more the blood runs, the more you can’t bring yourself to look away. Still, in many other cases (looking at you, and ), it’s felt like Roth was shamelessly lifting ideas from older, far better movies without adding anything new. Rather than feeling like homage, they’re closer to poor imitation. Instead of being remotely horrifying, the scariest thing about a growing number of Roth’s films — when they aren’t outright disasters like the baffling — is how derivative they are.

Such is the case with Ice Cream Man, Roth’s first film directed under his company, The Horror Section. Not to be confused with the 1995 horror movie of the same name starring Clint Howard, this is a film about the dangers of consuming too much ice cream that itself feels like it’s gobbled up too many past horror films and puked them out. However, what’s strange this time around is how his latest is not just indebted to horror of the distant past, but recent genre hits like the series and Zach Cregger’s . It’s once more not nearly as good as either of those, lacking the chaotic madness of Art the Clown in its killer and the more haunting yet humorous patience with which Cregger approached his stellar horror film. Instead, it’s just a sporadic smashing together of both of them, bringing together murderous kids trapped in a trance of some kind, and a silent though far less entertainingly expressive killer pulling their strings. The primary difference? The reason for the kids becoming murderous involves eating ice cream.

Credit where credit is due: This is not the worst premise on paper, and even sounds like it could be the start of a more campy, cheeky horror romp. Unfortunately, Roth never makes the most of this potential, resulting in a film that’s really cheap and less than clever. This cheapness extends both to the way it all looks as well as the way it’s constructed. From the opening moments surrounding a baseball game that will soon be the last any in this town ever play, it feels like you’re watching a YouTube sketch rather than an immersive horror film. There isn’t any richness or texture to the images, most of the scenes are bizarrely overlit, and lines of dialogue feel painfully cringeworthy in a way that only seems half intentional. The more that it goes on, the more the whole thing proves inescapably awkward and stiff rather than playfully unhinged. Even when a character later gets their cranium removed so that their brain can be scooped out and fed back to them, it elicits little more than a shrug. It’s a movie that inflicts plenty of head trauma but ultimately reveals itself as having no real brains of its own.

At the core of it all is young Jared (Charlie Zeltzer), who — despite being lactose intolerant — will still be tormented by the titular Ice Cream Man (Ari Millen) after he unleashes what is essentially a curse on the otherwise peaceful Bayleen Bay. There’s a vaguely Stephen King-esque feel to the town, but we quickly realize how limited in scope it all is. Rather than feel like a real place populated by memorable characters or with interesting environments for the horror to play out in, it’s all rather unimaginative and just about getting to the next burst of violence, which often does prove genuinely gruesome. Parents are murdered in their beds by their children, the school becomes a site of bloody violence, and the town is revealed as having a darker side that the community has (futilely) tried to keep hidden. Some of this is sufficiently preposterous, with kills involving microscopes, a ladder, and even a Segway all bringing plenty of blood to the table.

That’s where the film seems to be attempting to be more like Terrifier, but where that movie — for all its flaws and own budgetary limitations — boasted great performances in lead Lauren LaVera and David Howard Thornton as Art himself, as well as a real sense of go-for-broke mania, there’s nothing here that brings the necessary energy to make this ride come alive. Instead, we get Roth himself playing Jared’s father and delivering lines like, “Dare I say, he gives me the chills,” in reference to the Ice Cream Man, which repeatedly fall flat. Were the film more playful throughout, maybe moments like this could work; instead, this line lands awkwardly and is followed by one of the most truly strange dubbed lines you’ll ever hear when Roth’s character turns away. It’s all more amateurish than it is darkly absurd, giving you a “we have Terrifier at home” feeling.

The Ice Cream Man is no Art the Clown or Aunt Gladys, and Roth is no horror auteur.

Most disappointingly, when it comes to what this horror film attempts to serve up, there just isn’t that much to chew on. It’s never quite creatively ridiculous enough to go off the rails, and the scenes where we’re spoon-fed mounds of rather unnecessary exposition grind everything to a halt. Where the grim pleasures to be found in Weapons were balanced by a creeping sense of dread, Roth’s Ice Cream Man doesn’t earn either. It occasionally gestures towards playing around with some animated sequences, only for those to fall by the wayside. For all it throws at the wall to see what sticks, the surface stays pretty bare. Despite running less than 90 minutes, you will feel the length; a sudden swerve to dive into the backstory of its killer just results in a dreary drawn-out explanation.

In the end, despite how desperately it attempts to replicate what’s been done better elsewhere, the Ice Cream Man is no Art the Clown or Aunt Gladys, and Roth is no horror auteur. Where Weapons was restrained before ending with a bang, providing a dark cherry on top with one of the most satisfying yet sinister endings of recent memory, this film fails to build in any entertaining way and just leaves you with a sense of emptiness. The only real revelation that you come away with is that you could probably entirely skip this meal, including the dessert that is supposedly so important, and not miss much. You won’t be screaming in either joy or fear, but you open your mouth to yawn.

items.title: Beast of Reincarnation Review
items.author: Aimee Carr
items.content:
Like an above-ground swimming pool, Beast of Reincarnation is one of those things that feels like it should be great in theory, but leaves something to be desired once you actually spend some time in it. On a surface level, everything from the aesthetics and otherworldly apocalyptic setting to the battles against giant, diseased creatures has the makings of something really special. In practice though, this awesome collection of ideas only rarely approaches realizing that potential, as nearly every aspect proves to be quite shallow. Combat against both minion enemies and bosses alike is extremely one-note, the story succeeds much more at collecting tropes than evoking any kind of emotion, and there’s an overreliance on indistinguishable areas and enemies throughout the adventure. There’s still a decent action RPG in here somewhere, because when it occasionally does shine with a neat wrinkle in the story or a particularly cool fight sequence, it’s very easy to see how this could have been every bit as awesome as it looks at first glance, but highlights like those are certainly the exception to an action game that’s largely just okay.

Combining elements of a soulslike with a more traditional JRPG, this fast-paced action game feels like what you might end up with if you tried to combine Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice with the Final Fantasy VII Remake. Across the roughly 35-hour campaign, you’ll split your time between exploring levels of ruined buildings reclaimed by wildlife, parrying and dodging in tense combat encounters, and learning about the convoluted backstory of the world and characters that surround your protagonist, Emma. There’s loads of potential in that formula, and in its best moments, Beast of Reincarnation is both beautiful to look at and incredibly badass, as your katana-wielding elemental mage absolutely overloads the screen with over-the-top melee attacks, sending bolts of lightning and fire flying every which way to complement the artful swordsmanship.

That potential is only realized every once in a while though, as you’ll spend a lot of your time fighting the same handful of enemies far too often, plowing through even the most daunting encounters without much friction due to incredibly forgiving parry windows, and quickly mastering every opponent you come across owing to the fact that they all have just two or three attacks they repeat ad nauseum. Conceptually, ninja-dueling your way through this beautiful, destroyed world and its massive monsters should be sick as hell, but it only takes a couple hours for it all to feel quite skin deep, like how in its opening chapter you’re forced to fight the same giant elk boss multiple times, as it assails you with the one attack it seem to know over and over again in a fight that lasts much longer than it should.

There are still plenty of memorable moments sprout up every now and then, like one level where you’re scaling the inside of a creepy, rotating cube machine and fighting against the forgotten experiments left in the creepy structure, but most of your time will be spent in forgettable regions filled with the same robotic baddies, concluding in a boss fight against a creature you’ve already seen (and is in many cases just a larger version of an existing bestial enemy).

One aspect of combat that fares much better is the addition of Koo, your dire wolf companion, who battles alongside you with an arsenal of increasingly destructive magical abilities. Koo mostly does his own thing, but his behaviors and abilities can be customized and upgraded as you go, and it's important to build him up accordingly since he becomes a vital part of getting through some of the larger combat sequences much faster. He can also be controlled directly, as you pause time to select a special ability for him to use Final Fantasy VII Remake-style – you can even command him to assassinate enemies on your behalf, which really helps speed up some of those repetitive combat encounters and can burn through large chunks of a boss’ health bar as well. Plus, Koo is inexplicably one of the strongest characters, despite being a four-legged pooch with no dialogue. His high energy and unusually expressive face serves as a counterweight to the robotic mannerisms of the majority of the bipedal cast.

The paper-thin depth of Beast of Reincarnation only grows the longer you play.

Despite Koo’s best efforts though, the paper-thin depth of Beast of Reincarnation only grows the longer you play. Exploring the mostly-linear regions is beautiful and features some truly awesome music, but after just two levels I already felt overly familiar with the extremely monotonous checklist of loot to collect and camp sites to unlock before fighting the boss (almost always twice for some reason), then moving on to do it all again. That formula doesn’t evolve as you progress through levels either, as you only ever unlock new abilities to help you power through combat while exploration and platforming never gain any new tricks. Meanwhile, most of the combat pits you against sword-wielding automatons who have maybe one or two different attacks between them, which means you’ll be parrying and countering the same set of telegraphed attacks a dozen times in a single combat encounter.

Even things like the music (which again, is quite good), becomes stale as you quickly discover they’ve got one whole song playing on a loop for more than ten hours worth of levels. Emma, on the other hand, gains access to a bunch of passive abilities that buff her generally, and a bunch of special arts that unlock new moves and attack combos in combat. Most of this stuff does very little to make fighting feel better, as you’re still going up against enemies that just spam the same attacks for you to parry before countering with an attack of your own. They do help those fights go by much quicker, however, and eventually you’ll be able to take out a handful of enemies all at once with some seriously cool-looking attacks.

RPG mechanics don’t fare much better, as the shallow upgrades available for upgrading your katanas, ranged weapons, and accessories are fairly limited. For example, you’ll find new katanas on a regular basis, but even by the end of the story, you won’t come across any that are definitively better or have incentives to support a specific playstyle than those you found early on. So, you have little motivation to upgrade them except to diversify the special effects and status ailments various weapons offer. Skill trees, on the other hand, fare much better as Koo unlocks a whole host of abilities that blast enemies with tons of high-DPS spells and layer on status effects that do things like bind an enemy in place with magical plant vines.

Boss fights are especially disappointing, because they feel like they should be the major draw here, but instead only serve to magnify combat’s shortcomings (quite literally) as you fight a massive beast whose imposing presence is wasted on them being incredibly thoughtless adversaries who often repeat the same slow-moving attack twenty times in row. Bizarrely, you’re usually made to fight these creatures once partway through a level, only to face them again with zero changes at the level’s conclusion, before they transform into an even cooler-looking final phase that…attacks with an almost identical moveset. Worse yet, in the second half of the adventure, it seems to straight up run out of ideas as it starts sending repeat bosses at you. The fact that all of these fights are followed by the same cutscene of your character passing out then waking up in a bed certainly don’t help, making story progress fall into a predictable cadence.

Like any RPG worth its salt, a lot of the focus here is on the story, complete with cutscenes so lengthy you’ll want to remember to flick the joystick every so often to keep your screen lit up. As an emotionless warrior who also has amnesia (because of course you do), you’ll go around hunting down the aforementioned giant, blighted beasts alongside Koo, so you can stop the end of the world. As is the case with lots of things in Beast of Reincarnation, that idea is much stronger than the execution as Emma and the apocalyptic setting that gives rise to such conflict is poised to deliver a tale filled with interesting mysteries to unravel. Instead, Emma and her companions come with lifeless performances as they tell a story with every single genre trope in the book, including a quiet hero who has been chosen by prophecy, a heavy-handed nature vs. humans/technology theme, a Force-ghost little girl who isn’t actually there, and an amnesiatic character who at one point is stricken with a dose of amnesia so she remembers even less than before.

None of that would be a deal-breaker for me were it not for the fact that the execution of its trope-filled story isn't delivered with the kind of punch that can make up for it. It's on the weaker side with consistently weak dialogue and reveals I saw coming from about 10 miles away. If you’ve played a JRPG in the last twenty years, there’s nothing about this story that hasn’t been done better in numerous other games, and if you’re expecting the quality to be near the level of something like Xenoblade Chronicles, you’re almost certainly going to be disappointed. It’s especially weird just how flat most of the characters are; they rarely show emotion (sometimes with in-universe reasons, not that the justification makes it more interesting to watch). The robotic animations, lifeless eyes, and long silences in between dialogue makes nearly all the scenes between Emma and her found family pretty hard to sit through most of the time. And they do that thing where they show a washed out flashback to something that literally happened less than five minutes ago, which drives me up the wall way more than it probably should.

Its trope-filled story isn't delivered with the kind of punch that can make up for it.

Also, this isn't really a specific pain point, but I feel obligated to mention just how much of the dialogue is taken up by characters talking about food and the eating of it. It'd make sense if it was woven in thematically, but it's not and I’m not sure if the writers were just super hungry when they wrote this or what, but it’s pretty bizarre.

items.title: House of the Dragon Season 3, Episode 7 Recap and Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
There’s a great fundamental issue at the heart of House Targaryen that has too often gone unexamined and underexplained in House of the Dragon, despite its name, and that’s how the dragons work. This show has followed its predecessor’s example in leaning into the human drama of Westeros and away from its more fantastical aspects, but there’s a limit to how well that works, and in this engaging and generally fun episode (unless you’re Emma D’Arcy’s Rhaenyra), they finally get their teeth, and claws, into it.

The question is what, exactly, is the relationship between rider and dragon for House Targaryen and their allies? What are the obligations between rider and beast, if any? How (or how much) do they communicate? Do their feelings affect one another? There have been suggestions, occasionally, that having a dragon may affect one’s temperament (or that one’s temperament may affect one’s chance of bonding with a dragon); there’s a clear implication that losing your dragon is a form of emasculation for Tom Glynn-Carney’s Aegon II and the late Viserys (Paddy Considine). But it’s never been clear if it matters, and how much, beyond prestige in the internal Targaryen pecking order.

This time, however, we get some key hints that there’s more of a link than perhaps we were shown before. The scenes of dragon conflict, as when Rhaenyra finally discovers that her husband Daemon (Matt Smith) has been lying to her to protect his daughter Rhaena (Phoebe Campbell) and flies to confront both along with Addam (Clinton Liberty), suggest an emotional closeness. As the humans shout at one another, their dragons roar and bellow and, occasionally, threaten to flame, and it’s absolutely clear that they’re reflecting something human and vice versa. Later in the episode we see Aegon screaming in sync with his steed Sunfyre, both disfigured and defiant and apparently on the verge of madness, and the impression is confirmed.

The episode also begins with a dream of Helaena (Phia Saban) and in fact heavily features her dreams - or perhaps Dreams, of the prophetic kind. So what does it mean that she sees herself on her dragon, Dreamfyre, shouting “Dracarys!” as an angry mob rushes at them in the Dragonpit? What does it mean that she imagines a quiet life on the farm with her children (it looks like both Jaehaera and a younger boy, presumably the one she’s currently expecting) when an eclipse occurs? Rhaenyra is putting her younger half-sister under pressure to share her Dreams, desperate for reassurance that she is on the right path, but it’s not clear that Helaena has any such comfort to offer.

The question is what, exactly, is the relationship between rider and dragon for House Targaryen and their allies?

Of course, that’s far from the most screwed-up dream this episode. That prize goes to Aemond (Ewan Mitchell), who sees his mother Alicent (Olivia Cooke) arriving at Harrenhal and the two of them tumbling into bed together before realising it was all a dream. And then he wakes up and she has indeed arrived. Awkward! This may not be the dictionary definition of “headfuck” but it should be. Alicent babbles, Aemond is more taciturn, Alys (Gayle Rankin) is rightly suspicious of the newcomer. Aemond shares her wariness to a degree, enough to murder Alicent’s travelling companion (who, to be fair, is there to help assassinate him), but not enough to refuse the poisoned nightcap she offers after the world’s most awkward meet-the-mother-in-law dinner. Alicent creeps out of the castle and into the wind, figuring that the job is done and stricken by it, but Aemond stumbles to Alys at the first stomach pangs so he’ll probably recover.

Meanwhile Rhaenyra is still pulled in every direction and failing to deal with any of her problems, and it creates a vacuum at the seat of her power. Torrhen Manderly (Dan Fogler) is furious that he’s been left to hold the bag for everyone’s money woes – something that is literally his job -- and Mysaria (Sonoya Mizuno) is trying to make herself a conduit to the people and being rejected on all sides. She manages to, ahem, reconnect with Rhaenyra herself by the end of the episode (is that what the kids are calling it these days?), but she’s still caught in-between a regal rock and a common hard place, and that’s a tough situation to be in.

Daemon, too, is looking more woebegone than we have seen him before. He has belatedly realised that his daughter may desperately need him, which by Westeros standards makes him father of the year against almost zero competition, but in trying to protect her he has broken his wife’s heart. And also, he’s almost entirely failed to protect her; he’s just separated her from her dragon and gone home. He’s also increasingly floundering in council, suffering the same myopia as Rhaenyra and failing to look past his personal passions to the big picture.

It’s a mess. The only person laughing – and laughing a lot this time -- is Ormund (James Norton), who’s riding high despite the imminent arrival of the Rivermen outside his hastily built walls and the fact that he’s probably in last place in that aforementioned father of the year competition. He holds Corlys Velaryon (Steve Toussaint) captive, and cuts off his finger as proof of life to attempt to keep the Velaryon men from plugging the policing gap in King’s Landing (an efficient and speedy postal system still appears to be operating between Tumbleton and King’s Landing). He’s also keeping his ward Daeron (Benjamin Evan Ainsworth) and cousin Gwayne (Freddie Fox) in the dark about his plans, to their increasing frustration. And, in the episode’s final big reveal, he’s courting the dragon rider Ulf (Tom Bennett), trying to turn him from Rhaenyra’s service with the promise that he’ll become Lord of (Corlys’) Driftmark fortress, and also that he’ll be free to drink whenever he wants. It’s not clear which is the bigger inducement to the big ol’ lush but it could spell big trouble for Rhaenyra if he turns.

So the tally was six dragons for Rhaenyra (Syrax, Caraxes, Vermithor, Silverwing, Moondancer, Seasmoke) plus one unreliable wannabe ally (Sheepstealer). Then there was one MIA for the Greens (Vhagar) and one out of combat (Dreamfyre). Now there are five for Rhaenyra, two of them perhaps injured; two for the Greens (it looks like Ulf’s Silverwing and the resurgent Sunfyre) and potentially two MIA dragons (Sheepstealer and Vhagar, still) to potentially change that calculus further. It’s all at play going into the Season 3 finale, and it’s still not clear how far these flames could spread.
